en: Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Scroll One.
Composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Having shattered the cataracts of the cognitive obscurations, they exhaust all things in their multiplicity and their suchness;
yet amidst the reflections of the ultimate and conventional truths of all phenomena, deluded attachments compete to give rise to divergent views.
This arises from being forever free from all conceptual constructions;
through the light of stainless, pure wisdom, one attains supreme *sambodhi*.
With the habitual tendencies of afflictive obstructions severed, one abides eternally, acting effortlessly throughout the ten directions according to the inclinations of sentient beings.
He reveals the supreme and most vast means, such as the three doors of liberation;
through non-conceptualization and great compassion, he dwells in neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa.
By embracing sublime wisdom and skillful means, he ultimately achieves the ultimate benefit of both self and others.
Thus is that which the World-Honored One and others have awakened to, and the subtle Dharma they have revealed;
if one can practice this well, one will surely attain the state of tranquil nectar.
Those who slander [the Dharma] will certainly sink to the bottomless depths; for a very long time, they shall be unable to escape the great ocean of suffering.
The monks in training and those beyond training, who dwell in the fruits of the Path, universally surpass all other remaining monks.
The Sugata is a stainless river of merit; those who truly bathe within it become unsurpassed fields of merit for the world.
Even by casting into it a small amount of goodness, it immediately becomes as vast as the earth and space; through this, the wise attain liberation.
Therefore, with utmost sincerity of body, speech, and mind, I repeatedly cultivate the practice of unerring refuge and prostration.
Now that the masters who serve as our guides have diminished, and the true Dharma and correct principles are largely muddied,
it is all due to those of clever intelligence yet false pride, who rely on their own speculative reasoning and lose sight of the scriptural authority and realization.
My teacher, here, was neither before nor after; He encountered and served the Holy One, the Greatly Compassionate Honored One.

Relying upon the immovable supramundane state, He manifested the samādhi of the great light of Dharma, Proclaiming the wondrous Dharma and spreading a pure reputation, Like the sun extending its radiance throughout the ten directions.
The light of its words is stainless and most profound, in accord with all sūtras of definitive meaning.
Its vast phrases and meanings are all subtle and wondrous, entirely adorning itself with exquisite ornamentation.
It can cause those who are intelligent to melt their hearts; free from flattery and pride, they give rise to love and reverence.
With wisdom that penetrates the most difficult teachings without obstruction, He does not dwell amidst gain, offerings, or praise;
His mind is ever free from attachment to pleasure, And thus he is named "One of Certain Virtue."
The noble sages always draw near to him; there is no one in all the world who does not know him.
His fame is renowned everywhere without attachment, and his manifest merits are praised by all alike.
The rain of the nectar of the subtle Dharma—its words and meanings—showered by those such as the Inexhaustible Eloquence;
though I have heard much from them, my own power is slight, and what I have received is but little, like a bird seeking rain.
From a small portion of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, I have provided this brief verbal explanation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
May this work bring universal benefit to those who are intimidated by the vast ocean of words.
The treatise states:

In the *Abhidharma Mahāyāna Sūtra*, prior to the Bhagavān, for the sake of revealing the greatness of the essence of the Mahāyāna, it was spoken by a bodhisattva who had already attained skillful entry into the Mahāyāna.
This refers to the tenfold excellence of the sublime speech of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, based upon the Mahāyāna.
The commentary asks:
"Based upon what meaning?"
On what basis is this statement made?
Regarding the vast and profound nature of reality (*dharmatā*) that is to be known, who—apart from the majestic power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—could compose an explanatory treatise upon it?
Furthermore, for what reason are these matters stated at the beginning of this treatise?

It is for the purpose of ensuring that, were it not for the citation of the words from the *Abhidharma-mahāyāna-sūtra*, one would not understand that this treatise is the word of the Buddha (*āptāgama*). For this reason, [the citation is made].
Furthermore, it is to manifest the title of the sūtra—just as one says "the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*"—that the phrase "thus [in] the Abhidharma Mahāyāna Sūtra" is spoken.
Moreover, there is another meaning: in order to manifest that this sūtra is the sacred teaching (*āgama*), the phrase "thus [in] the Abhidharma Mahāyāna Sūtra" is stated at the outset.
The purpose for composing this treatise now is to enlighten those who are ignorant.

The term *abhidharma* is cited to reveal its specific name; the word "sūtra" is cited to reveal its general name; and the "Mahāyāna" is further cited to distinguish it from the *abhidharma* of the Śrāvakas.

For there are also non-noble Abhidharmas spoken today; for instance, there are those who, through their own analytical wisdom, claim that a certain work is the Buddha’s teaching on Abhidharma, or the teaching of a Śrāvaka, or the creation of a worldly sage.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "Mahāyāna sūtras," this is intended to distinguish them from those of the śrāvakas and others, and because they are intended to demonstrate that they are included within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, the Abhidharma is also cited.
Furthermore, regarding inclusion within the Pitakas: it refers to entering the Sūtra Piṭaka of one's own school to manifest the cessation of one's own afflictions.
As for the Vinaya Piṭaka, this refers to the afflictions of Bodhisattvas within the Mahāyāna, because the various conceptual discriminations of Bodhisattvas constitute their afflictions.
It does not contradict the most excellent Abhidharma, for its characteristics are vastness and profundity.
Within this context, the Three Piṭakas are: first, the Sūtra Piṭaka; second, the Vinaya Piṭaka; and third, the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
Since these three collections (tripiṭaka) are distinguished as the Lesser Vehicle and the Greater Vehicle, they constitute two collections:
first, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka; second, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
For what reason are these three and these two called "collections" (piṭaka)?
Because they are capable of encompassing [all teachings], that is to say, they encompass all objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
Furthermore, for what reasons are the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*) established?

They are established by way of nine reasons: namely, the Sūtra Piṭaka is established as an antidote to doubt; for if there is doubt regarding various meanings, it is for the sake of definitively proclaiming those respective meanings.

The Vinaya Piṭaka is established as an antidote to the enjoyment of the two extremes: that is, to prevent attachment to the extreme of sensual pleasure by prohibiting what is blameworthy, and to permit the enjoyment of the extreme of not afflicting oneself by allowing what is blameless.
The Abhidharma Piṭaka is established as an antidote to the dogmatic adherence to one's own views, for it illuminates the unerring characteristics of all phenomena.
Furthermore, the Sūtra Piṭaka is established because it can expound the three trainings;

the Vinaya Piṭaka is established because it accomplishes higher ethics and higher mind—meaning that one who possesses ethical discipline (*śīla*) is free from remorse and so forth, and can gradually attain meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
and the Abhidharma Piṭaka is established because it accomplishes higher wisdom—meaning it can definitively discern the non-erroneous meaning.
Furthermore, the Sūtra Piṭaka is established because it can expound the meaning of the Dharma;

the Vinaya Piṭaka is established because it can bring the meaning of the Dharma to fulfillment—meaning that those who diligently practice for the sake of subduing the afflictions are able to penetrate both of these [Sūtra and Vinaya];
and the Abhidharma Piṭaka is established because it possesses skill in the discernment of the meaning of the Dharma.
Based on these nine conditions, the establishment of the Three Piṭakas is permitted.
Furthermore, all of these are for the purpose of liberation from birth and death.
How, then, can they bring about such liberation?
Through perfuming, awakening, tranquility, and penetration, one attains liberation.

That is to say, by means of the mind being perfumed by hearing, by means of awakening through reflection, by means of tranquility through the cultivation of *śamatha*, and by means of penetration through the realization of *vipaśyanā*, one is able to attain liberation.

Furthermore, to speak briefly, each of these collections—the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma—possesses four meanings; if a bodhisattva fully understands them, they will be able to realize the nature of omniscience.
Even a śrāvaka, by understanding the meaning of just a single verse from them, attains the exhaustion of outflows.
How do these three each possess four meanings?
That is to say, they are called *sūtra* because they are able to penetrate [the truth] by way of basis (*āśraya*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), dharma (*dharma*), and meaning (*artha*).
In this context, "basis" refers to that which is spoken of, the means by which it is spoken, and the purpose for which it is spoken.
"Characteristics" refers to the characteristics of conventional truth and the characteristics of ultimate truth.

"Dharma" refers to the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), truths (satya), nutriments (āhāra), meditative absorptions (dhyāna), immeasurables (apramāṇa), formless attainments (ārūpya), liberations (vimokṣa), bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), bases of totality (kṛtsnāyatana), factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa), analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), the absence of contention (araṇa), and so forth.
Regarding the meaning: it follows the intentional terminology (*saṃdhāya*).

Because it is "confrontational" (*abhi*), because it is "numerical" (*prati*), because it is "subduing" (*vi*), and because it is "pervasive" (*dharma*), one should know that it is called *Abhidharma*.

That is to say, *Abhidharma* is also named *Pratidharma*; this *dharma* is directed toward non-abiding *nirvāṇa*, as it is able to explain the [Four] Truths, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), the gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), and so forth.

Abhidharma is also called "the enumeration of dharmas" (*dharmasaṃkhyāna*), because it repeatedly explains and defines each individual dharma through an infinite variety of distinctions, such as their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Abhidharma is also called "the subduing dharma" (*abhibhava-dharma*), because it is fully equipped with the bases of discourse (*sthāna*) and other such factors, enabling it to overcome and subdue the arguments of others.
Abhidharma is also called "the penetrating dharma" (*abhivinaya-dharma*), because it is able to penetrate and explain the meaning of the Sūtras.
It should be known as *vinaya* (the discipline) by virtue of transgression, origination, purification, and renunciation.
Herein, "transgression" refers to the five classes of offenses.
Regarding the origination [of offenses]: it refers to committing various transgressions due to ignorance, negligence, the intensity of afflictions, or a lack of respect.
Regarding purification: it refers to restoration through one's internal intention (*āśaya*) rather than through punitive measures, as when one undertakes a formal vow (*saṃvara*).
Regarding renunciation (*naiṣkramya*), there are seven kinds:
first, confessing each respective transgression before its counterpart;
second, vowing to undergo disciplinary punishment, such as being granted the *śikṣādattaka* status.
Third, there is that which is subject to obstruction: a training rule (*śikṣāpada*) is first established, but later, through a different circumstance, it is again permitted;
fourth, there is that which is specifically suspended: when the Saṃgha is in harmony, they collectively relinquish what was established;
fifth, there is the change of basis: because a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī undergoes a change of gender, they relinquish the offenses unique to their respective classes.
Sixth, by means of contemplation of reality, which refers to the contemplation of the various characteristics of the summary verses (*udāna*) on the sublime dharmas;

seventh, by means of obtaining through the nature of things (*dharmatā*), which refers to obtaining freedom from even the most minor of minor offenses by virtue of seeing the truth of the nature of things.
It should be understood that the Vinaya further possesses four meanings:
first, in terms of the *pudgala* (individual),
for whom the Blessed One established the rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).
Second, because of its formal establishment;
that is to say, once a particular individual has committed an offense, the Great Teacher assembles the Saṃgha and establishes the training rule (śikṣāpada).
Third, because of its detailed analysis; that is to say, after the training rule has been established, there is a further extensive explanation of what was previously stated in brief.
Fourth, because of the definitive determination (*viniścaya*); that is to say, herein one definitively judges what has been transgressed, determining what constitutes an offense and what does not.
Now, the main text shall be explained.
The term "Bhagavat" indicates that there is someone to be revered; therefore, no other word is used.

"One who has well entered the Mahāyāna" refers to the meaning of having already attained supreme qualities such as *dhāraṇī*; because it manifests that these various qualities have been attained, one is able to correctly uphold and correctly reveal both the meaning and the text—it is for this reason that one is called a Bodhisattva.
For what purpose is it taught?
It is taught in order to reveal the greatness of the essence of the Mahāyāna.
As for "revealing," it means to open up and manifest the truly existent great essence of the Mahāyāna.
"Relying on the Mahāyāna" means that what is spoken arises based upon the Mahāyāna.

Regarding "the speech that is preeminent through ten aspects of excellence," this refers to the speech that is made preeminent by those very ten kinds of excellence; thus it is called "the speech that is preeminent through ten aspects of excellence."
The term "excellent" (*viśiṣṭa*) has the sense of differentiation; it is relative, as when one says that this meaning is more excellent than that.
Furthermore, the sense of being "supreme" (*parama*) is also the sense of being "excellent."
Alternatively, it refers to a different category, namely the meaning; because the cause is preeminent, the fruit of speech is likewise preeminent.
We shall now explain these ten distinct characteristics.
The treatise says:

First, the discourse on the excellence of the basis of the knowable; second, the discourse on the excellence of the characteristics of the knowable; third, the discourse on the excellence of entering the characteristics of the knowable; fourth, the discourse on the excellence of the cause and fruit of that entry; fifth, the discourse on the excellence of the distinctions in the cultivation of those causes and fruits; sixth, the discourse on the excellence of the superior morality within such distinctions in cultivation; seventh, the discourse on the excellence of the superior mind within this [superior morality]; eighth, the discourse on the excellence of the superior wisdom within this [superior mind]; ninth, the discourse on the excellence of the abandonment which is its fruit; tenth, the discourse on the excellence of the gnosis which is its fruit.
By these various phrases from the sūtras spoken by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, it is demonstrated that the Mahāyāna is truly the word of the Buddha.
The commentary states:

Regarding the phrase "the basis of what is to be known" (*jñeya-āśraya*) as being "superlative and superlatively expressed": it is called "what is to be known" (*jñeya*) because it is that which ought to be known; namely, the phenomena of affliction and purification, which are the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

"Dependent upon" (*āśrita*) has the meaning of "cause. This basis of the knowable is itself preeminent; therefore, it is called the "preeminence of the basis of the knowable. Because of this preeminence, the discourse is preeminent.

This basis is precisely the ālayavijñāna; thus, it is a *karmadhāraya* (attributive) compound. This applies even up to the "excellence of the resultant wisdom," meaning that the resultant wisdom itself is the excellence, and is therefore termed the "excellence of the resultant wisdom," and so forth.
The "characteristics of the knowable" (jñeyalakṣaṇa) refers to the meaning of the intrinsic nature of that which is known.
Since the knowable itself is the characteristic, it is called the "characteristics of the knowable," namely the three natures (trisvabhāva).

"Entering the characteristics of the knowable" refers to the ability to enter or the actual entering into those characteristics of the knowable, which is the very nature of representation-only (vijñaptimātratā).
Regarding "entering its cause and fruit": it is called "entering that" because one is able to enter it; this refers to the realization of the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*).
"Cause" refers to the mundane perfections (*pāramitā*), such as generosity and so forth, at the time of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
The "fruit" refers to the supramundane perfections (pāramitās), such as generosity, at the time of thorough penetration.

Regarding the distinction in the cultivation of those causes and fruits: they are called "those causes and fruits" because they are precisely those [causes and fruits]; it refers to the specific distinctions in the cultivation thereof within this very context.

"Cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) refers to repeated practice; this very repeated practice becomes increasingly superior throughout the various stages (*bhūmi*), and is therefore called "distinction," which refers to the ten stages.

Within such distinctions of cultivation, "higher training in ethical discipline" (*adhiśīla*) means learning by relying upon ethical discipline within the ten stages; thus it is called higher training in ethical discipline. This refers to all the vows (*saṃvara*) of the bodhisattvas, wherein they no longer entertain the intention to commit unwholesome acts.
Higher mind (*adhicitta*) refers to training either within the internal mind or by relying upon the mind; thus it is called higher mind, which consists of the various *samādhis*.

Higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) refers to the wisdom that proceeds toward realization, and is thus called higher wisdom; alternatively, it is so named because one trains by relying on wisdom, which is none other than non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

Regarding the excellence of abandonment (*prahāṇa-viśeṣa*): this refers to the most supreme distinction, wherein one internally relinquishes both the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which is precisely non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*).
Regarding the excellence of wisdom (*jñāna-viśeṇa*) and the excellence of speech: unobstructed wisdom is called the excellence of wisdom;

while that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) has something to be countered, this Buddha-wisdom is now free from all obstructions and their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). This is what is meant by the excellence of Buddha-wisdom over that non-conceptual wisdom.
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, how is it manifested?

Because these ten points, as here explained, have never been seen taught in the Śrāvaka vehicle, but are seen taught in various places within the Mahāyāna—namely, the *ālayavijñāna*, which is designated as the essence of the "basis of the knowable" (*jñeyāśraya*).

The three natures—first, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); second, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); and third, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)—are designated as the essence of the characteristics of the knowable.
The nature of consciousness-only is called the essence of entering the characteristics of the knowable.
The six pāramitās are called the essence of the cause and fruit of that entry.
The ten stages of the bodhisattva are called the essence of the distinctions in the cultivation of that cause and fruit.
The bodhisattva vows are designated here as the essence of higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*).
The various samādhis, such as Śūraṅgama and Gaganagañja, are designated here as the essence of higher mind (*adhicitta*).
Non-conceptual wisdom is designated as the essence of superior insight therein.
Non-abiding nirvana is designated as the essence of its fruit, which is abandonment.

The three bodies of the Buddha—the first being the svābhāvika-kāya (essential body), the second the sambhogika-kāya (enjoyment body), and the third the nairmāṇika-kāya (emanation body)—are designated as the essence of its fruit, which is wisdom.

By means of these ten points thus explained, it is shown that the Mahāyāna differs from the Śrāvaka-yāna, and furthermore, it is shown that the most excellent Blessed One taught them solely for the sake of bodhisattvas; therefore, one should know that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten modes of speech that are preeminent and most preeminent, based exclusively upon the Mahāyāna.
The commentary says:
"How can it be made manifest? asks by what reason [this is so].

Regarding the statement that the six *pāramitās* are called the essence of the cause and fruit of entry into that [reality]: this means that when one enters the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) by means of the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), the worldly *pāramitās* such as generosity and the rest are termed "purifying causes," because they are capable of inducing the supramundane.
Once one has entered the stages (*bhūmi*), those very perfections (*pāramitā*) such as generosity become supramundane; this is termed the "result of purification.

Regarding the statement that the ten bodhisattva stages are called the "distinctive nature of the cultivation of their cause and result": this means that the ten bodhisattva stages constitute the distinct nature of the cultivation within the two positions of cause and result of the aforementioned perfections.

Regarding the statement that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is designated here as the essence of superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā*): if śrāvakas are free from the conceptualization of the four inversions, it is called "non-conceptual";
if bodhisattvas are free from the conceptualization of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), it is called "non-conceptual. Such is the distinction between these two types of non-conceptuality.
Regarding the statement that "non-abiding nirvana is called the essence of the abandonment of those fruits": this refers to the fruits of the three trainings, and is thus termed "those fruits.
These fruits are themselves abandonment; hence, it is called "the abandonment of those fruits."
This nature is called the essence of the abandonment of those fruits; that is to say, it is the meaning of the abandonment of the two obstacles: the afflictive and the cognitive.

Regarding the statement that the three bodies of the Buddha are called the essence of the wisdom of those fruits: they are called "those fruits" because they are the fruits of the three trainings; that fruit is itself wisdom, hence "wisdom of those fruits," and this nature is called the essence of the wisdom of those fruits.
In this context, if the svabhāvakāya did not exist, the dharmakāya would not exist, just as, for example, the visual faculty [does not exist without its basis];
and if the dharmakāya did not exist, the saṃbhogakāya would not exist, just as, for example, visual consciousness [does not exist without its basis].
It should be understood that here the basis and the based serve as the example by way of shared properties (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
If the enjoyment body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) did not exist, the assembly of bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages (*mahā-bhūmi*) would lack the enjoyment of the Dharma-joy;
if there were no enjoyment of the Dharma-joy, the provisions for awakening (*bodhi-sambhāra*) would not reach fulfillment.
For example, it is like seeing forms.

If there were no transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), then bodhisattvas on the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*) and śrāvakas of inferior resolve would have no initial point of departure for their practice; therefore, it is certain that there must be three bodies.
To demonstrate how the Mahāyāna differs from the Śrāvaka-yāna: this is because it is not taught in the Śrāvaka-yāna.
Furthermore, to demonstrate its supremacy: it is shown that within the Mahāyāna, this is likewise supreme.
The Commentary says:

Furthermore, how is it that by means of these ten marks of excellence, the speech of the Tathāgata is shown to be truly the word of the Buddha regarding the Mahāyāna, while the Śrāvaka vehicle is excluded from being of the nature of the Mahāyāna?
These ten points have never been taught within the Śrāvaka vehicle, but are found taught everywhere in the Mahāyāna.

That is to say, these ten points are most capable of inducing the nature of great enlightenment; they are well-established, consistent and non-contradictory, and serve as the means for realizing the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
Within this, there are two verses:
The basis of the knowable and the characteristics of the knowable, Its entry, its cause and fruit, and its diverse cultivation,
The three trainings, their fruits, abandonment, and wisdom— Subsumed within the Supreme Vehicle, these are its excellences.
This teaches what is seen here and what is not seen elsewhere;
because it is the most excellent cause for supreme enlightenment, the Mahāyāna is accepted as the true word of the Buddha, being superior due to its teaching of the ten topics.
The commentary says: What does this mean?
It means that these ten points thus explained are most capable of inducing the nature of great enlightenment; they are well-established, conformable, and non-contradictory.
"That which is most capable of inducing the nature of great enlightenment" means that it is the cause capable of inducing great enlightenment.
"That which is well-established" refers to its being analyzed through valid means of cognition such as correct reasoning, just as one perceives the characteristics of the path shown by a guide.
"Conformity" means that when one diligently practices in order to realize [the goal], one dwells in conformity with it, just as one dwells in conformity with the right path taught by a guide.
"Non-contradiction" refers to the absence of obstructive causes within the various stages (*bhūmi*), just as there are no obstacles such as bandits along the path shown by a guide.
Alternatively, the two states of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are mutually non-contradictory.

Furthermore, there is another perspective: that which is most capable of inducing the nature of great enlightenment (mahābodhi) is this very capacity to induce non-conceptual wisdom free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca-jñāna).
"Being well-established" means that it is not in contradiction with the four principles.
"Conformable" means that it is not in contradiction with the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
"Non-contradictory" means that what was previously conformable does not later become contradictory.
As a verse says:
"Initially upholding love and compassion, yet subsequently following what is unwholesome—
this view of self, being neither black nor white, is both beneficial and harmful."
"Being able to realize all-knowledge" means that within all phenomena, one gives rise to the supreme, uninterrupted knowledge of all aspects of conduct (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Regarding "well-established" and so forth, there is another meaning: it refers to being well-established in accordance with [the truth], without contradiction, and providing successive definitions and explanations.
How is it well-established?
It is because it is able to accord with [reality].
How is it able to accord with [reality]?
This means that there is no contradiction in their sequence.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, why are these ten bases explained in such an order?
This means that bodhisattvas must first become thoroughly proficient in the causes of all phenomena before they should attain skillfulness regarding dependent origination.

Subsequently, they should become skilled in the characteristics of the phenomena produced by conditions, so as to be able effectively to avoid the faults of the two extremes of superimposition and denial.
Thereafter, a bodhisattva who has thus cultivated well should correctly penetrate the well-grasped signs, causing the mind to be liberated from all hindrances.

Subsequently, having penetrated the signs of the knowable, the six pāramitās of the prior stage of application (prayoga-avasthā) should be further perfected through realization, because the superior intention (adhyāśaya) has attained purity.

Subsequently, one should diligently cultivate the six pāramitās, which are embraced by the pure intention (*śuddhāśaya*), with their specific distinctions throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*); that is to say, this must be accomplished over the course of three incalculable great eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
Thereafter, one should bring to perfection the trainings of the three bodhisattvas.
Once these are perfected, one should manifest the realization of their fruits: nirvāṇa and unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Therefore, the ten bases are taught in this specific order.
The commentary asks:

"What is meant by teaching them in such an order? It means that Bodhisattvas must first become thoroughly proficient in the causes of all phenomena, and so on, up to the point where they should manifest and realize their results—namely, *nirvāṇa* and unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Answer: One must first thoroughly understand the causes of all phenomena before subsequently attaining skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Because there must be a cause for a result to arise—and it does not arise from an *Īśvara* or other such [unconditioned] agents—one thereby attains the two types of knowledge concerning cause and effect.
Next, one should understand the characteristics of all phenomena produced from causes.
What are these characteristics?
To falsely perceive as existent that which is actually non-existent—the thoroughly imagined nature—is called "superimposition."
Since there is no increase, one realizes that the truly existent perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is not subject to diminution.
Because one is thus free from the faults of these two extremes, it is called "skillfulness.
Next, regarding these various signs of the grasped object, one should correctly penetrate their nature as mere consciousness (vijñapti-mātratā) and attain non-obstruction.

Next, regarding the entry into the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) in accordance with reality, those six mundane perfections (*pāramitā*) realized at the conventional level should be further realized from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This is what should be practiced; it is the meaning subsumed by the pure superior intention (*adhyāśaya*).

Next, one should diligently cultivate the specific distinctions of each stage of the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*), which requires passing through three incalculable great eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*). This is not like the Śrāvakas, who, through diligent cultivation of remedies for at most three births, quickly realize liberation.
Subsequently, within such cultivation, one should bring the three trainings of a bodhisattva—beginning with higher ethical discipline—to perfection.

Finally, regarding the fruit of those trainings, which is nirvāṇa, one should realize the eternal severance of afflictions, as well as unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and the manifestation of the three bodies of a Buddha; it is for these reasons that the ten topics are taught in this sequential order.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, within this teaching, all Mahāyāna systems attain their ultimate consummation.
The Commentary explains:
All Mahāyāna teachings reach their ultimate conclusion at this point.
Why is this? If one wishes to explain dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), it is subsumed within the entry into the ālayavijñāna.
If one wishes to explain the various characteristics, they are subsumed within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
If one wishes to explain realization, they are subsumed within the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*).
If one wishes to explain the perfections (*pāramitā*), they are subsumed within the perfections.
If one wishes to speak of the stages (*bhūmi*), they are subsumed within the inclusion of the stages.
If one wishes to speak of the trainings (*śikṣā*), they are subsumed within the inclusion of the trainings.
If one wishes to speak of abandonment and knowledge, they are subsumed within non-abiding *nirvāṇa* and the three bodies of the Buddha (*trikāya*).
This is designated as the word of all Buddhas; therefore, it is taught solely in this sequential order. 2.
The Section on the Basis of the Knowable (*Jñeyāśraya-vibhāga*). Commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, Part Two, Section One: The Basis of the Knowable. The treatise states:
Herein, first of all, the basis of the knowable is explained, which is the ālayavijñāna.
In what place did the Blessed One speak of the *ālayavijñāna* by the name of *ālayavijñāna*?
It is said that the Bhagavat spoke in a verse of the *Abhidharmamahāyānasūtra*:
"The element (*dhātu*) from beginningless time, The common support for all phenomena,"
"From this arise the various realms of existence, as well as the realization of nirvāṇa.
The commentary states:
Among these, that which realizes [the truth] is the ālayavijñāna; its essence is definitively the ālayavijñāna.
Regarding the *Āgama*, it refers to the verse spoken by the Bhagavat in the *Abhidharma-mahāyāna-sūtra* at its very beginning:
"The *dhātu* means cause; it is that upon which all phenomena depend."

Since it is observed in the world that terms such as "element" (*dhātu*) are applied to gold ore and the like, and because this is the reason [for the term], it is the cause upon which all phenomena depend;
its essence is precisely the meaning of being that which is depended upon.
"Existence by virtue of this" means existence as the basis for all phenomena and so forth.
"The various destinies" refers to all the destinies within saṃsāra.
"Destiny" refers to the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala).

Due to this fruit, one may be of a nature that is dull-witted, foolish, or mute; or one may possess the power to understand the meaning of well-spoken and ill-spoken teachings; or one may be able to realize and attain the supreme realization.
Furthermore, it serves as the basis for the afflictions; because of this, there arise intense afflictions and long-lasting afflictions.
Since it is the basis for these four kinds of distinctions in maturation (*vipāka*), it lacks functional capacity (*karmanya*).
One should know that the opposite of this is termed "possessing capability.

It is not only because of this that the various realms of existence come to be; it is also because of this that one realizes nirvāṇa, for it is precisely by means of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) that one attains nirvāṇa.
The treatise says:
Within this very context, a verse is further spoken:
"Because it stores and conceals all phenomena, it is the consciousness of all seeds."
"Therefore it is named Ālaya; this I have revealed to the Victorious Ones. Commentary:

Having already cited the Āgama to prove that the ālayavijñāna is the substance of the support for all that is known (*jñeya-āśraya*), he further cites the Āgama to prove that the ālayavijñāna is named *ālayavijñāna*.
In this verse, the second line explains the first.
"Victors" refers to the assembly of bodhisattvas.
The Commentary states:
Thus, having first cited scriptural authority from the Āgamas, for what reason is this consciousness called the *ālayavijñāna*?
Because all dharmas belonging to the category of defilement (*saṃkleśa*) that arise through birth are stored within it as their fruit-nature;
and because this very consciousness is, in turn, stored within them as their cause-nature, it is therefore called the *ālayavijñāna*.
Because sentient beings grasp and conceal this consciousness as a self, it is therefore called the *ālayavijñāna*.
The commentary states:
This now explains the etymological derivation of the name *ālaya* for this consciousness.
"All that has birth" refers to all categories of sentient beings who possess birth.
"Defiled phenomena" (saṃkleśa-dharma) are so called because they function as an obstruction to the meaning of purification; thus, they are termed "concealment" (saṃvṛti).
Alternatively, for those sentient beings who grasp and conceal this consciousness as a self, it has the sense of "clinging.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, this consciousness is also called the *ādāna-vijñāna* (appropriating consciousness).
Regarding the Āgama herein, as stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*:
"The ādāna-vijñāna is profound and subtle; Containing all seeds like a torrential stream, I do not reveal it to the foolish and ignorant, Fearing they would conceptually grasp it as a self."
The commentary states:
Furthermore, it cites the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.
Within this very Āgama, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vighuṣṭamati, saying:

O Wisdom of Extensive Intelligence, you should know that within the cycle of birth and death across the six realms of existence, various sentient beings fall into their respective classes of beings, where their physical bodies arise—whether by birth from an egg, birth from a womb, birth from moisture, or birth by transformation.
Within this, first of all, the mind-consciousness containing all seeds matures, evolving through successive integration, increasing and expanding, based upon two types of appropriation (*upādāna*):

first, the appropriation of the material sense-faculties and their bases; second, the appropriation of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of signs, names, conceptual discrimination, and the proliferation of verbal discourse.
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), this consciousness possesses both types of appropriation; in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it does not possess both.
O Vipaśyin! This consciousness is also called the *ādānavijñāna*.
Why is this? Because this consciousness follows and sustains the body;
it is also called the ālayavijñāna.
Why is this? Because this consciousness, in relation to the body, performs the functions of grasping, concealing, and sharing a common fate;
for these reasons, it is also called "mind" (*citta*).
Why is this? Because by means of this consciousness, form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and so forth are accumulated and nourished.
O Broad Wisdom!
Based upon and established by the *ādānavijñāna*, the sixfold group of consciousnesses arises—namely, eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness.
Within this process, with the eye and visible forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises;
and simultaneously with that eye-consciousness, there arises a conceptualizing mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that functions concurrently, sharing the same time and the same object.

There is consciousness; conditioned by the ear, nose, tongue, body, as well as sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, there arise the ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousnesses, along with which a conceptual mental consciousness arises simultaneously, at the same time, and with the same object, following in their wake.
Vipula-mati!
If at that time a single visual consciousness arises, then at that very moment there is only one conceptual mental consciousness that arises with the same objective range as the visual consciousness.

If at that time two, three, four, or five groups of consciousness arise, then at that very moment there is only a single conceptual mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that arises with the same objective range as those five groups of consciousness.
Vipula-mati!
It is like a great torrent of water: if the conditions for the arising of a single wave appear, only one wave arises;
if the conditions for the arising of two or many waves appear, many waves arise.
Yet this torrential stream flows perpetually from its own kind, without interruption or exhaustion.
Furthermore, it is like the surface of a perfectly pure mirror: if the conditions for a single reflection to arise are present, only that one reflection appears.
If the conditions for the arising of two or many reflections are present, then many reflections appear.
It is not that this mirror surface undergoes transformation into the reflections, nor is there any depletion or exhaustion of its capacity to be experienced.
Thus it is, Broad Wisdom!

Because the appropriating consciousness (*ādānavijñāna*), which resembles a torrential stream, serves as the basis and support, whenever at that time the conditions for the arising of a single visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) appear, at that very moment a single visual consciousness proceeds.
If, at that time, the conditions for the arising of even the five groups of consciousness (pañca-vijñāna-kāya) are present, then at that very moment the five groups of consciousness function.
O Vipaśyin!

In this way, although a bodhisattva relies upon and is established by means of the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthititā-jñāna), they become skillful regarding the secrets of mind, mentation, and consciousness (citta-manovijñāna).
However, the Tathāgatas do not designate all such [bodhisattvas] as being "skillful in all the secrets of mind, mentation, and consciousness" based on this alone.

O Viśālamati! If bodhisattvas, within themselves individually, do not perceive the ādāna as it truly is, nor perceive the ādāna-vijñāna; do not perceive the ālaya, nor perceive the ālaya-vijñāna; do not perceive the accumulation, nor perceive the mind (citta); and do not perceive the eye and forms and eye-consciousness; do not perceive the ear and sounds and ear-consciousness; do not perceive the nose and odors and nose-consciousness; do not perceive the tongue and tastes and tongue-consciousness; do not perceive the body and tangibles and body-consciousness; and do not perceive the mind, mental objects, and mind-consciousness—these are called bodhisattvas who are skillful in the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
The Tathāgata designates him as a bodhisattva skilled in the ultimate meaning.
O Viśālamati!

To this extent one is called a bodhisattva skilled in all the secrets of mind, mentation, and consciousness; it is to this extent that the Tathāgata designates him as a bodhisattva skilled in all the secrets of mind, mentation, and consciousness.
This verse reiterates that meaning.
"Ādānavijñāna" is an alternative name for what has been explained.
It is "profound and subtle" because it is difficult to comprehend.
"All seeds are like a torrent" means they evolve in succession; that is, all seeds evolve in a continuous stream from moment to moment, just like the flow of a torrential river.
Fearing that those who conceptually grasp [this] as a self might find such grasping possible because it functions through a single mode of appearance,
the treatise asks:
"For what reason is this consciousness also called the *ādāna-vijñāna* (appropriating consciousness)?"
Because it appropriates all material sense-faculties and serves as the basis for grasping all personal existences. Why is this so?
Because the material sense-faculties, being appropriated by this [appropriating consciousness], remain without decay and persist throughout the duration of life.
Furthermore, at the moment of the actual linking of rebirth within the continuum, because it grasps that birth, it appropriates the physical body;
for this reason, this consciousness is also called the *ādāna-vijñāna* (appropriating consciousness).
The commentary states:
Regarding the phrase "because it appropriates all material sense faculties," why is this so?
It is explained that the material sense faculties are appropriated by this [appropriation] and persist throughout one's life. This serves as the explanation.
This means that because the physical sense faculties, such as the eye, are sustained by the ālayavijñāna, they do not undergo states such as bluish discoloration like a dead body.
When death occurs, this [ālayavijñāna] abandons them, and consequently, those states of bluish discoloration and so forth arise.
Therefore, it is certain that because this [appropriation] exists, the life-limit is not lost or destroyed.

Regarding the phrase "because it is the basis for the grasping of all personal existences," this is explained as follows: at the moment of the actual linking of rebirth within the continuum, one grasps that birth and thereby appropriates the personal existence. This serves as the interpretation.

This means that because this consciousness is a continuous consciousness, at the time of the actual linking of rebirth within the continuum, it is able to appropriate the self-body for the duration of one lifetime; furthermore, it is itself appropriated by this [ālayavijñāna], because the habitual impression (*vāsanā*) of the self-body for one lifetime resides within the ālayavijñāna.
Because its substance arises, it is called "its arising.
Because one experiences that arising, it is called "grasping at its arising.
By means of this grasping, it appropriates the personal existence; for this reason, the *ālayavijñāna* is also called the *ādānavijñāna*.
The Treatise says:
This is also called "mind" (*citta*), as the Blessed One has taught:
"Mind, mentation (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—these three."
In this context, there are two meanings:
first, it serves as the basis for the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*); that is, consciousness which has just ceased can serve as the generative basis for mental consciousness.
Second, the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) is always associated with four afflictions:

first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); second, the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*); third, self-love (*ātmasneha*); and fourth, ignorance (*avidyā*). This is the basis for the defilement of consciousness.
Furthermore, consciousness arises from that first basis; it is the second [basis], which is defiled, because its meaning is the discernment of objects.
Because of the meaning of "immediately antecedent" and the meaning of "cognition," the mind (*manas*) is established as two kinds.
The commentary states:
That which is also called "mind" (citta) is the very essence of the ālayavijñāna.

While the two meanings of "intellect" (manas) and "consciousness" (vijñāna) can be distinguished as having distinct characteristics, one should know that the meaning of "mind" likewise possesses distinctions; this is shown for the sake of clarifying this point.

In this context, its nature as a cause functioning as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) refers to the consciousness that has just ceased acting as the cause for mental consciousness; this is the first meaning of "mind" (*manas*).
Its being constantly defiled by the four afflictions is the second meaning.
In this context, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) refers to the grasping at a nature of self;
by the power of this, pride of self (*asmimāna*) arises.
Relying on "I" and "mine," one exalts oneself; the craving for a self that arises toward what is actually selfless is called self-love (*ātmasneha*).
Thus, these three types take ignorance as their cause.
What is called "ignorance" is precisely the absence of wisdom and cognition.

Furthermore, regarding how the second defilement arises from that first basis: the consciousness that has just ceased is termed "mind" (*manas*); because it provides a locus for the reception of the consciousness about to arise, it serves as its generative basis.

The second is the afflicted manas (*kliṣṭamanas*), which serves as the basis for defilement because it clings to a self even within virtuous states of mind, because its function is the discernment of objects, and because its function is reflection (*manana*).

Thus, the manas is twofold: that which is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) in the sense of apprehending objects; that which is called the "first manas" in the sense of being the locus [of the preceding moment]; and that which is called the "second manas" in the sense of constituting defilement through the clinging to a self and so forth.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, how is it known that there is a defiled mind (*kliṣṭamanas*)?
It is because if this did not exist, non-associated ignorance (*āveṇikāvidyā*) could not exist, which would result in a logical fallacy.
Furthermore, the five [mental consciousnesses] having the same nature [as the sensory consciousnesses] is also impossible, as it would entail logical fallacies. Why is this?
Because the five groups of consciousness must necessarily have simultaneous supports (sahabhū-āśraya), such as the eyes and so forth.
Furthermore, the etymological definitions [of these states] would also be untenable, as this would result in logical fallacies.
Moreover, there would be no distinction between the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) and the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), which likewise results in a logical fallacy.
This means that the state of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) is manifested by the afflicted mind (kliṣṭa-manas), whereas the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) is not;
for if it were otherwise, there would be no distinction between these two attainments.

Furthermore, within a single lifetime in the Heaven of No-Perception (asaṃjñi-sattva), there would have to be no defilement, which would result in the fallacy that neither self-grasping (ātma-grāha) nor the conceit of "I" (asmimāna) exists therein.
Furthermore, because the activity of the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) is observable at all times— namely, within minds that are wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral— if this were not the case,
then the afflictions of "I" and "mine" would manifest only in association with unwholesome minds, and not in wholesome or neutral ones.
Therefore, if one posits that it is a simultaneous manifestation rather than an associated manifestation, this fault does not arise.
Here, the verse says:
"If it were non-common ignorance, And shared the same characteristics as the five [aggregates],"
Regarding the two determinations of the exegesis, if [the self] were non-existent, both would result in fallacies.
There would be no birth in the Realm of Non-conception, and the persistence of the grasping at a self would become a fallacy;
for the grasping at a self would constantly follow [the person], yet it would be entirely absent [if the self were non-existent].
If the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) did not exist, two or three [mental factors] would be contradictory;
since it does not exist anywhere, the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*) should not occur.
It constantly acts as an obstacle to the arising of the mind directed toward the true meaning (*tattvārtha*).
It accompanies all factors; this refers to the unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*).
Because this mind is defiled, it is of the nature of obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), and it is always associated with the four afflictions.

Just as the afflictions of the two entanglements—those of the form and formless realms—are subsumed under the category of obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) nature, because the entanglements of the form and formless realms are concealed by śamatha;
so too is this manas, for it follows [the object] subtly at all times.
The commentary states:
This passage further establishes the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) by means of another principle.
What is this establishing principle?
This means that if this [ignorance] did not exist, the non-common ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) could not exist.
What is the characteristic of non-common ignorance?
It is the delusion that has not yet been countered by its remedy and which obstructs true knowledge.
This is logically inconsistent with the nature of the five consciousnesses, because there is no possibility for an obstruction to exist therein.
Furthermore, where a counteragent exists, the corresponding object of that counteragent cannot exist.
If it were held that this [affliction] does not exist within the afflicted mental consciousness (*kliṣṭa-manovijñāna*), then the manifestation of other afflictions would fail to be established.

If one were to posit these afflictions as residing in the afflicted mental consciousness, then that consciousness would necessarily be perpetually afflicted in nature; how, then, could the mind engaged in giving and so forth be established as virtuous?

Because it is constantly associated with these afflictions, if one were to say that there is a mental consciousness functioning simultaneously with wholesome dharmas, this would mean it is associated with those very afflictions; thus, it would be illogical for such a defiled mental consciousness to induce the arising of its antidote.

If it is said that there is a wholesome mind functioning simultaneously with the afflicted manas, then this wholesome mind induces its antidote; since the former arises and the latter ceases, there is no fault.
Furthermore, this is because of the five common characteristics.

Why is this so? For example, just as the five consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness, must necessarily have the five sense organs, such as the eye, as their simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*), so too must mental consciousness necessarily have a simultaneous support.
Furthermore, it is because of its etymological definition. Why is this so?
Because it is capable of cogitation, it is called "manas" (mind).
Upon what basis is this etymological explanation founded?
It is not logical that those six consciousnesses serve as the support for the immediately preceding consciousness (anantara-vijñāna), because they have already ceased and perished.
Furthermore, there is a distinction between the two meditative attainments. Why is this so?

If it were definitively stated that the afflicted manas exists, then it would follow that this manas exists within the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) but not within other attainments; thus, there would be a discrepancy.
If it were otherwise, there would be no distinction between the two meditative attainments, because the sixth mental consciousness does not function in both of them.
Furthermore, there would be no grasping at a self within the state of non-conception.
Why is this so? If the afflicted manas were absent during that state [of meditative absorption], there would be no grasping at a self throughout that single lifetime.
If that were the case, it would not be something censured and loathed by the Noble Ones.
Since they have been thus rebuked and reviled, it is certain that they possess self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*).
Furthermore, because self-grasping persists. Why is this so?
Furthermore, because the latent tendency of ego-grasping (*ātmagrāha-anuśaya*) definitely persists even during states such as giving,
it would be illogical for this latent tendency of ego-grasping to exist apart from ignorance (*avidyā*).

This ignorance cannot exist independently of its support, and since this support is nothing other than the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), one must necessarily admit the existence of the afflicted mind.

If this were not admitted, there would be the aforementioned fault; therefore, to further clarify that point, four verses are spoken, beginning with "if it were non-associated ignorance," and so forth, as explained at length.

In this context, "unshared ignorance" refers to the innate ignorance associated with the afflicted manas (kliṣṭamanas) that arises simultaneously within all states of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral afflictions and secondary afflictions;
if it were absent, a great fault would ensue.
Its functional activity consists in constantly obstructing the arising of wisdom regarding suffering and so forth; this demonstrates the fault of lacking such functional activity.

Regarding the "five similar dharmas": the sixth consciousness (manovijñāna) shares certain common characteristics with the five groups of sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñānakāya*); for those [five], there are the five sense organs (*pañcendriya*), and the *ālayavijñāna* serves as their simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*).
This case is likewise: there is the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), which takes the *ālayavijñāna* as its simultaneous support (*sahabhv-āśraya*).
These five [mental factors] share this same nature; they definitely do not exist apart from the afflicted mind, which thus reveals the fault of their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva-doṣa*).
If it is argued that there is no fault in the definition, it is because it apprehends the characteristics of its objects and reflects upon them;
since it can grasp its object at the moment immediately following [the cessation of the preceding consciousness], it is called "mind" (manas).
Since that which has passed away is already extinguished and beyond conceptualization, how could it possess a nature capable of conceptualization?
Since there would be no basis for such a definition, this would result in a great logical fallacy.

As for the distinction between the two meditative attainments: within the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), there is no afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*); within the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), there is an afflicted mind.
If this [defiled mind] were non-existent, there would be no distinction between these two meditative attainments, which would constitute a great logical fallacy.

Furthermore, if the defiled mind did not exist, there would be no grasping at a self within the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñika*), for it is not logically tenable that an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) should temporarily be free from grasping at a self within their own continuum.
Since all such faults must necessarily be avoided by means of a defiled mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), one must certainly admit the existence of a defiled mind.
To clarify this point, it is further stated that "there is no [second]" and so forth.
The second is the unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) and the five similar dharmas.

Regarding the three contradictions: namely, the etymological interpretation, the distinction between the two meditative attainments, and the fact that within the state of birth in the non-percipient realm (*asaṃjñisattva*), the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) constantly persists apart from the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*). These three matters all constitute contradictions.

If this [defiled mind] did not exist, self-clinging would not be possible in all circumstances; for apart from the defiled mind, self-clinging would not be able to constantly accompany one throughout all states, such as those that are wholesome. Therefore, one must certainly admit the existence of the defiled mind (*kliṣṭamanas*).
The remainder of the text is easy to understand and requires no further explanation.
The Treatise states:
Regarding the third [category], the substance of the mind—if one were to exclude the ālayavijñāna, nothing else could be found.
Therefore, the *ālayavijñāna* is established as the essence of the mind; with this as its seed, the *manas* and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) arise.
The commentary states:

regarding the third essence of the mind, if it were apart from the *ālayavijñāna*, there would be no other nature; with this as the cause, both the *manas* and the evolving consciousnesses are able to arise.
One should know that the evolving consciousness of the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) likewise grasps the second *manas*. Why is this?
Because at the moment it is about to cease, it receives the name of *manas*.
The treatise says:
For what reason is it also called "mind" (citta)?
Because it is accumulated by the seeds perfumed by various dharmas.
The commentary states:
Furthermore, wishing to explain the etymology, this question is posed.
"By means of various phenomena" refers to phenomena belonging to their respective categories.
The "perfuming seeds" are the causes for the differentiation of functional capacities.
"Because they are accumulated" means that they constitute the sense of an extremely dense aggregation of a unified whole.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, for what reason is this mind not taught in the Śrāvakayāna under the name *ālayavijñāna* or *ādānavijñāna*?
It is because it is comprised within an extremely subtle and profound objective sphere.

Why is this so? Because the śrāvakas do not operate within the sphere of all objects and knowledge; therefore, although they would attain wisdom and achieve liberation even without this teaching, it was not taught to them.
If bodhisattvas are certain to engage with the sphere of all objects of knowledge and wisdom, it is for this reason that it is taught;
for apart from this wisdom, it is not easy to realize the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (sarvajñajñāna).
The commentary states:
Regarding "that which is subsumed under this profound and subtle object," it means that because this very object is profound and subtle, it is called a "profound and subtle object.
This is because it is subsumed within the profound and subtle sphere of experience and is difficult to comprehend.

It is not that the śrāvakas practice with right diligence for the sake of seeking the knowledge of all objects; rather, they seek only their own welfare, for by means of the coarse and shallow correct knowledge of suffering and so forth, they are able to permanently sever the afflictive obstructions.

This is taught for the sake of those bodhisattvas who, for the benefit of themselves and others, seek to sever the afflictive obstructions and the obstructions to omniscience, and thus practice with right diligence.
*Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Fascicle One;
*Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Fascicle Two.
Composed by Vasubandhu Bodhisattva;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Part Two of the Second Section: The Basis of the Knowable. The Treatise says:
Furthermore, within the Śrāvakayāna, the ālayavijñāna has also been taught through various indirect methods (paryāya) and with intentional meaning (saṃdhi).
As it is said in the *Ekottarika Āgama*:
"The sentient beings of the world love the ālaya, delight in the ālaya, rejoice in the ālaya, and find pleasure in the ālaya."
In order to sever such an *ālayavijñāna*, when the True Dharma is taught, one listens with reverence, dwells in a mind seeking understanding, and practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is thus a most marvelous and rare event, through which the True Dharma appears in the world.
In the Śrāvakayāna, within the *Tathāgatotpattisambhava-caturguṇa-sūtra*, the ālayavijñāna has been revealed through this alternative terminology and intentional meaning (*saṃdhi*).

Furthermore, in the Āgamas of the Mahāsāṃghika school, it is also spoken of through an alternative terminology and intentional meaning as the "root-consciousness" (*mūlavijñāna*), just as a tree depends upon its root.

Within the Mahīśāsaka school as well, this is referred to by another name through intentional terminology as the "aggregates that exhaust saṃsāra" (*ātyantika-saṃsārika-skandha*). While there are instances and times where form and mind are seen to be interrupted, it is not the case that the seeds within the ālayavijñāna are ever interrupted.
The commentary states:
"Worldly sentient beings who love the *ālayavijñāna*" is the general introductory statement.
Subsequently, the remaining phrases explain it specifically according to the three periods of time—present, past, and future—in their respective order.
Furthermore, there is another meaning: namely, one craves the ālayavijñāna in the present and delights in the ālayavijñāna in the past.
Because of having delighted in the ālayavijñāna in previous lives, one again takes pleasure in the ālayavijñāna in this present life.
Because one delights in and rejoices in the *ālayavijñāna*, one will take pleasure in the *ālayavijñāna* in future lives.
One who practices in accordance with the Dharma acts according to the teachings.

Within the Mahāsāṃghika school, it is called the "root-consciousness" (*mūlavijñāna*), just as a tree depends upon its roots; this is because the root-consciousness is the fundamental cause of all consciousnesses, just as a tree root is the general cause for the trunk and other parts.
If one is separated from its root, the stem and so forth do not exist.
One should know that the ālayavijñāna, called the "root-consciousness," is likewise so.

Within the Mahīśāsaka school, it is described by another name as the "aggregate that exhausts birth and death" (ātyantika-saṃsāra-skandha); to explain the reason for this, it is said that there exists the "basis" (sthāna) and so forth.
To say there is "place" means that in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) there are no forms.
To say there is "time" means that within various states such as the state of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), there are no mental states.
The statement that "the seeds within the ālayavijñāna are not severed" means that the perfuming of form and mind within the ālayavijñāna serves as the cause by which form and mind arise again.
The Commentary states:

Thus, regarding this basis of the knowable (*jñeyāśraya*), it is taught that its nature is the ālayavijñāna, its nature is the ādānavijñāna, its nature is the mind (*citta*), its nature is the ālaya, its nature is the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), and its nature is the aggregate that persists until the end of saṃsāra (*ātyantika-saṃsārika-skandha*).
"By this alternative formulation, the ālayavijñāna becomes the great royal highway.
The commentary explains:
"By this alternative formulation, the ālayavijñāna becomes the great royal highway" refers to its extremely vast significance.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, there is a class [of thinkers] who claim that *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna* are identical in meaning despite differing in expression.
This position is untenable; since distinct differences in meaning are observable between *manas* and *vijñāna*, one should know that the meaning of *citta* must likewise differ [from them].

Furthermore, there is another class [of persons] who say that what the Blessed One spoke of as "sentient beings' attachment to the *ālaya*," and so forth at length—in this context, the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) are designated by the name *ālaya*.
Others again claim that the feeling of pleasure associated with craving is the ālayavijñāna;
still others claim that the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is the ālayavijñāna.
These various teachers hold such views because they are ignorant of the ālayavijñāna both through scripture and through realization.
Establishing the name "ālaya" in this manner is also inconsistent with the principles established according to the Śrāvaka-yāna.
However, for one who is not deluded, if they grasp the ālayavijñāna and establish it by the name "ālaya," such an establishment is the most excellent.
What is the most excellent [explanation]?

If the five aggregates of clinging were called the *ālaya*, it would be unreasonable for them to be so designated, because they are the most loathsome and repulsive places within the miserable realms where beings are born, and where sentient beings never give rise to affection or delight; since beings constantly seek to abandon and leave them, it is illogical for them to be "stored" therein.

If the feeling of pleasure associated with craving were called the *ālaya*, it would not exist from the fourth dhyāna upward; moreover, sentient beings possessing those states would always experience aversion toward it, and thus it would be illogical for them to harbor [the seeds] within it.

If the view of a transitory collection (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) were called the *ālaya*, it would be constantly repugnant to those who have faith and understanding in the selflessness of this True Dharma; therefore, it would also be unreasonable for it to be that which is grasped and stored within.

Although the ālayavijñāna is comprised within the nature of an internal self, and even when one is born in the miserable realms where there is constant suffering and seeks to escape that suffering-aggregate, one is nevertheless perpetually bound by the craving for a self directed toward the ālayavijñāna, never seeking to abandon it.

Although those born in the fourth dhyāna or above always feel aversion toward the pleasure associated with craving, they are nevertheless constantly bound by the attachment to self within the ālayavijñāna.

Although those who have faith and understanding in this True Dharma and who loathe the view of self may turn away from it, they remain bound by the attachment to a self within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Therefore, establishing the name *ālaya* for the *ālayavijñāna* is most excellent and definitive.
The commentary states:
"Those who are not deluded" refers to the bodhisattvas, because the principle of the ālayavijñāna as proclaimed by them is established.
"Within the miserable destinies" refers to within the various miserable destinies of hungry ghosts (preta), animals (tiryagyoni), and hell-beings (naraka).
Regarding "a place of exclusively suffering," this refers to a place where one exclusively experiences the results of unwholesome karma (*an-iṣṭa-karma-phala*).

While pleasant feelings (*sukha-vedanā*) may occasionally arise there as a result of concordant cause (*niṣyanda-phala*), the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) experienced by those born there is exclusively suffering.
That which does not exist from the fourth dhyāna upward refers to the fourth dhyāna itself and all higher stages.
"Possessing those sentient beings" refers to those who have acquired them through birth.
Regarding "the ālayavijñāna being comprised within the nature of an internal self": this refers to all sentient beings grasping this consciousness as an internal self-nature.
"Seeking to leave behind the aggregates of suffering" means seeking to leave behind painful sensation.

"However, regarding 'being bound by the attachment to self within the storehouse consciousness' (ālayavijñāna), this means that one clings to the ālayavijñāna as a self, giving rise to attachment that binds one so that one does not depart from it.
The Commentary says:
"Thus has the establishment of the various synonyms for the ālayavijñāna been explained."
How can these characteristics be established and perceived?
Briefly, there are three ways to establish these characteristics:

first, the establishment of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); second, the establishment of causal characteristics (*hetulakṣaṇa*); and third, the establishment of resultant characteristics (*phalalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the establishment of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the ālayavijñāna herein: it refers to its being the cause for the arising of all phenomena belonging to the category of affliction (*saṃkleśapakṣa*), by virtue of its capacity to maintain the corresponding seeds (*bīja*).

Regarding the establishment of the causal characteristic (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*) of the ālayavijñāna herein: it refers to this very ālayavijñāna, which consists of all seeds, acting at all times as the cause for the manifestation of those phenomena belonging to the category of defilement (*saṃkleśa-pakṣya*).

Regarding the establishment of the resultant characteristic (*phala-lakṣaṇa*) of the ālayavijñāna herein: it means that the ālayavijñāna arises in continuous succession based upon all the perfumations (*vāsanā*) of those factors belonging to the category of affliction (*saṃkleśapakṣa*) that have existed since beginningless time.
The commentary states:
Thus far, the various designations for the establishment of the ālayavijñāna have been explained.

However, merely explaining these designations does not lead to an understanding of its characteristics; therefore, the intrinsic nature, causal nature, and resultant nature of this consciousness are explained next.

Regarding the establishment of its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) herein: it has as its intrinsic nature the consciousness that possesses the differentiation of functional capacities capable of producing those [phenomena], based upon all the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the category of defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśapakṣadharma*).
In order to demonstrate such a capacity, it is said that [the storehouse consciousness] is associated with the retention of seeds;
that is to say, based upon all the perfumings (*vāsanā*) of the factors belonging to the category of total affliction (*saṃkleśapakṣa*), it serves as the productive cause for those very factors.
That which "appropriates and maintains the seeds" refers to its specific functional capacity.
"Concomitance" has the meaning of cultivation.
This is called the establishment of the self-characteristic of this consciousness.

Regarding the establishment of the characteristics of the cause herein: it refers to the aforementioned ālayavijñāna, which possesses all seeds; through the perfuming of various phenomena belonging to the category of defilement, it acquires specific functional capacities that serve as the causes for the arising of those very phenomena.
This is called the establishment of the causal characteristic (*nimitta-lakṣaṇa*) of this consciousness.

Regarding the establishment of its resultant characteristic (*phala-lakṣaṇa*) herein: it refers to the fact that, based upon the beginningless habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of those factors belonging to the category of affliction (*saṃkleśa-pakṣa*), this consciousness arises in succession and is able to maintain that beginningless habitual perfuming.
This is called the establishment of the characteristic of the fruit of this consciousness.

Herein, its specific characteristic is that it takes the beginningless perfuming of all factors belonging to the category of affliction as the cause for its arising; it has as its intrinsic nature the consciousness that sustains seeds, being established by way of both the state of fruit and the state of cause.

In this context, the characteristic of the cause consists of the differentiation of functional capacities formed by the perfuming of those dharmas belonging to the category of affliction; it serves as the cause for their arising and is established solely as the nature of causality.

In this context, the characteristic of the fruit arises from the continuity of the *ālaya-vijñāna*, which has been perfumed since beginningless time by various phenomena belonging to the category of affliction (*saṃkleśa*); it is established solely as that which possesses the nature of a fruit.
These are the three distinctions.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, what is called "perfuming" (vāsanā)?
Regarding the perfuming of the expressive [words], what is the expressed?
It refers to that which arises and ceases simultaneously with those phenomena; within this, there exists the causal nature capable of producing them—this is called the expressed.

For example, when there is the perfuming of a flower within a *tila* seed, the *tila* seed and the flower arise and perish together; thus, those *tila* seeds are produced carrying the causal capacity to generate that fragrance.

Furthermore, as in the case of those established as practitioners of greed and so forth, the latencies (*vāsanā*) of greed and so forth depend upon that [mind] which arises and ceases simultaneously with the greed; this mind arises bearing the causes for the production of those [defilements].

Alternatively, for one who is learned, the perfuming of learning arises and ceases simultaneously with the mental attention based on hearing; this mind arises bearing the causal seeds of that [learning], and because it is able to maintain them through this perfuming, such a person is called a "holder of the Dharma."
It should be understood that the principle of the perfuming of the ālayavijñāna is likewise.
The commentary explains:
"That which arises and perishes simultaneously with those dharmas, and within which there exists the causal nature capable of producing them—this is what is meant by the term [perfuming]."

It refers to the fact that, based upon that ālayavijñāna which arises and perishes simultaneously with those various defiled phenomena, there exists a causal nature capable of producing those phenomena; this is called "perfuming" (vāsanā).
The treatise says:
Furthermore, regarding the seeds of all phenomena belonging to the category of affliction within the ālayavijñāna, do they abide as distinct entities or are they not distinct?
It is not that there are separate, substantial entities among those seeds abiding therein, nor is it that they are not distinct.

However, when the ālayavijñāna arises in this manner, it possesses a specific functional capacity capable of producing those [phenomena], which is termed the "all-seed consciousness" (*sarvabījaka-vijñāna*).
The commentary asks:
Within the ālayavijñāna, are the seeds of the defiled phenomena (saṃkleśa-dharma) different from it, or not different?
If that were so, what would be the fault?

If there were a difference [between the seeds and the consciousness], those seeds would have to be distinguished as separate entities, and the principle that the ālayavijñāna perishes moment by moment would also not be established, because they would be distinct from one another.
Due to the power of perfuming by the wholesome and unwholesome, the seeds should themselves become wholesome or unwholesome in nature; yet they are admitted to be neutral (*avyākṛta*).
If [the seeds] were not distinct [from their natures], how could there be many of them?
This is not reasonable;
therefore, both positions possess faults.
