It is not that the seeds exist as distinct real entities residing within this [consciousness], nor are they non-different from it—even when referred to as the "all-seed consciousness"—for one does not definitively take them to be either different or non-different in order to avoid the faults mentioned previously.
"Arising in such a manner" means arising by way of such categories.

"There is a specific functional capacity capable of producing them" refers to the principle that there exists a specific functional capacity corresponding to the production of phenomena belonging to the category of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
Because it is associated with the capacity to produce those [states], it is called the "all-seed consciousness.
Regarding this meaning, there is a present analogy: just as a barley seed possesses the nature of a seed because it has the capacity to produce its own sprout.

If, over time, the grain becomes stale or is affected by fire, the functional capacity (*śakti*) of this barley fruit is impaired; at that time, although the physical characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the barley remain as they were, because its potency has been destroyed, it lacks the nature of a seed (*bījatva*).
The ālayavijñāna is likewise: it possesses the functional capacity to produce all defiled phenomena; because it is associated with this capacity, it is called the "all-seed consciousness."
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, how is it to be understood that the ālayavijñāna and those various defiled phenomena act as mutual causes for one another simultaneously?
It is, for example, like a bright lamp, wherein the flame and the wick arise and burn simultaneously, acting as mutual causes for one another.
Furthermore, just as bundles of reeds support one another so that they do not fall simultaneously, one should observe that the principle of mutual causality here is likewise.

For example, the *ālayavijñāna* is the cause of all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*), and all defiled phenomena are also the cause of the *ālayavijñāna*; this is established solely on the basis of such causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), because no other causal conditions can be found.
The commentary states:

Furthermore, as for how it is to be understood that the ālayavijñāna and those various defiled phenomena act as mutual causes for one another simultaneously, this question is posed in order to clarify the matter through an analogy.

For example, regarding the statement that the flame and the wick of a bright lamp arise and burn simultaneously and act upon one another: this means that in a single moment, the lamp-wick serves as the basis for the production of the lamp-flame; thus, the lamp-wick is the cause for the arising of the flame.
At that same moment, the flame is further able to burn the lamp-wick upon which it depends; thus, the lamp-flame is the cause for the burning of the wick.
The other metaphors are likewise.
Thus it is shown that there is a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), because the fruit is seen to arise precisely while the cause remains present.

Regarding the statement from "the ālayavijñāna being the cause of the defiled phenomena" up to "other causes and conditions being unobtainable," this indicates that the ālayavijñāna and the defiled phenomena are mutual causes for one another, and this constitutes the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The Commentary says:
How can perfuming (*vāsanā*), which is itself without distinction or mixture, serve as the cause for those various phenomena that possess distinction and mixture?
It is like a cloth being dyed with various dyes; at the very moment of dyeing, although there is as yet no distinction or mixture, it cannot be perceived as being of a single category.
After entering the dyeing vat, at that time, various and diverse patterns of interwoven colors appear upon the cloth, manifesting as more than a single type of hue.

The ālayavijñāna is likewise: it is perfumed by various and diverse perfuming agents (*vāsanā*), and although no such diversity can yet be perceived at the time of perfuming, once the result has emerged and the dyeing vat is present before one, there appear immeasurable categories of phenomena characterized by such diversity.
The commentary states:

As for the question, "How can perfuming (vāsanā), which is itself undifferentiated and unmixed, serve as the cause for those various phenomena that are differentiated and mixed?"—this question is posed in order to clarify this principle through an analogy.

It is like a cloth dyed with various mordants: at the time of dyeing, although no distinct or variegated patterns can be seen, once it has entered the dye-vat, distinct and variegated patterns then become visible.
The ālayavijñāna is like a cloth to be dyed; since it is the vessel for the production of results, it is called the "vessel for the production of results.
"Entering" (praveśa) signifies being encompassed by conditions.

Although there is no differentiation or admixture at the time of perfuming, once the stage of the ripening of the fruit is reached, the causal nature of various dharmas of more than one category manifests, just like a cloth that has already been dyed.
The treatise says:
Such dependent origination is extremely subtle and profound within the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, to speak briefly, there are two types of dependent origination:
The first is the dependent origination of the discrimination of self-nature; the second is the dependent origination of the discrimination of the agreeable and the disagreeable.

Among these, the arising of all phenomena based upon the ālayavijñāna is called the dependent origination of the discrimination of self-nature, because it functions as the causal nature by being able to discriminate various self-natures.

Furthermore, there is the twelve-linked dependent origination, which is called the "dependent origination that distinguishes the agreeable and the disagreeable," because it serves as the causal nature for distinguishing the various individual existences—both agreeable and disagreeable—within the happy and miserable realms of rebirth.
The commentary states:

Regarding this dependent origination, which is extremely subtle and profound within the Mahāyāna, it is called "extremely subtle" because it is difficult for the cognitive wisdom of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to comprehend.
Because it is difficult for even Arhats and others to fathom its depths, it is called "profound.
Furthermore, if one were to briefly explain dependent origination, there are two types; this is the enumeration.

First is the dependent origination of the differentiation of self-nature; second is the dependent origination of the differentiation of the agreeable and the disagreeable—these are the listing of the names.

In this context, that which relies upon the ālayavijñāna means that all phenomena arise with the ālayavijñāna as their cause; this is called the dependent origination of the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva-pratītyasamutpāda*), because it functions as the causal nature by being able to imagine the natures of various distinct categories.

If ignorance and so forth are present, this is called the dependent origination of the pleasant and the unpleasant through discrimination, because they function as the causal nature by being able to discriminate various types of self-entities as pleasant or unpleasant.
The treatise states:

Within the *ālaya-vijñāna*, regarding the first dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there are those who are deluded and conceptualize either self-nature as the cause, or past karma as the cause, or the transformations of a sovereign lord (*īśvara*) as the cause, or a real self (*ātman*) as the cause, or else they conceptualize it as being without cause or condition.
If one is deluded regarding the second dependent origination, one further discriminates, thinking "I am the agent" and "I am the experiencer.
It is, for example, like a group of many congenitally blind men who have never seen an elephant, and someone else explains and demonstrates it to them by means of the elephant.
Among those born blind, some touched the elephant’s trunk, some its tusks, some its ears, some its feet, some its tail, and some its backbone.
When people ask, "What is the appearance of an elephant?
some say it is like a plow-handle; others say it is like a pestle, or like a winnowing basket, or like a mortar, or like a broom; and still others say that an elephant is like a rocky mountain.

If one does not understand these two types of dependent origination, then ignorance is likewise like one born blind; some falsely conceive of intrinsic nature as the cause, some conceive of past karma as the cause, some conceive of Īśvara as the cause, some conceive of a real self as the cause, some conceive of no cause and no condition, and some conceive of a self as the agent and a self as the experiencer.
The intrinsic nature, causal nature, and resultant nature of the ālayavijñāna are like one who does not understand the nature of an elephant.
The commentary states:
Some distinguish past karma as the cause; because they do not admit the existence of the *puruṣakāra-hetu* (the cause of human effort), they fall into erroneous attachment.
To illustrate these points, the analogy of one born blind is given.
"Born blind due to ignorance" means that by virtue of ignorance, one becomes like one born blind.

Regarding the fact that the self-nature, causal nature, and resultant nature of the ālayavijñāna are not understood—just as [the blind man] does not understand the nature of the elephant: the aforementioned specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) established for this consciousness are called its "self-nature" (svabhāvatā); the established causal characteristics are called its "causal nature" (hetutā); and the established resultant characteristics are called its "resultant nature" (phalatā). Through the power of ignorance, one fails to understand these.
Because they do not understand the dependent origination of the discrimination of self-nature within the ālayavijñāna, they cling to self-nature and so forth as the cause of all phenomena.
Because they do not understand the second [type of] dependent origination—the discrimination of the pleasant and the unpleasant—they cling to a self as the agent and the experiencer.
In this context, the cause refers to the ālayavijñāna, because it maintains the perfumation (*vāsanā*) of all phenomena within itself.
The result is the ālayavijñāna itself, because it is that which has been perfumed by those very phenomena.
The treatise says:

Furthermore, to state it briefly, the ālayavijñāna, functioning as the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), has all seeds as its intrinsic nature; it is capable of encompassing all individual existences and all realms of rebirth within the three worlds.
The commentary states:

Regarding the fact that the ālayavijñāna has the maturation-consciousness (vipākavijñāna) with all seeds as its intrinsic nature, this means that it acquires its own substance through the ripening of heterogeneous [karmic] results, and because the seeds of all dharmas are perfumed within it.
"All destinies" refers to the five destinies and so forth.
"All individual existences" refers to the various distinctions between homogeneous and heterogeneous categories within each of those destinies.
The treatise states:
Herein are five verses:
"External and internal [objects] are not clearly manifest; regarding these two, they exist only conventionally."
The seeds of the ultimate truth should be known to be of six kinds:
they are momentary, co-existent, ever-continuing,
dependent on various conditions, determined, and capable of producing only their own specific fruits.

That which is stable, indeterminate, and capable of being perfumed, Which is associated with the perfuming agent— The object perfumed is not different from this; This is the characteristic of perfuming.
The six consciousnesses lack such association, And their three distinctions are contradictory.
Two moments of thought do not coexist; by this analogy, other cases would result in error.
Furthermore, one should know that seeds—both external and internal—are capable of both producing and projecting [rebirth].
Death occurs due to the projecting force, because [the body] perishes spontaneously thereafter.
To demonstrate that internal seeds are not like external seeds, two verses are further spoken:
One should know that external [seeds], which may lack perfuming, Are not like internal seeds;
for if there were no perfuming By hearing and so forth, the arising of a fruit would be illogical.
"Regarding what is done and not done, and loss and gain, because of these errors they become contradictory.
External seeds take the internal as their condition, due to depending upon that perfuming.
Commentary:
Having thus explained that the ālayavijñāna is the true seed of all phenomena, these five verses are now spoken to further reveal the essential nature of those seeds.
Among these, "external" refers to rice grains and the like;
"internal" refers to the ālayavijñāna.
"Not clearly manifest" means that external seeds have the sense of being *avyākṛta* (neutral).
Regarding the phrase "in both": the ālayavijñāna is clear and manifest with respect to the two natures of wholesome and unwholesome, because it pervades all that is determinate (vyākṛta).
Furthermore, there is another specific meaning: it is clear and manifest with respect to both defilement (saṃkleśa) and purification (vyavadāna).
Regarding "only conventionally," this means that external seeds are designated as seeds solely from a conventional standpoint. Why is this?
Because they, too, are all manifestations produced by the ālayavijñāna.
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is precisely the ālayavijñāna. Why is this so?
Because it is the true seed of all phenomena (*dharma*).
It should be understood that all these seeds further possess six characteristics.
Regarding "momentary destruction" (*kṣaṇika-nirodha*): it means that both types of seeds necessarily perish immediately after they have arisen.
Why is this so? That which is of a permanent nature cannot serve as the essence of a seed, because its nature remains as it was at all times without any differentiation.
As for the term "simultaneous" (*sahabhū*), it means that what is neither past nor future, nor separated [from the result], can function as a seed.
Why is this? Because if the seed exists at this time, the fruit arises at that very moment.

"It should be known to persist continuously" means that from the time the *ālaya-vijñāna* arises until its antidote is produced, the seeds of external phenomena persist until the roots remain or until they reach maturation.

Regarding "determination," it means that these seeds are each individually determined; they do not arise from everything, nor does everything arise from them. Rather, from a specific kind of entity, only that same kind of entity is produced.

"Waiting for various conditions" means that this seed must wait for its own specific collection of conditions before it can produce a fruit; it cannot produce everything at all times. Rather, when it encounters its own specific collection of conditions at a particular place and time, its own fruit is produced at that very place and time.

"Only that which can induce its own fruit" means that a seed induces only its own fruit; for example, the seeds of the *ālaya-vijñāna* can only induce the arising of the *ālaya-vijñāna*, just as rice seeds and the like can only induce rice fruits and the like.
Thus far, the meaning of the arising of seeds and fruits has been clarified; now, the distinct characteristics of perfuming shall be further demonstrated.
That which is "firm" must be firmly established in order to receive perfuming, unlike moving air.
Why is this? Because the nature of wind is sparse and mobile, it cannot sustain [perfumes]; thus, all perfumed vapors [carried] for one *yojana* do not continue to follow along with it.
However, *campaka* oil can sustain fragrances for a hundred *yojanas*, and those fragrances are likewise able to follow along with it.
Regarding the term "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*), it refers to the sense that its fragrance or stench cannot be defined.
By this principle, garlic does not absorb perfumes because it is extremely foul-smelling;
likewise, highly fragrant substances do not absorb perfumes because they are already extremely fragrant.
If a thing is not characterized by extreme fragrance or stench, it can receive perfuming (*vāsanā*).

That which is said to be "capable of being perfumed" means that it must be capable of receiving perfuming before it can be habituated; it is not something incapable of receiving perfuming, such as metal or stone.
That which cannot receive perfuming is called "unperfumable.
If at this time it is able to receive perfuming, then at that very moment it is called "perfumable," just like a substance capable of being perfumed.

Regarding "that which is associated with the perfuming agent": only that which is associated with the perfuming agent is termed "capable of being perfumed," not that which is dissociated from it; one should know that this refers precisely to the meaning of arising immediately thereafter.

Regarding the term "that which is perfumed" (*bhāvyam*): the *ālayavijñāna* possesses the four aforementioned qualities and is thus fit to receive perfuming; therefore, it is called "that which is perfumed," whereas the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and so forth are not.

"Not different from this" means that if one were to exclude this *ālayavijñāna*, nothing else would be perfumable; therefore, that which is perfumed is precisely this [consciousness] and nothing other than it.

Regarding what constitutes the characteristic of perfuming (*vāsanā-lakṣaṇa*): it means that the ālayavijñāna possesses the characteristics of perfuming, such as momentary cessation (*kṣaṇika-nirodha*) and so forth. This is because it is momentary; because it exists simultaneously with all the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*); because it continues to function until its antidote arises; or because it continues to function throughout the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); because it is determinately the causal nature for the wholesome and so forth; and because, depending on the conditions of meritorious, non-meritorious, or immovable karma, it matures into various types of rebirth within the good or evil destinies.
All such meanings as these must be established regarding all diverse phenomena within the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
Therefore, it is only this *ālayavijñāna* that is endowed with such superior qualities and is capable of receiving perfuming (*vāsanā*).
The six consciousnesses lack association because those various consciousnesses are subject to movement and fluctuation.
The three types of distinct characteristics are mutually exclusive, meaning that those various consciousnesses have distinct bases, distinct objects, and distinct acts of attention.
Furthermore, there is another meaning: because the individual modes of activity (*ākāra*) arise one by one.

To refute the position of the Dārṣṭāntika masters—who wish to have a preceding moment of consciousness perfuse a subsequent moment—it is stated that two moments cannot coexist; for two moments do not exist simultaneously, as perfuming (*vāsanā*) would have to abide through simultaneous arising and simultaneous cessation.
If it is argued that this consciousness, being of such a nature, can mutually perfuse one another despite not being associated, on the grounds that they belong to the same category of consciousness—
then applying this logic to other cases would result in logical fallacies.

This means that other types of cases should likewise be treated in this way; since the sense organs such as the eye belong to the same category of translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*), they too should mutually perfuse one another.
This implies that because the two organs of the eye and ear both possess translucent phenomena, these two translucencies should mutually perfuse each other, and the same applies to the others.
However, you do not allow this; for although they share the same pure nature, because their continuums are distinct, they cannot mutually infuse one another.
Consciousness should be treated likewise: although it shares the same nature as consciousness, how could it possibly mutually infuse itself?
Regarding these two kinds of seeds thus described—namely, the external and the internal—one should know that both possess the capacity to produce and the capacity to project.
Among these, external seeds act as the producing cause until the fruit ripens; internal seeds act as the producing cause until the limit of the lifespan.

External seeds can induce a continuity that persists even after withering, and internal seeds can induce the remains of a corpse even after death; it is due to this inducing cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) that they continue to abide for a long duration.

If these two types of seeds possessed only the productive cause (*janana-hetu*), then once this cause perished, the fruit would immediately cease to exist, and there would be no possibility of its abiding in continuity for even a brief moment.

If it is argued that moments arise in a continuous succession, where the preceding moment acts as the cause and the succeeding moment follows accordingly, then the final moment should not be subject to total cessation; therefore, there must necessarily be a projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
These two seeds are, for example, like a bent bow released from its string as the cause, whereby the arrow does not fall but reaches a distant destination.
The treatise says:

Furthermore, it should be understood that the remaining *pravṛtti-vijñānas* (active consciousnesses), throughout all their respective bases and realms of existence (*gati*), are designated as the "experiencers."
As stated in a verse in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*:
"The first is called the consciousness of conditions; The second is named the experiencer.
Within this, there is that which experiences, And the mind and mental factors that perform discrimination and investigation."
The commentary states:
Herein, "enjoyment" has the sense of "arising.
That which exists within enjoyment is called the "enjoyer."
To clarify this meaning, the verse from the *Madhyāntavibhāga* is cited as scriptural authority (*āgama*).
The treatise states:
"In this way, these two consciousnesses serve as mutual conditions, as stated in a verse within the *Mahāyānābhidharma-sūtra*:"
All phenomena reside within the storehouse-consciousness, and the consciousness likewise resides within all phenomena;
they are mutually the nature of effect and also eternally the nature of cause.
Commentary:

The ālayavijñāna and all phenomena are mutually cause and effect at all times, arising from one another in a continuous succession: if at this time the ālayavijñāna is the cause of all phenomena, then at that very moment all phenomena are the effect;
if at this time the ālayavijñāna is the effect of all phenomena, then at that very moment all phenomena are the cause.
The treatise says:

If, in the first dependent origination, these two consciousnesses thus serve as mutual causes and conditions for one another, then in the second dependent origination, what kind of condition do they constitute?
This is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Of how many conditions are these six consciousnesses produced?
They are produced by the dominant condition, the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

These three types of dependent origination—namely, that which extends to the limits of saṃsāra, that which pertains to agreeable and disagreeable destinies, and that which pertains to experience—possess four conditions.
The commentary states:
herein, the first type of dependent origination refers to the mutual relationship of cause and condition between all habitual tendencies within the ālayavijñāna and those various phenomena.

The second dependent origination refers to ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth acting as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), because formations (*saṃskāra*) and the rest arise through the predominant power of ignorance and the others.
Furthermore, the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are called the "dependent origination of enjoyment," as they are produced by three conditions.

That is to say, visual consciousness takes the eye as its dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and takes visible form as its object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and its equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), meaning that this consciousness arises immediately following that [moment].
Why is this so? Because if there were no place for it to be accommodated, this [consciousness] would not arise;
the same applies to the other consciousnesses as well.
The treatise says:
Having thus established the various synonyms and characteristics of the ālayavijñāna,
how is it known that these synonyms and such characteristics apply exclusively to the ālayavijñāna and not to the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna)?

If one were to distance oneself from such an established ālaya-vijñāna, neither defilement nor purification could be established; that is to say, because the defilement of afflictions, the defilement of karma, and the defilement of birth would all fail to be established, and both mundane purification and supramundane purification would likewise fail to be established.
The commentary states:

Thus far, the various designations for the establishment of the ālayavijñāna and its defining characteristics have been explained. Now, it shall be demonstrated that these two pertain exclusively to the ālayavijñāna and are consistent with correct reasoning, rather than applying to anything else; this will be determined through logical analysis.
The treatise says:
Why is it that the defilement of afflictions is not established?

Because it is illogical for the substance of those seeds—which are produced by the perfuming of the primary afflictions and secondary afflictions—to exist within the sixfold collection of consciousnesses.

Why is this so? If one were to establish that visual consciousness arises and ceases simultaneously with afflictions and secondary afflictions such as craving, then these must be produced by the perfuming of those very afflictions, and not by anything else. However, once this visual consciousness has already ceased and been interrupted by other consciousnesses, neither such perfuming nor its basis can be found. Since the previously ceased visual consciousness no longer exists in the present—having been interrupted by other consciousnesses—it is illogical for it to have arisen simultaneously with those cravings and other afflictions, because that past consciousness lacks any existing entity in the present.

Just as it is illogical for a maturation fruit to arise from an action that has no substance in the present after having passed away, so too this perfuming co-arising with craving and so forth within this visual consciousness is not established. This perfuming does not reside in the craving itself, because that craving is the dependent and is not stable; nor can it reside in the other consciousnesses, because their bases are distinct and they do not necessarily perish simultaneously.
Nor can it abide within its own substance, because that substance is definitively devoid of simultaneous arising and ceasing.
Therefore, it is illogical for the visual consciousness to be perfumed by afflictions and secondary afflictions such as craving.
Furthermore, this consciousness is not perfumed by other consciousnesses.
As it has been said regarding visual consciousness, the same applies to the remaining evolving consciousnesses; this should be understood accordingly.
The commentary states:
In this context, "this" refers to this very visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
"By that which perfumes it" means by the perfuming of craving and so forth.
"To become a seed" means to constitute the nature of a cause.
"Is not other than [the auditory consciousness]" means it is not the auditory consciousness and so forth.
"Interrupted by other consciousnesses" means interrupted by the auditory consciousness and others.
"Such perfuming" refers to the perfuming of greed and so forth.
Regarding the basis for perfuming (*vāsanā*), it refers to the visual consciousness itself.

As for the statement that "the visual consciousness arises simultaneously with those [afflictions] such as greed," this means that it is not logical for the visual consciousness to arise simultaneously with greed and so forth from a past cause that currently lacks substantial existence.
Just as it is illogical for a maturation fruit to arise from past karma that currently lacks substantial existence, so too is it illogical in this case; it is likewise unreasonable.
Furthermore, there are other masters who maintain that it possesses substantial existence; namely, the proponents of divergent views who wish to establish that the past is of a truly existent nature.
However, neither the designator nor the designated of the past can be apprehended.
Why is this so? If a phenomenon were substantially existent, how could it be called "past"?
Therefore, it is unreasonable for [the result] to arise from that maturation fruit, because there is no perfuming.

Furthermore, regarding this visual consciousness—namely, that the perfuming (vāsanā) inherent in the visual consciousness arising simultaneously with greed and so forth is not established—it means that such perfuming is not even established; how much less could the visual consciousness arising later in time together with greed ever be established?
However, regarding the statement that this perfuming does not abide within greed: it is illogical for the perfuming of visual consciousness to reside within greed. Why is this?
Because that greed depends upon the visual consciousness.
"Because it does not abide firmly, it also cannot abide in other consciousnesses" means that this perfuming cannot reside within the consciousnesses of the ear and so forth. Why is this?
Because the bases of those various consciousnesses are distinct, and due to this distinction of their bases, there is no principle of their necessarily arising and ceasing together.

That is to say, visual consciousness depends on the eye, auditory consciousness depends on the ear, and so on, up to mental consciousness depending on the *manas*; since these bases are remote from one another, it would be illogical for the remaining latencies (*vāsanā*) to reside in locations other than where they originated.

Furthermore, it cannot abide within its own substance; that is to say, this visual consciousness cannot also be perfumed by visual consciousness, because two visual consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously.
Because they are non-dual, it is certain that there can be no sense of simultaneous arising and ceasing.

By this principle, visual consciousness must certainly not be perfumed by afflictions (*kleśa*) or secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) such as greed, nor is visual consciousness itself perfumed by visual consciousness.
The treatise says:

Furthermore, when one dies from the higher realms such as the Realm of Non-conception (asaṃjñika) and is reborn in this world, the initial consciousness at that time is defiled by afflictions (kleśa) and secondary afflictions (upakleśa). This consciousness would have no seed when it arises, because both its basis (āśraya) and its perfuming (vāsanā) have already passed away and lack any present substantiality.
The commentary states:
"The consciousness that is first defiled" refers to the very first consciousness produced upon arriving here [in this realm].
"When this consciousness arises, it would have no seed" means that the initially produced consciousness would arise without a cause.
The "basis" refers to that which serves as the basis.
The "perfuming thereof" refers to the perfuming of afflictions.
The Treatise says:

Furthermore, when the consciousness that serves as the antidote to the afflictions has arisen and all other worldly consciousnesses have ceased, it would be illogical for the seeds of the remaining afflictions and secondary afflictions to reside within this antidotal consciousness if the ālayavijñāna were absent.

Because this counteractive consciousness is liberated by its very nature and does not arise or cease simultaneously with other afflictions (*kleśa*) or secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), when a subsequent worldly consciousness arises later on, if the ālayavijñāna were absent, those various latencies (*vāsanā*) and their basis would have long since passed away and would currently lack substantial existence; thus, it would follow that they could arise again without seeds.
Therefore, if one were separated from the ālayavijñāna, the defilement of afflictions (kleśa-saṃkleśa) could not be established at all.
The commentary states:
"If the consciousness that serves as the antidote to afflictions has already arisen and all other worldly consciousnesses have already ceased" means that the six consciousnesses have already ceased.

Regarding the point that it is illogical for the seeds of the remaining afflictions and secondary afflictions to exist within this counteractive consciousness (*pratipakṣa-vijñāna*): it means that the counteractive consciousness is not the cause for the arising of subsequent worldly consciousnesses.
"Furthermore, at a later time" means after this supramundane mind.
"Those various perfumings" refers to all the perfumings belonging to the remaining afflictions and secondary afflictions.
Regarding "and that which is supported," this refers to the consciousness that serves as the support.
"It would arise without seeds" means that if the ālayavijñāna did not exist, it [the supported consciousness] would arise without a cause.
In this context, afflictions are themselves the defilements; therefore, they are called "afflictive defilement.
According to the reasoning presented above, afflictive defilement cannot be established.
The treatise says:
Why is it that the defilement of karma is not established?
Because it is inconsistent for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) to serve as the condition for consciousness (*vijñāna*).
If this were non-existent, then "existence conditioned by grasping" would also be inconsistent.
The commentary states:
In order to demonstrate that the defilement of karma cannot function as a causal condition, it next asks: why does the defilement of karma fail to be established?

Regarding the statement that "consciousness does not correspond [with karma] because karma serves as its condition": this means that once meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable formations have arisen and subsequently ceased, if one does not accept the existence of the ālayavijñāna, in what location could the perfuming (vāsanā) be established?
As has already been fully demonstrated regarding the various afflictions and defiled phenomena, the six groups of consciousness are incapable of sustaining any habitual perfumations.
If this [storehouse consciousness] were non-existent—that is, if there were no consciousness conditioned by formative action—[the process of rebirth could not occur].
Regarding the statement that "existence conditioned by grasping is also inconsistent," this means that there is no such thing as existence conditioned by grasping.
For what reason?
It is because the consciousness perfumed by the preceding formations, through the power of grasping, causes the perfuming to increase and transform into existence.

In this context, karma itself is the nature of defilement, and is thus called "karmic defilement"; alternatively, there is defilement that exists in dependence upon karma, and this is also called "karmic defilement.
If one does not believe in the existence of the ālayavijñāna, this karmic defilement cannot be established.
Commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, Scroll Two;
Commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, Scroll Three.
Composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Section Two: The Basis of the Knowable, Part Three. The Treatise says:
Why is it that the defilement of birth is not established?
Because they are not associated at the time of the reconnection of the continuity.
The commentary states:
If one does not believe in the existence of the ālayavijñāna, then even the defilement of birth cannot be established; this shall now be demonstrated.
Regarding the phrase "because it is not associated at the time of linking the continuity": this means that it is not associated with the acquisition of a personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
The treatise states:

When one dies from a state that is not in meditative equipoise (*asamāhita-bhūmi*) and is reborn, a defiled mental consciousness (*kliṣṭa-manovijñāna*) arises based on the mind during the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) to link the continuity of birth. This defiled mental consciousness ceases within the intermediate state, and the consciousness (*vijñāna*) then merges with the *kalala* in the mother’s womb.

If the mental consciousness itself were to conjoin with that [intermediate state], then once conjoined, this consciousness would serve as the basis for the arising of mental consciousness within the mother’s womb.
If that were so, there would necessarily be two mental consciousnesses arising simultaneously within the mother’s womb.

Furthermore, it is unreasonable that the consciousness which is conjoined with those [afflictions] should be of the nature of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because it would depend upon defilement, its occurrence would be uninterrupted, and the objects of mental consciousness could not be apprehended therein.

If the consciousness of conjunction (*saṃmūrcchana-vijñāna*) is indeed the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), is this mental consciousness of conjunction itself the all-seed consciousness (*sarvabījaka-vijñāna*), or is it that other mental consciousnesses arising based upon this [consciousness] which are the all-seed consciousness?

If this combined consciousness (*saṃhatavijñāna*) were the all-seed consciousness (*sarvabījaka-vijñāna*), it would be the ālayavijñāna, yet you establish it under the different name of "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*).

Furthermore, if the consciousness that serves as the support (*āśraya*) were the all-seed consciousness, then the supporting causal consciousness would not be the all-seed consciousness, while the supported resultant consciousness would be the all-seed consciousness; this is logically untenable.

Therefore, this accomplished harmonious consciousness is not the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), but is rather the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), which is the consciousness of all seeds (*sarvabījaka-vijñāna*).
The commentary states:
"The non-equipoised stage" refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
"Passing away" means death.
"Defiled mental consciousness" refers to the mental consciousness that functions in conjunction with the afflictions.

"Linking of rebirth" refers to the appropriation of a self-body; this defiled mental consciousness takes the conditioned state of existence (*bhava*) as its object and ceases within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

Regarding "conjunction" (saṃnipāta): consciousness and the red and white [elements] share a single fate; if this conjunctive consciousness were the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), then based upon it, another mental consciousness would arise. In that case, two mental consciousnesses would function simultaneously—namely, the conjunctive consciousness which serves as the support (āśraya) and the other mental consciousness which depends upon it (āśrita).
Furthermore, it is not logical that the synthesizing consciousness (*saṃprayukta-vijñāna*) should be of the nature of mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*). Why?
Because it is based on defilement and because its continuity is uninterrupted.

This means that this mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is defiled because it takes as its object a realm of existence produced by dependent origination, being itself defiled by afflictions such as craving (*rāga*) which rely upon the *manas*. Thus, it is called "defiled based" (*saṃkliṣṭāśraya*) because it relies upon this very [defiled *manas*].
In this state, the foundational retribution-consciousness cannot be defiled, as it is neutral (avyākṛta).
This synthesizing consciousness is constantly uninterrupted, as it evolves under the influence of karma.

Regarding the statement "because the object of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) cannot be apprehended": the object of the mental consciousness is clearly apprehended, namely, all phenomena (*dharmas*).
This combined consciousness (*saṃhatavijñāna*) does not possess such a clearly apprehended object; therefore, it is illogical for this consciousness to be of the nature of mental consciousness.
The Commentary says:

Furthermore, once the continuity of rebirth has been established, if one were to exclude the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), the appropriation of the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) would also be impossible.
This is because the other various consciousnesses each have distinct bases and lack stable persistence; therefore, these material sense-faculties should not be separated from consciousness.
The commentary states:
"Having already undergone the continuity of rebirth" means that one has already acquired a self-body (*ātman*).
"If apart from the maturation consciousness" means apart from the *ālayavijñāna*, because the other various consciousnesses each have their own distinct bases.
"Because they do not abide firmly" means that the other six consciousnesses each have their own distinct bases and are easily shifted.

For instance, the eye-consciousness has the eye as its specific basis; likewise, the other various consciousnesses, such as the ear-consciousness and so forth, have the ear and other material sense-faculties as their respective distinct bases.
By this reasoning, these various consciousnesses should only be held as the support for their own respective bases.

Furthermore, because these consciousnesses are easily shifted and may at times be absent, if they were apart from the ālayavijñāna, the eye and other sense organs would have no capacity to be maintained and would consequently decay.
The treatise says:

If one were to exclude the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), the mutual dependence of consciousness and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)—which functions like bundles of reeds leaning against one another—would likewise be untenable.
The commentary states:
If one were separated from the maturation consciousness—that is, if it were separated from the *ālayavijñāna*—it could not be established; this shall now be demonstrated.
As the Blessed One said:
Consciousness conditions name-and-form, and name-and-form conditions consciousness.
Herein, "consciousness conditions name" refers to the four non-material aggregates among the six consciousnesses.
"Consciousness conditions form" refers to the kalala.
If the ālayavijñāna were not taught, what would be designated as "consciousness conditioned by name-and-form"?
It is that which flows on in an uninterrupted stream, proceeding through a moment-to-moment succession of similar states based upon name-and-form.
The treatise says:
If one were apart from the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), the consciousness-nutriment (*vijñānāhāra*) for sentient beings who have already been born would not be established. Why is this?
Because it is impossible for any one of the six consciousnesses, taken individually, to perform the function of nutriment for sentient beings already born within the three realms.
The commentary states:
These words demonstrate that the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) is not established.
As the Blessed One has said:
"There are four kinds of nutriment: first, edible food; second, contact-nutriment; third, volitional-nutriment; and fourth, consciousness-nutriment."
Among these, edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is that which undergoes transformation; by means of this transformation, it benefits the physical basis (*āśraya*).

As for the nutriment of contact (*sparśa-āhāra*), it is that which apprehends objects; because it briefly perceives objects such as visible forms, it immediately causes the physical basis to flourish and thrive.

The food of mental volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra*) is that which is capable of aspiring; by means of this aspiration, it benefits the basis [of existence]. It is like seeing water from afar: although one is thirsty, one does not die.

The food of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) is that which is capable of maintaining [the body]; by means of this maintenance, the basis endures for a long time. Were it otherwise, it would be like a corpse, soon to rot and decay.
Therefore, one must admit that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is also a nutriment (*āhāra*), because it performs the function of benefiting its basis.

Among these, the nutriment of contact (*sparśa-āhāra*) belongs to the six groups of consciousness; as for the nutriment of mental volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanā-āhāra*), it belongs to the mind characterized by aspiration. What other distinct consciousness could be said to constitute a nutriment?

Furthermore, if one is without mind, asleep, fainting, or has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the six groups of consciousness have ceased; what else could remain to maintain the body and prevent it from decaying?
If one were to discard the ālayavijñāna, the body would necessarily perish.
The treatise says:

When passing away from this state and being reborn in a meditative absorption (samāhita-bhūmi), the continuity of rebirth is established by a defiled mental consciousness (manovijñāna) that is not in a state of meditative absorption.

This is not a defiled mind in a state of non-equipoise (asamāhita) belonging to that level; apart from the ripening consciousness (vipākavijñāna), the substance of other seeds cannot possibly be found.
The commentary states:
Thus it has been explained that the linking of rebirth (pratisandhi) in a level of non-equipoise cannot be established apart from the ripening consciousness.
It will now be demonstrated that [rebirth] cannot be established even in the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*).

That is to say, in this case, the continuity of rebirth is linked by means of a defiled consciousness (*kliṣṭa-vijñāna*); whereas in the state of meditative equipoise, the continuity of rebirth is linked by means of a non-equipoised defiled mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Regarding "defiled," it refers to being defiled by the afflictions (*kleśa*) of that particular stage.
Those afflictions of that stage refer to such things as relishing the flavor of meditative concentration (*samādhi-rasa*).
This defiled mind resides in the non-concentrated stage (*anāgamya-bhūmi*).
When one passes away from an indeterminate stage (*aniyata-bhūmi*), once one has passed away from that stage, how can the mind of that very stage manifest?
Since it does not manifest, how will one achieve the reconnection of birth (*pratisaṃdhi*)?

By this reasoning, one must certainly admit that from beginningless time there has always existed the perfuming of that stage and this mind within the ālayavijñāna; from this perfuming, this mind manifests as active functioning, and by means of this mind, rebirth and continuity are established.
The Commentary says:

Furthermore, regarding birth in the formless realm, if the all-seed maturation-consciousness were absent, then defiled and wholesome minds would lack seeds, and defiled and wholesome minds would lack a supporting basis.
The commentary states:
"Those born in the formless realm" refers to those who have already attained liberation.
"Defiled and wholesome minds regarding form" refers to the ability to relish [form] as well as meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
"Should have no seeds" means that there should be no cause.
"Should have no support" means that there should be no basis.
Furthermore, there is another meaning: if these two minds were without seeds, from what would they arise?
If there were no support, upon what would it depend to function?
Because it is sustained by the ālayavijñāna and because it arises from its own seeds as its basis, this dependent [consciousness] continues to evolve.
The treatise says:

Furthermore, regarding those very states, when supramundane consciousness is directly present, all other mundane minds are completely extinguished; therefore, at that time, one should indeed be extinguished and depart from those realms of existence.
The commentary states:
Within that very realm, when supramundane consciousness manifests, all other remaining mundane consciousnesses are extinguished at that time.
In that case, those destinies would be eternally severed, and one would spontaneously realize nirvana without remainder without effort.
Since this is not logically tenable, one should not deny the existence of the ālayavijñāna.
The treatise says:

If one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception or the sphere of nothingness, when a supramundane mind manifests before one, both realms of existence should be entirely extinguished and abandoned.

This supramundane consciousness does not take the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as its basis, nor should it take the sphere of nothingness as its basis, nor does it take nirvana as its basis.
The commentary states:

If one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, at times one may give rise to a supramundane mind of the sphere of nothingness, causing it to manifest before one, because the mind of that [lower] sphere is extremely clear and sharp.

Furthermore, because the mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is dull and obscure, when one dwells in that state, an extremely clear and sharp supramundane mind must arise and be brought into presence. This supramundane mind cannot take those first two [levels] as its basis or object, for both of those stages are mundane; moreover, since one arises in another stage and brings forth the mind of that other stage into presence, it is illogical for either of the two to serve as its basis or object.
Furthermore, this very mind cannot have nirvana as its objective support, because there remains a basis for clinging (sopadhiśeṣa).
Since these three types [of states] cannot be established as objective supports, if one does not believe in the existence of the ālayavijñāna, upon what would this supramundane mind depend?
The treatise states:
Furthermore, at the time of death, whether one has performed virtuous or non-virtuous deeds, the physical basis (āśraya) gradually becomes cold from either the lower or upper parts of the body.
If the existence of the ālayavijñāna were not accepted, none of these phenomena could be established.
Therefore, if one were separated from the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) which contains all seeds, the defilement of this birth could not be established either.
The commentary explains:

at the time of passing away, whether one has performed virtuous or non-virtuous deeds, the lower or upper parts of the body gradually become cold; for those who have performed virtue will certainly ascend, while those who have performed non-virtue will certainly fall downward.
If the existence of the *ālaya-vijñāna* as the appropriator were not admitted, how could there be a gradual cooling of the physical basis?
Because the *ālaya-vijñāna* is the appropriator, the body becomes cold at the respective points where it is relinquished, either from the bottom up or from the top down, according to the sequence.
The treatise says:
Why is it that mundane purification is not established?

It refers to one who has not yet abandoned the greed associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and has not yet attained a mind associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), yet diligently practices preparatory application (*prayoga*) by means of a wholesome mind associated with the desire realm for the purpose of abandoning the greed associated with the desire realm.

Because this preparatory mind bound to the desire realm does not arise and perish simultaneously with the mind bound to the form realm, it is not perfumed by the latter; therefore, it is illogical for it to serve as the seed for that [form-realm mind].

Furthermore, since the mind bound by the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*) has been separated from the present concentrated mind by many past births and other intervening states of mind, it cannot serve as the seed for this present concentration, because it no longer exists.

Therefore, it is established that the *vipākaphala-vijñāna* containing all seeds—which has been transmitted through a continuous succession—serves as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the present concentrated mind, while the preparatory wholesome mind (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*) serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
In this manner, it should be understood that throughout all the stages of detachment from desire,
such worldly purification would be logically impossible if it were devoid of the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) containing all seeds.
The commentary states:
We shall now demonstrate how the principle of worldly purification cannot be established.

That is to say, in order to distance oneself from the greed associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), when one cultivates preparatory application (*prayoga*) with a wholesome mind of the desire realm, this very wholesome mind of the desire-realm application has never been perfumed by a wholesome mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), because they do not arise and perish simultaneously. Consequently, the mind of the form realm should now arise spontaneously without any seed.

Furthermore, the wholesome mind bound by form (*rūpāvacara*) in past lives has been interrupted by many births and separated by other consciousnesses; because it no longer exists and has already passed away, it cannot serve as the seed for the present concentrated mind.
That which has been transmitted through successive stages to serve as the present causal condition is because the *ālayavijñāna* maintains those seeds.
Now, the mind bound by the realm of form arises from its own seed; it is not that the mind of applied effort (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*) lacks efficacy.

As for what is called "efficacy," it is merely a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); it is through that dominant power that this mind bound by the realm of form arises. One should understand accordingly how, in this way, greed and other afflictions bound to the realm of form are abandoned.
The Treatise says:
Why is supramundane purity not established?

It is because the Blessed One taught that, based on the speech and sounds of others and one's own internal, individual correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), right view arises with these as its causes.
Does this correct mental attention toward the sounds of another's speech perfume the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*), or both?
If one is correctly reflecting upon those dharmas at that time, the ear-consciousness cannot arise, and the mental consciousness is also interrupted by various other distracted cognitions.

If, at the time when [a mind] arises in association with correct mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*), this consciousness—which was perfumed by hearing and whose perfuming has long since ceased into the past—is definitively without substantial existence, how could it again serve as the seed capable of producing the subsequent mind associated with correct mental attention?

Furthermore, this mental attention (manasikāra) associated with correct reasoning is a mundane mind, whereas that which is associated with right view is a supramundane mind; since they have never arisen or ceased simultaneously, this [mundane] mind is not perfumed by the latter.
Since it cannot be perfumed, it is illogical for it to serve as their seed.
Therefore, supramundane purity cannot be established if it is separated from the resultant consciousness that possesses all seeds.
Regarding the statement that "the perfuming by hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) herein is incompatible with the appropriation of those seeds," the commentary explains:
we shall now demonstrate how supramundane purity would otherwise be unestablished.
Regarding "proper mental attention toward these sounds of others' speech," this refers to mental attention that corresponds with those sounds.

As for the phrase "the mental consciousness is also interrupted by various distractions and other cognitions," this means that the supramundane mind associated with right view is separated [from its continuity].
Regarding "when it arises in association with appropriate mental attention," this refers to a later time.

As for the claim that this consciousness, which has been perfumed by hearing, and its corresponding perfumation, are definitively without substance once they have long since ceased and passed away—meaning they have already perished after a long duration and are separated by time—they are certainly without substance.

How can that which serves as the seed capable of producing at a later time a mind associated with appropriate attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*)—that is, something which has long since ceased and currently lacks any substantial entity—function as a cause? It cannot.

Regarding the statement that "the permeation of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) herein is incompatible with the grasping of those seeds," this means it exists within the worldly mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
As for the term "permeation of hearing herein," it refers to the correct permeation of hearing based upon the sounds of others' speech.
Regarding "appropriating those seeds," it means that within the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), one appropriates the supramundane pure seeds.
As for "because they are incompatible," this refers to the fact that what they have conceptualized is illogical; how, then, can it be said that these [seeds] arise from that?
The treatise says:

Furthermore, how can the maturation-consciousness (vipākavijñāna), which possesses all seeds and serves as the cause of defilement, also serve as the seed for the supramundane pure mind that acts as its antidote?
Furthermore, because the supramundane mind has never been practiced in the past, its latencies (*vāsanā*) must certainly be non-existent; if there are no latencies, from what seed could it arise?
Therefore, one should answer:
It arises from seeds of the correctly heard latencies that flow forth from the most pure *dharmadhātu*.
The commentary states:

As for what is meant by "contradictory," it refers to the fact that the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is the cause of that which is to be remedied; therefore, it is illogical for it to serve as the cause of the remedy.
Furthermore, regarding the supramundane mind (*lokottaracitta*) which has not been previously practiced, this means that it has not arisen before.
Regarding the statement that "those perfumings must certainly not exist," for this reason, it is certain and beyond doubt that those supramundane minds have no perfuming.

The phrase "arising from the seeds of the perfuming of correct hearing that flows equally from the most pure *dharmadhātu*" is intended to show that the *dharmadhātu* is distinct from that of the *śrāvakas* and others.

It is called "most pure" because the Dharma-realm realized by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has eternally severed the afflictive and cognitive obstructions; thus, the teachings such as the sutras that flow forth from this most pure Dharma-realm are termed "outflows of the most pure Dharma-realm."
Listening to such sūtras and other teachings without error is therefore called "correct hearing.
The perfuming (*vāsanā*) produced by this correct hearing is termed "perfuming.
Alternatively, correct hearing itself is the perfuming; thus it is called "the perfuming of correct hearing."

This very perfuming, which persists as a continuum within the ālayavijñāna acting as its cause, is able to give rise to supramundane mind; therefore, it is said to be produced from the seeds of the perfuming of correct hearing that flow forth from the most pure dharma-dhātu.
The treatise says:
Is this perfuming by hearing of the nature of the ālayavijñāna, or is it not of the nature of the ālayavijñāna?
If it were of the nature of the ālayavijñāna, how could it be the seed for its antidote?
If it were not of the nature of the ālayavijñāna, how could the basis for these seeds of the perfuming of hearing be perceived?

Up until the realization of the bodhi of all Buddhas, these seeds of the perfuming of hearing abide in whichever one of the bases they are associated with; they reside within the vipākavijñāna, evolving in conjunction with it like water and milk.
Nevertheless, they are not the ālayavijñāna, because they are of the nature of seeds that serve as its antidote.
The commentary states:
Is this permeation by hearing the very nature of the ālayavijñāna, or is it not the nature of the ālayavijñāna?
If so, what fault would there be?
If it is of the same nature as the ālayavijñāna, how can it serve as the seed for the antidote to the ālayavijñāna?
If it is not of the same nature as the ālayavijñāna, then this seed of the cultivation through hearing must have a separate basis.
"Up to the point of realizing the bodhi of all Buddhas" means up to the attainment of the unsurpassed bodhi realized by all Buddhas.
This "perfuming of hearing" is precisely the perfuming of correct hearing that flows from the most pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
"Abiding in whichever locus of support it may be" means abiding in whichever continuum it may be.

"Residing within the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), merging and evolving together with it like water and milk" means that although this cultivation through hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) is not of the same nature as the ripening consciousness, it resides within that consciousness and evolves together with it, just like water and milk merged together.

Regarding the phrase "yet it is not the ālayavijñāna, etc.": although these [factors] arise in combination as if they were of a single nature, they are nonetheless not the ālayavijñāna itself, because they possess the nature of seeds that serve as the antidote to the ālayavijñāna.
The Commentary states:

Herein, based on weak-grade perfuming, middle-grade perfuming is established; based on middle-grade perfuming, superior-grade perfuming is established; for by extensively practicing through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, one attains correspondence with the truth.
The commentary states:

Herein, the categories of inferior, middling, and superior should be understood as being explained in reference to the wisdoms consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, because each of these possesses three types.

Furthermore, there is another interpretation: wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) is of inferior grade, wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) is of middling grade, and wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) is of superior grade.

Regarding the phrase "because one attains correspondence through extensive practice based on hearing, reflection, and cultivation," this means that one practices repeatedly and with intensity by relying upon hearing and the others.

Furthermore, within this context, that which is of inferior grade serves as the cause for attaining the middling grade, and that which is of middling grade serves as the cause for attaining the superior grade.
The treatise states:

Moreover, these seeds of the熏習 (vāsanā) from correct hearing—in their inferior, middling, and superior grades—should be understood as the seeds of the *dharmakāya*. They are contrary to the *ālayavijñāna*, are not subsumed within the *ālayavijñāna*, and because they are of the nature of the outflow from the most pure supramundane *dharmadhātu*.
Although this is worldly, it possesses the nature of the seed for supramundane mind.

Furthermore, even before the supramundane mind has arisen, it is already able to counteract the entanglements of all afflictions, it is already able to counteract all perilous evil destinies, it acts as the antidote that causes all existing evil karma to decay, and it is further able to accord with and serve all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Although these belong to the mundane world, it should be understood that what is attained by bodhisattvas who are beginners is also subsumed within the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), whereas what is attained by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is subsumed solely within the liberation-body (*vimuktikāya*).
Furthermore, this perfuming is not the ālayavijñāna, but is subsumed within the dharmakāya and the vimuktikāya.

As the perfuming gradually increases through the stages of inferior, middling, and superior, so too does the ripening-result consciousness (vipākaphala-vijñāna) gradually diminish, whereby the basis is transformed (āśraya-parāvṛtti).
Once the basis has been transformed in all its aspects, the maturation-consciousness and all seeds proceed without seeds, and all seeds are forever severed.
The commentary states:
"Having already been able to counteract the entanglements of the afflictions" means being able to sever the active causes of predominant greed and so forth.

"Having already been able to counteract the perilous miserable destinies" means that if one can sever the entanglements of the afflictions, one is thereby able to counteract the perilous miserable destinies.

"Having performed the remedy that causes all previously committed evil karma to decay" means that even if there is karma to be experienced in a future life that would otherwise lead to rebirth in the miserable realms, one is able to create the cause for its decay.
To state the essentials: this perfuming of hearing can counteract all past, future, and present evil karma.

Furthermore, that which accords with and enables one to encounter and serve all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas refers to the cause for encountering virtuous friends in the future and attaining it within oneself.

Regarding the statement that "although these belong to the mundane world, one should know that what is attained by a bodhisattva who is newly engaged in practice is also subsumed within the dharmakāya": this refers to those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who are bodhisattvas; they are called "bodhisattvas newly engaged in practice" because they are the seeds of the dharmakāya, and thus it is said that they are also subsumed within the dharmakāya.

Regarding the statement that what is attained by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is comprised solely of the body of liberation (*vimuktikāya*): this means that for the Śrāvakas and others, the permeation of hearing the True Dharma (*saddharma-śruta-vāsanā*) serves exclusively as the cause for liberation; they attain only the body of liberation and do not attain the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, how is it like water and milk?

It is not that the non-ālayavijñāna and the ālayavijñāna evolve simultaneously in the same location, yet the seeds of all types within the ālayavijñāna are exhausted while the seeds of all types within the non-ālayavijñāna increase.
It is like a swan drinking milk from water.

Furthermore, it is like when one attains freedom from desire in the world: the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the non-concentrated states gradually diminish, while the latencies of the concentrated states gradually increase, whereby the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) is attained.
The commentary states:
Although the non-ālayavijñāna and the ālayavijñāna function simultaneously in the same locus, when the ālayavijñāna is exhausted, the non-ālayavijñāna remains.
This is further illustrated by the analogy of the water and milk mixed together that were drunk by the goose, wherein the milk was consumed and only the water remained.

Furthermore, just as in the world when one attains freedom from desire (*vairāgya*), within a single *ālayavijñāna*, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the non-concentrated states (*asamāhita-bhūmi*) gradually diminish while the habitual tendencies of the wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*) of the concentrated states (*samāhita-bhūmi*) gradually increase, resulting in the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*); it should be understood that the transformation of the basis here is likewise so.
The Commentary states:
Furthermore, it is taught by the Noble Ones that when one enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), consciousness does not depart from the body.
In this context, the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) must be what does not depart from the body, for this attainment does not arise as an antidote to it.
The commentary states:

The statement that consciousness does not depart from the body when entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is intended to establish the actual existence of the *ālayavijñāna*.

When the Blessed One says that consciousness does not leave the body, this cannot be established by any consciousness other than the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), because the arising of the counteractive active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) within the absorption of cessation renders that state extremely tranquil. Thus, this absorption is regarded as being utterly peaceful.
The treatise says:

Furthermore, this consciousness does not arise again upon emerging from meditative absorption, because once the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) has been interrupted, it cannot be regenerated apart from the reconnection of the continuum.
The commentary states:
If one maintains that this consciousness arises again upon emerging from meditative absorption, and on that basis claims that consciousness does not depart from the body, this is unreasonable;
for consciousness does not arise again once one has emerged from absorption.

Once the ripening-result consciousness (*vipākavipāka-vijñāna*) has been interrupted, it cannot enter another birth after having severed its continuity, because there is no such thing as being born twice.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, if there were those who maintain that because of the presence of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), there is mind within the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

This mind is not established because it would necessarily fail to be established; because its object and mode of activity (*ālambana-ākāra*) cannot be apprehended; because it would entail the fault of being associated with wholesome roots; because it would be illogical for it to be unwholesome or neutral; because it would entail the fault of the manifestation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedanā*); because contact (*sparśa*) is apprehended therein; because it possesses efficacy within meditative concentration (*samādhi*); because it would entail the fault of being merely the cessation of thought; because it would entail the fault of the manifestation of volition (*cetanā*), faith (*śraddhā*), and other wholesome roots; because it would be illogical to extract that which depends [upon it] while leaving the basis behind; because there is a supporting analogy; and because, unlike the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), it does not exist in all states.
The commentary states:

Furthermore, if there is an adherence to the view that because of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) possesses a mind, and this [mental consciousness] is not established [as such], then for one who wishes to avoid the previously explained ālayavijñāna with its specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and instead maintain that the meditative absorption of cessation possesses a mind by means of other evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), this is unreasonable.
Why is this? Because meditative concentration (samādhi) would not be established, and because we have never observed a mind existing apart from mental factors (citta-dharma).
Just as with other mental factors, so too with perception (saṃjñā) and feeling (vedanā); they should likewise not cease.

However, since this meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) is manifested by the simultaneous cessation [of both mind and mental factors], it follows that this absorption should not be established.
If one posits that there is only the ālayavijñāna, then this fault does not arise.

Those who seek peaceful abiding give rise to this meditative concentration in order to counteract those enemies—the other minds and mental factors—and not for the purpose of counteracting the lack of clarity in the ālayavijñāna.
Furthermore, within this meditative absorption there is no other mind. Why?
Because its objects and mental modes cannot be apprehended.
The continuity of all minds and mental factors is never severed and must not be separated from their objects and modes of apprehension.
If there were a mind within this meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it too would necessarily not be separated from its object and mode of apprehension.
However, since these two types [of mind] are both unobtainable, this meditative absorption is therefore devoid of any other mind.
If one posits only the *ālayavijñāna*, there is no such difficulty, for it is that which manifests as the basis of appropriation (*upādāna*).

Furthermore, if there were evolving consciousnesses within this meditative absorption, these consciousnesses would necessarily possess distinctions such as being wholesome and so forth; that is, they would be either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
However, in this context, consciousness is not [itself] wholesome, because it would entail the fault of being associated with wholesome roots, which would be contradictory.

Nor is this consciousness wholesome by nature (*svabhāva-kuśala*), because its status as wholesome is established by its non-separation from association with wholesome roots, given that the concentrated mind is established as being of a wholesome nature.

To claim that [this state] is associated with wholesome roots such as non-greed (*alobha*) because it is not something one desires is untenable; for it would be indistinguishable from other wholesome minds, and this fault would consequently apply universally to all cases.
Furthermore, within this state, neither the unwholesome nor the indeterminate can exist, for it is illogical for the unwholesome or indeterminate to be present there.
At the time of detachment from desire, all unwholesome roots are permanently severed; thus, it is not unwholesome, nor is it indeterminate, because this concentration is wholesome.
Furthermore, it is not tenable to establish that this mind is wholesome, for there would be the fault of the manifestation of perception and feeling [which are unwholesome].
Since a wholesome mind does not exist apart from the wholesome roots, it follows that the wholesome roots must manifest.
In this context, if wholesome roots were to manifest, then perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) would likewise have to manifest, as there is no distinct cause [for their non-manifestation].
However, this is not logical, because when that which is to be countered manifests, the counteragent cannot exist.
For example, when greed and the like are actively manifesting, contemplations such as the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) are necessarily absent.

Furthermore, within this meditative absorption, no other mind can exist apart from the *ālayavijñāna*, for it would otherwise inevitably entail the presence of contact (*sparśa*), which must be perceived.

Just as there is no doubt when one abides in other meditative absorptions—namely, that within those other absorptions they are associated with wholesome roots, and when other consciousnesses arise, contact is necessarily present, characterized by the pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) produced by concentration, and being either conducive to pleasant feeling or conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
With this contact as a condition, either a pleasant feeling arises, or else a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.
Why is this? Because such a capacity exists within other samādhis.

In other meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), one observes that these two types of contact (*sparśa*) necessarily possess the functional capacity to produce the two types of feeling (*vedanā*); this case should likewise be so, as there is no obstructing cause.
That contact serves as the condition for feeling would logically follow here as well, yet it is not reasonable.
Why is this? Because it would entail the fault that only perception (*saṃjñā*) is extinguished.
If one were to admit that feeling (*vedanā*) arises with this contact as its condition, then within this meditative absorption, only perception should be extinguished.
However, one should not admit that perception and feeling are both extinguished, for this is what the Noble One has taught.
Furthermore, if there were any other consciousness within this meditative absorption, it would necessarily be associated with contact.
This is not reasonable. Why?
Because if there were contact, there would be the fault that volition, faith, and other roots of goodness would be manifesting.

If there is the functioning of consciousness associated with contact, there must necessarily be volition (*cetanā*) and other factors arising simultaneously with it, because this has been taught by the Noble Ones; therefore, in this case, volition must be present as an active manifestation.

If, within this meditative absorption, there were the active manifestation of volition (*cetanā*) constructing a wholesome mind, there would necessarily be the active manifestation of wholesome faculties such as faith (*śraddhā*); however, this must not be admitted.

If one wishes to avoid the various faults previously mentioned as well as the fault of contradicting the *Āgamas*, and thus—merely out of a desire for renunciation regarding mental factors (*caitta*) and wishing to exclude them alone—asserts that in this absorption there is only mind (*citta*) and no mental factors, this too is incorrect.
Why is this? It is because it is illogical to extract that which depends (the supported) from its basis (the support).

The support is the mind, and that which depends upon it is the mental factors; since beginningless saṃsāra, the mind as support and the mental factors as that which depends have never been separated from one another.
Because it is induced by these [factors], it must necessarily be associated with wholesome roots such as non-attachment (*alobha*).
