If one were to argue that because this meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and the preparatory means for absorption (*samādhy-upāya*) are contrary to wholesome roots such as non-attachment, wholesome roots do not function within the absorption, but only a wholesome mind functions therein.
This has never been seen elsewhere.
If that dharma were associated during the time of the cause, it would also be associated during the time of its outflow fruit; therefore, this is not logical.
Furthermore, this is unreasonable because there is a scriptural analogy.
That is to say, the Blessed One has stated:
"The formations of body cease, the formations of speech cease, and the formations of mind cease."

In this context, bodily formations refer to inhalation and exhalation; vocal formations refer to vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought); and mental formations refer to perception, volition, and so forth.
Just as when vitarka and vicāra cease, speech necessarily does not arise.
The mind is also like this: if mental formations (*manasaṃskāra*) cease, the mind should likewise not arise.

If you think that just as when bodily formations cease one remains established in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the body does not cease, so too with the mind—it should remain unceased even though mental formations have ceased—[that is not so].
This is also not the case.
Why? Because it does not exist, just as [a factor] that is not universal (asarvatraga) does not exist [in all instances].
As the Blessed One has said:
Apart from bodily formations, there is a cause for the persistence of the body, namely food, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so forth.
By means of these, the body remains stable even in the absence of inhalation and exhalation.

The mind is not so; apart from the mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*), there is no other cause that can sustain the mind and cause it to abide. For this reason, one should reach the state called "mindless absorption" (*acittaka-samāpatti*) because consciousness is absent; yet, the resultant maturation consciousness (*vipākaphala-vijñāna*) exists within this state.

The World-Honored One has taught that consciousness does not depart from the body; thus, from this very consciousness containing all seeds, the evolving consciousnesses arise again upon emerging from meditative absorption. Therefore, we know that the ālayavijñāna definitely exists.
The treatise states:

Furthermore, regarding those who maintain that there is a mind within this meditative absorption due to the presence of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), such a mind—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—cannot be established; therefore, their position is unreasonable.
The commentary states:
Having already extensively established and refuted [the views on] whether the attainment of cessation possesses consciousness, we shall now briefly elucidate the meaning of the second verse.
If one wishes to eliminate the ālayavijñāna and maintain that the attainment of cessation possesses consciousness by means of the manovijñāna:
This mind cannot be established as being either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate; therefore, it is not logical.

Why? Because this meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) is by nature wholesome, and thus it is certainly not unwholesome; the same applies to the indeterminate. Furthermore, the indeterminate states of deportment (airyāpathika), craftsmanship (śailpasthānika), and transformation (nairmāṇika) can certainly not exist [within it].
If it is said that this is the maturation-unspecified (*vipāka-avyākṛta*), then by logic it must be the ālayavijñāna; for apart from this, there is no fifth unspecified [type of consciousness].

Furthermore, if the mind in this meditative absorption were wholesome, it would have to be associated with wholesome roots such as non-attachment. Since the defiled manas has ceased and only a wholesome mind remains, at that time the wholesome mind’s basis and object are both present. With these three factors in conjunction, why would contact (*sparśa*) not arise therein?
Since contact exists, how could mental factors such as feeling not arise?
In that case, the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) could not be established, because all mental states and mental factors would fail to cease.

Furthermore, if one maintains that this meditative absorption is wholesome because it is induced by the power of the wholesome mind drawn forth by the preparatory application (*prayoga*) preceding the absorption,
then the wholesome mind within the absorption would not be associated with wholesome roots such as non-attachment (*alobha*).
Furthermore, if the conjunction of the three [faculties] possesses functional capacity, it can also produce feeling (*vedanā*);
if the conjunction of the three lacks functional capacity, it produces only contact (*sparśa*).
Therefore, although there is a wholesome mind within meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), it is not associated with wholesome roots such as non-attachment, nor is there feeling and so forth.

This argument is not tenable; since the wholesome mind of skillful means is already dissociated from wholesome roots such as non-greed, why would the resultant flow-of-similarity (niṣyanda-phala) mind induced by it not be likewise?

Furthermore, it is illogical to extract the dependent from its basis; for since beginningless time, the mind and mental factors have at all times been inseparable from one another, and it is therefore impossible to now extract the dependent and cause it to separate from its basis.
Why is this? Because there is an analogy:

in the world, from birth until destruction, throughout all times, things are mutually inseparable; it is impossible to extract the dependent [the supported] and cause it to be separated from its basis [the support].
For example, just as it is impossible for derived matter to exist apart from the primary elements that produce it, so too it is with mental factors:
they cannot be made to exist apart from the mind upon which they depend.
Therefore, it is illogical to claim that within this mindless absorption (acittaka-samāpatti) there are no mental factors (caitta-dharma), but only a virtuous mind (kuśala-citta).

Furthermore, if one were to argue that although it is illogical to separate the supported from its support, ideation (saṃjñā) and sensation (vedanā) obstruct this absorption and are thus loathed during the preparatory stage (prayoga); [this is not so].
It is illogical that only these two do not function while other dharmas, which are not like them, are able to manifest.
Why is this? Because, unlike the universal factors (*sarvatraga*), these [two] are not present there.
Those that are not universal can be extinguished herein, but because the two [types of] universal [factors] are pervasive, they cannot be extinguished.
If the universal factors were extinguished, the mind would also follow in being extinguished, as there would be no separate cause [for their persistence].
Therefore, that which is referred to here as "possessing mind" is the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), and it is certainly not the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The treatise states:

Furthermore, if there were those who maintain that the seeds of all phenomena are produced from the immediate succession of form and mind, this cannot be established, as has already been explained previously.
Furthermore, it would be illogical for one to pass away from the formless realms or the realm of non-perception, or to emerge from the meditative attainment of cessation and so forth.
Moreover, the final mind of an Arhat would not be established, as there would only be room for the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
The commentary states:

Furthermore, if there were those who maintain that matter and mind arise in immediate succession as the seeds of all phenomena—meaning, for instance, that one maintains the matter of the preceding moment can serve as the seed from which the matter of the subsequent moment arises, and that the same applies to the relationship between preceding and succeeding moments of consciousness.
This has already been refuted previously.
Furthermore, when one passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the realm of form, since form has been extinguished for a long time, how could there be a seed?

When one passes away from the Heaven of No-Thought, or emerges from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and so forth, and the mind arises again, since the mind has been extinguished for a long time, what could serve as its cause?
If this were the case, the Arhats would ultimately never attain *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, because the two causes—form and mind—would never be exhausted.

One should know that while there may be the condition of immediate antecedence (*samanantarapratyaya*) between preceding form and subsequent form, or between preceding consciousness and subsequent consciousness, there can be no causal condition (*hetupratyaya*).
The treatise states:
Thus, if one were to be separated from the maturation-consciousness (vipākavijñāna) which contains all seeds, neither defilement nor purification could be established.
Therefore, it is proven that the ālayavijñāna, possessing the characteristics previously described, definitely exists.
The commentary states:
By means of the immeasurable principles explained above, it is therefore established that the ālayavijñāna definitely exists.
The treatise says:
Regarding this, there are three verses:
If a bodhisattva, within a pure mind, Is far removed from the five consciousnesses,
And undergoes the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) without remainder— How could you possibly achieve this?
If the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) were merely the counteractive [path], it would not be established because it is not a cessation;
there would be no distinction between cause and fruit, and a fault would arise regarding its definitive abandonment.
If one were to assert that the transformation of the basis consists in the absence of seeds or the absence of an entity, [the following would apply].
Because those two do not exist, the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is not logical.
The commentary states:
Just as when one abides in the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna), the transformation of the basis is not established; this is demonstrated by the three verses.
The Bodhisattva’s state of pure mind refers to the meaning of a wholesome mental consciousness associated with supramundane remedies.
"Being far removed from the five consciousnesses" means that this [state] is free from the five consciousnesses of the eye and so forth.
Regarding the term "without remainder" (*anavaśeṣa*): it refers to the absence of wholesome, out-flowing (*sāsrava*), and defiled mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Having already mentioned the pure mind, the term "without remainder" is further employed in order to exclude wholesome, out-flowing consciousness.

As for the question, "What is meant by the transformation of the basis of the mind? if you believe that there exists an *ālayavijñāna* which can serve as the seed for all defiled phenomena, then the state of being without seeds is called the transformation of the basis of the mind.
If it were not so, how could it be established?
If the arising of an antidote were called "transformation of the basis" (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), this would be unreasonable. Why is that?
If the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) were not through abandonment, it would not constitute the cessation of affliction.

It is called the "transformation of the basis" precisely because it is the permanent abandonment; the antidote itself is not the permanent abandonment, for it is merely the cause of that permanent abandonment.
If this were necessarily the case, it would lead to the fallacy that there is no distinction between cause and fruit.
The fruit is the permanent cessation termed *nirvāṇa*, while the cause is the remedial factor termed the "Noble Path."

If the antidote were itself the permanent abandonment, it would entail the fault of the fruit and its cause becoming one and the same; as soon as the antidote arises, there would have to be nirvāṇa immediately.

If you claim that the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) consists in the absence of seeds or the absence of essence—meaning that if one posits the absence of seeds within the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*), or if one claims that the absence of essence itself constitutes the transformation of the basis—[this is untenable].
Because those two do not exist, the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) would be illogical;
for in this state, the defiled evolving consciousnesses cannot exist, and there would likewise be no seeds that could be rendered non-existent.
It is not logical to claim that there is a "transformation of the basis" (āśraya-parāvṛtti) when there is nothing to be eliminated.

If the ālayavijñāna definitely exists, then although the afflicted evolving consciousnesses cannot exist during this state of meditative concentration, their seeds remain entirely within the ālayavijñāna; thus, it is possible for them to become "without seeds" and "without substance."
Since it is unreasonable for you to effect the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) [without it], one must therefore believe that the ālayavijñāna exists.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, what are the distinctions of this ālayavijñāna?
In brief, it should be understood that there are either three kinds or four kinds.

Among these, the three kinds refer to the distinctions among the three types of perfuming (*vāsanā*): first, the distinction of the perfuming of names and phrases (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*); second, the distinction of the perfuming of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); and third, the distinction of the perfuming of the members of existence (*bhava-aṅga*).

Regarding the four types: first, the distinction of manifestation; second, the distinction of maturation; third, the distinction of causal characteristics; and fourth, the distinction of appearance. The commentary states:
Having thus established the *ālayavijñāna*, we shall now clarify its various categories of differentiation.

Among the three types of distinctions in perfuming (*vāsanā*), regarding the distinction of the perfuming of names and conventions (*nāma-vyavahāra-vāsanā*): it refers to the perfuming of the name "eye," which, residing within the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), serves as the cause for the arising of the eye.
When the eye born of maturation arises from that [cause], it takes that as its cause and is still designated by the name "eye.
The same applies to all such linguistic distinctions, including the ear and so forth.

Regarding the differentiation of the perfuming of the view of self: by the power of the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) within the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), the perfuming of self-clinging arises within the ālayavijñāna.
Based on this as a cause, there arises the distinction between regarding oneself as "self" and regarding others as "other.

Regarding the distinctions in the perfuming of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga-vāsanā*): by the power of wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable formative forces (*saṃskāra*), there is the differentiation of cyclic wandering (*saṃsāra*) among the various realms of existence.
These three will be analyzed in detail later, at the beginning of the section on the "Characteristics of the Knowable.
The treatise states:
Among these, the differentiation of "induced" refers to newly arisen perfuming.
If this were non-existent, then consciousness conditioned by volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence conditioned by grasping (*upādāna*) would not be established.
The commentary states:
"The distinction of production" refers to the capacity to produce specific categories of distinctions.
Regarding "newly arising perfumation," this refers to the very first perfumation that arises.

If there were no differentiation within the ālayavijñāna capable of inducing it, then the perfumations of the arising and ceasing of the *saṃskāras* would not constitute consciousness; consequently, the existence (*bhava*) that is produced through the grasping and appropriation of the *upādānas* could not manifest. Since this produced existence has the power to bring about future birth, it is called "existence" (*bhava*).
This aforementioned grasping, whether wholesome or unwholesome, is the fruit of habitual practice.
The treatise states:

Regarding the differentiation of maturation (*vipāka*) herein, it refers to the differentiation of maturation within the various realms of existence (*gati*), conditioned by formations (*saṃskāra*) and becoming (*bhava*).
If this did not exist, there would be no seed, and the arising of subsequent dharmas would be impossible.
The commentary states:
"The differentiation of maturation" refers to the maturation projected within the various realms of existence by conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as conditions.

If these specific manifestations of the ālayavijñāna were non-existent, there would be no cause for the various dharmas of future existence, such as the material sense organs like the eye; thus, their arising as results of maturation (vipākaja) would be impossible.
One should know that this is the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
The treatise says:
Regarding the distinctions among the characteristics of the objects of perception herein, they refer to the characteristics of the objects of the grasping at a self within the mind.
If this did not exist, the objective referent (*ālambana*) for the grasping at a self within the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) would be impossible to establish.
The commentary explains:

regarding the distinction of the characteristics of the objective referent, it means that this *ālayavijñāna* is precisely the characteristic of the objective referent for the view of self and the grasping at a self, which are dependent upon the afflicted mind.

If these distinct aspects of the ālayavijñāna as objects did not exist, then the grasping at a self within the afflicted manas—which has the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as its cause—would be unable to establish its objective referent.
It should be understood that this is the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
The treatise says:

Regarding the distinctions among these characteristics, it means that this very consciousness possesses both common characteristics (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) and non-common characteristics (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*), as well as the characteristic of seeds for the production of sensationless states (*anupabhoga-janman-bīja-lakṣaṇa*) and the characteristic of seeds for the production of states involving sensation (*upabhoga-janman-bīja-lakṣaṇa*), and so forth.
The commentary states:

There are many categories of distinctions in characteristics; that is to say, within these there are common characteristics and uncommon characteristics, as well as characteristics that lack the seeds for rebirth and characteristics that possess the seeds for rebirth, and so forth.
This is a brief enumeration; it shall be explained in detail later.
The Treatise says:
"The common characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) refers to the seeds of the receptacle world (bhājana-loka)."
The specific characteristic (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the seeds of the individual internal bases (*ādhyātmika-āyatana*).
The common characteristic (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) is the seed for birth without sensation (*vedanā*), whereas the specific characteristic is the seed for birth with sensation.
When the antidote arises, only that which is to be countered by its specific characteristic (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) is extinguished;
however, that which is common to others (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) is maintained by the conceptualizations of others, and thus only the pure aspect is perceived.
Just as yogins have various resolute convictions (*adhimukti*) regarding a single object, all that is seen through their true seeds (*tattva-bīja*) is established.
Regarding this, there are two verses:
"Difficult to sever and difficult to fully know, These should be known as common fetters;
The mind of the yogin differs [from others] Because external signs are so vast."
Although the pure does not cease, one perceives purity therein;
furthermore, the pure buddha-fields exist because the Buddha perceives them as pure.
There is another verse that, in response to what was cited previously, establishes that various resolute convictions (*adhimukti*) and various perceptions are all validly established.
Yogins, with respect to a single object, have various and differing resolute convictions;
thus, their various perceptions are all established, and we know that what is apprehended exists only as consciousness.
If this did not exist, the various distinctions in the arising of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) and the sentient world (*sattva-loka*) would be impossible to establish.
The commentary states:
In this context, if the *ālaya-vijñāna* were the causal substance for the common receptacle world of all sentient beings, it would be that which lacks seeds for the production of rebirth.
If the ālayavijñāna were the causal substance for the individual and unique bases such as form and so forth, it would then possess seeds for the production of sensation.
If one were to exclude such an ālayavijñāna characterized by commonality, the receptacle world—the cause for the collective enjoyment of all sentient beings—could not come into existence.
Likewise, if one were to exclude the second, unique ālayavijñāna, the world of sentient beings would also fail to be established;
consequently, they would have to be born like wood or stone.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, there are the characteristics of heaviness and rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*) and the characteristics of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
As for the characteristic of heaviness and rigidity, it refers to the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
The characteristic of pliancy refers to the seeds of contaminated wholesome dharmas.
If these were absent, the resultant maturation would lack functional capacity; thus, the distinction of the basis that possesses such functional capacity could not be established.
Furthermore, there are the characteristics of the exhaustion of feeling with remainder and the exhaustion of feeling without remainder.
The characteristic of the exhaustion of feeling with remainder refers to the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karma whose matured results (*vipāka-phala*) have already been realized.

The characteristic of the non-exhaustion of experience refers to the seeds of linguistic proliferation (*abhilāpa-vāsanā*), which are the seeds for the circulation of various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) from beginningless time.
If these did not exist, the exhaustion of the results of the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—already performed would be impossible to establish.
Furthermore, the arising of new linguistic designations (*nāma-vikalpa*) through perfuming (*vāsanā*) would be impossible.

Moreover, there is the characteristic of being illustrated by analogies; that is to say, this ālayavijñāna is illustrated by the analogies of a magical illusion (*māyā*), a mirage (*marīci*), a dream (*svapna*), and a visual impairment (*timira*).
If this were non-existent, then because it would lack the seeds of unreal imagination, the correspondence with inverted conditions could not be established.

Furthermore, there are the characteristics of being complete and the characteristics of being incomplete: those who are bound by all fetters are said to possess the characteristics of completeness, while those in the world who have abandoned desire are said to possess the characteristics of diminution.

Those who are śrāvakas in training and bodhisattvas are termed "those whose portion [of the afflictions] has been eternally uprooted"; arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and all tathāgatas are termed "those whose afflictive obstructions have been entirely and eternally uprooted," and "those whose afflictive and cognitive obstructions have been entirely and eternally uprooted," as appropriate to each case.
If this did not exist, the sequential cessation of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) would be impossible.
The commentary states:
"The characteristic of *dausthulya* (dysfunction) refers to the lack of functional capacity within the basis (*āśraya*)."
The characteristic of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) refers to the capacity within the basis [of consciousness].

If there were no characteristic of the exhaustion of experience (*vedanā-kṣaya*), then the Ālayavijñāna, having repeatedly performed both wholesome and unwholesome karma, would be unable to achieve the exhaustion of its results through experience.

Regarding the statement that "the seeds of the perfuming of names and phrases are characterized by inexhaustibility," this has already been explained in the section on the distinctions of the perfuming of names and phrases.

Regarding the phrase "because they are the seeds for the circulation of various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) from beginningless time," this means they are the common causes for verbal discourse from beginningless time.
If such an ālayavijñāna did not exist, the arising of the newly produced perfumations of names and phrases would be impossible.
Why? Because if there were no prior perfumations, the present names and phrases would likewise not exist.
If something were originally non-existent in the world, it would be illogical for that which was originally non-existent to come into being now.
As for the characteristic of the simile: just as, due to causes such as magical illusions and the like, there can arise the appearance of inverted conditions, such as elephants and so forth.

The ālayavijñāna is likewise: by virtue of the characteristics of the aforementioned similes, because it contains the seeds of unreal pervasive conceptualization, it possesses the characteristic of inverted conditions.
If this did not exist, the correspondence with inverted conditions could not be established.
The treatise asks:
For what reason do wholesome and unwholesome dharmas produce maturation, while their maturation fruit is unobscured-neutral?

Because the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) is unobscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), it is not mutually contradictory with the wholesome or the unwholesome; for the wholesome and the unwholesome are mutually contradictory.

If the maturation fruit were of a wholesome or unwholesome nature, the process of the cessation of affliction (*saṃkleśa-pratipraśrabdhi*) could not be established. Therefore, the maturation consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is exclusively unobscured and indeterminate.
The commentary states:

Regarding "unobscured-unspecified" (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), here "unobscured" refers to the absence of defilement; thus, that which is both undefiled and unspecified is called "unobscured-unspecified. This is not like the afflictions produced in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), which, though unwholesome (*akuśala*), are designated as unspecified.

If the cessation of defilement through the nature of maturation fruits being both wholesome and unwholesome were not possible, then because the wholesome would give rise to further wholesome and the unwholesome to further unwholesome, the cycle of birth and death would have no end; for the defilement of cyclic existence extends even to wholesome states associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Scroll Three;
Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Scroll Four.
Composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Part Three: The Characteristics of the Knowable (Jñeyalakṣaṇa), Section One. The Treatise says:
The basis of the knowable has already been explained.
Furthermore, how should the characteristics of the knowable be viewed?
Briefly, there are three kinds:
first, the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*); second, the imputed nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*); and third, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*).
The commentary states:
These words are spoken based on the characteristics of the objects of knowledge (*jñeyalakṣaṇa*).
"Briefly" means essentially.
The treatise says:
Among these, what is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)?
It refers to all consciousnesses comprised within false discrimination, which have the ālayavijñāna as their seed.
What, then, are these? They are:

the consciousness of the body, the consciousness of the self as the possessor of the body, the consciousness of the experiencer, the consciousness of that which is experienced, the consciousness of that which experiences, the consciousness of time, the consciousness of number, the consciousness of place, the consciousness of verbal expression, the consciousness of the distinction between self and others, and the consciousness of death and rebirth in good and evil destinies.

Among these, the consciousness of the body, the consciousness of the self, the consciousness of the experiencer, the consciousness of that which is experienced, the consciousness of the experiencer thereof, the consciousness of time, the consciousness of number, the consciousness of place, and the consciousness of verbal expression arise from the seeds of the habitual perfuming of names and conventions.
If it is the consciousness of the distinction between self and other, this arises from the seeds of the perfuming of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
If it is the consciousness of death and birth in the happy or miserable realms, this arises from the seeds of the perfuming of the links of existence (*bhava-aṅga*).

By means of these various consciousnesses, all that is comprised within the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*)—the false conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa*) subsumed under the defilements of all realms and destinies—is made manifest.

These consciousnesses are all comprised within false conceptualization, have the nature of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*), and serve as the basis for the manifestation of non-existent, unreal objects; this is called the dependent nature.

The commentary states: Regarding "the various consciousnesses subsumed under false discrimination," this means that these various consciousnesses take false discrimination as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

"Body, the possessor of the body, the experiencer, and the consciousness"—here, "body" refers to the five elements (*dhātu*) beginning with the eye; "possessor of the body" refers to the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*); "experiencer" refers to the mind element (*mano-dhātu*); "the consciousness of what is experienced" refers to the six external objects (*viṣaya*) such as form; "the consciousness of the experiencer" refers to the six consciousness elements (*vijñāna-dhātu*); "consciousness of time" refers to the nature of the uninterrupted continuity of birth and death; "consciousness of number" refers to the nature of calculation; "consciousness of place" refers to the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*); and "consciousness of discourse" refers to the four kinds of discourse: seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.

All such consciousnesses take as their cause the specific distinctions in the habitual tendencies of names and expressions (nāma-vyañjana-vāsanā) as explained in the section on the "basis of the knowable" (jñeya-āśraya).

As for the consciousness that distinguishes between self and others, it refers to the distinction of the basis; this takes as its cause the specific distinctions in the habitual tendencies of the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi-vāsanā) previously mentioned.

Regarding the consciousness of death and birth in the good and bad realms of existence: this refers to the various distinctions among the destinies of birth and death, which arise from the seeds differentiated by the previously mentioned perfuming of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
"By these various consciousnesses" refers to the various consciousnesses explained immediately preceding.

"Encompassed by the defilements of all realms and destinies" means that they fall within the defilements of the three realms and five destinies; because they are of the same nature as those [defilements], they are said to be "encompassed."
The dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*) means that the dependent nature constitutes its essence, such that false discrimination (*abhūta-parikalpa*) manifests in all its forms.

Regarding the statement that these various consciousnesses are all comprised within false discrimination and have the nature of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*): it means that because these various consciousnesses are the very self-nature of false discrimination, they are said to be "comprised" [within it]; they are non-existent and are the manifestation of what is not a real object.
The "basis" refers to the cause for the manifestation of that which is non-existent and lacks true reality.
It is called "non-existent" because it is not real; just as the self as it is grasped does not exist, it is called "that which lacks true reality" because it is the object of apprehension.
This means that while there is no such self as it truly exists, it nevertheless appears as a self.
Regarding the term "basis" (*āśraya*), it refers to the basis of manifestation, which carries the sense of being the cause.
This is precisely what is called the *paratantra-lakṣaṇa* (the dependent nature).
The treatise says:
What herein is the characteristic of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva)?
It refers to that which appears as an object within what is merely consciousness, despite the absence of any external object.
The commentary states:
"Regarding 'that which lacks an object' (anartha), this means that there is no grasped object, as it truly lacks selfhood.

'Existing only within consciousness' (vijñaptimātra) means that within a consciousness that appears as an object despite lacking a real object, it is like a consciousness that manifests as if it were a self."
"Appearing as an object" means appearing with the semblance of an apprehended object; it is like the appearance of a self where, in reality, there is no self.
The treatise asks:
What herein is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)?
This means that within that very dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*), there is the eternal absence of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) regarding the appearance of objects.
The commentary explains:

Within the cause for the manifestation of what is not truly existent—that is, the unreal object—there is an eternal absence of an intrinsic nature because the appearance of the semblance of an object is in fact non-existent. This is like the semblance of a self (*ātman*): although it is eternally non-existent, the notion of "self" still exists.
The treatise says:
Among these, the body, the sense of self, and the perceiving consciousness should be understood as the six internal bases, such as the eye and so forth.
The consciousness of what is experienced should be understood as the six external bases, such as form and so forth.

That which is capable of receiving [objects] is the consciousness; one should know that this is precisely the six consciousness-elements (ṣaḍ-vijñāna-dhātu), such as the eye-consciousness and so forth.
One should know that all other consciousnesses are merely specific distinctions of these [six].
Furthermore, all these consciousnesses consist solely of consciousness itself, for they are entirely devoid of external objects.
By what analogy is this demonstrated?
It should be understood that dreams and the like serve as the analogies.

That is to say, just as in a dream there is no external object whatsoever, but only consciousness alone; although various forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, houses, forests, lands, and mountains appear as reflections of objects, there is in fact no object at all within them.

By means of these metaphors, one should understand accordingly that at all times and in all places there is only consciousness; this should be understood through the use of such terms as "and so forth.
Furthermore, there are other metaphors, such as illusions, mirages, and cataracts.
If, during the waking state, at all times and in all places, everything is like a dream and so forth—
consisting of nothing but consciousness— then one is like someone awakened from a dream, who realizes that within the dream there was nothing but consciousness.
Why does it not function in this way during the waking state?
True wisdom functions in this very same way during the waking state.
Just as this awareness does not function while one is dreaming, but only functions upon awakening from the dream, so it is here.
In this way, as long as one has not yet attained the awakening of true wisdom, this realization does not arise; only upon attaining the awakening of true wisdom does this realization arise.
For those who have not yet attained the awakening of true wisdom, how can they infer [the nature of reality] within the context of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only)?
This should be understood through both scripture and reasoning.
Regarding scripture, as the Bhagavān stated in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*: "These three realms are mind-only."
Furthermore, the Blessed One’s *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* also speaks in this way; that is, in that sūtra, the Bodhisattva Maitreya asks the Bhagavān:
"Regarding the images that are the objects of various samādhis, should one say they are different from this mind, or should one say they are not different?"
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"One should say they are not different. Why is this?"
"Because those images are nothing but consciousness, I say that the object of cognition is merely what is manifested by consciousness.
World-Honored One,
if the image traversed in samādhi is not different from this mind, how can this mind take itself as its own object?"
Maitreya! There is not even the slightest dharma that can apprehend another dharma.

However, when this very mind arises in such a manner, there appears an image corresponding to it, just as when a physical object serves as a condition, one sees the object itself yet thinks, "I am now seeing an image," and believes that an image distinct from the object has appeared before one's sight.
This mind is also like this: when it arises in such a manner, there appears a reflection that seems similar yet distinct.
By this very teaching, the underlying principle is also made manifest. Why is this so?

Within the state of meditative concentration, whatever cognizable images such as bluish discoloration (vinīlaka) one perceives, none of them are distinct entities separate from the bluish discoloration itself; rather, one sees only one's own mind.
By this reasoning, a bodhisattva should infer that within all consciousnesses there is only consciousness and no external objects.
Furthermore, regarding such things as the livid corpse and so forth, it is not a memory-consciousness (*smṛtivijñāna*) that perceives the object of observation appearing before one.

Since the two types of recollective consciousness produced through hearing and reflection also take the past as their object, the images that appear therein are established as being "consciousness-only.
By means of this inference, although a bodhisattva has not yet attained the awakening of true wisdom, they should be able to infer the nature of consciousness-only.
The commentary states:
This [reality] is consciousness-only, as demonstrated by scripture.
As the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* says: "Thus, these three realms are all mind-only."

In the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, when I state that "the objects of consciousness are manifested solely by consciousness," this means that the objects of consciousness are manifested solely by consciousness and have no separate objective referents.

To raise the term "consciousness" once more is to clarify that what I have taught is that the object of consciousness is determined by consciousness itself; it is manifested as representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and possesses no separate substantial entity.
As for the phrase "when this very mind arises in such a manner," it means when it arises from this specific category [of seeds].

Regarding the appearance of what seems to be distinct from the object seen: this refers to that which appears as a clearly manifest apprehended object, seemingly separate from consciousness, within the sphere of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "within such [objects] as the bluish discoloration (*vinīlaka*), it is not a memory-consciousness (*smṛti-vijñāna*) that sees the perceived object appearing before one": this means that the bluish discoloration and so forth are images within the range of *samādhi*, and are not a memory-consciousness.
Because of this, one does not remain in that same location; rather, one recollects exactly as it was previously experienced, for this dwelling is present and seen with clarity.
What is seen by the consciousness of recollection is dim, whereas what is seen by this present dwelling is distinct.

If someone were further to claim that, just as in the case of the wisdoms of hearing and reflection, although the object has passed away due to repeated practice, it arises just as before as soon as one directs the attention toward it—
and that this [wisdom of cultivation] is likewise so.

Since the objects of both the wisdoms of hearing and reflection have already passed away and lack any substantial entity in the present, when they arise again within that absence of entity, they do so merely as reflections of consciousness appearing as if they were those very objects.

The wisdoms derived from hearing and reflection do not take as their objects past realms that have already ceased; therefore, the fact that there are no external objects of apprehension is further demonstrated by this, and the principle is thus established.
The treatise states:

Having thus explained the various consciousnesses through analogies such as dreams and the like, it can be established that within this very context, the visual consciousness and other such consciousnesses are but consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Since the various consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, possess form, how can it be seen that they too are "only consciousness"?
This is also explained, as before, by means of scripture and reasoning.
The commentary states:
The consciousnesses such as visual consciousness and so forth are all non-material (*arūpin*), and thus can be established as mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*);
yet since the eye-consciousness and other such consciousnesses possess materiality (*rūpin*), how can they be mere consciousness?

This too is as previously explained through scripture and reasoning: these eye-consciousnesses and others, as demonstrated by the aforementioned scriptural citations and logical arguments, are likewise established as mere consciousness.
The treatise says:
If these various consciousnesses are also in essence consciousness, why do they manifest as having the nature of form?
Because they persist in a uniform manner, remaining stable and evolving in a continuum, serving as the basis for various defiled phenomena such as the inverted views.
If it were not so, the inversion of perceiving meaning where there is no meaning could not occur.
If this were absent, the defilements of the two obstructions—those of afflictions and those of the cognizable—could not exist.
If this did not exist, then all pure phenomena would likewise not exist.
Therefore, the various consciousnesses should evolve in this manner.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
The confused appearance and the confused substance should be admitted as being both consciousness of form and consciousness not of form;
if one does not exist, the other likewise does not exist.
Commentary:

Regarding "a single class that persists and evolves in continuity": it is called "a single class" because its members are similar; it is said to be "persisting" because it remains for a long duration.
All material consciousnesses evolve in a continuous stream that is similar over a long period of time.

"Perverted views and so forth" refers to the inclusion of all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*), which serve as the causal nature for the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
"As a basis" means serving as their causal nature.
If those various consciousnesses were devoid of such transformations, the cognitive inversion that perceives objects where there are no objects would be impossible.

If this [inversion] did not exist, then neither the various defiled phenomena of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) nor the various defiled phenomena of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) could exist.
In this verse, the following meaning is revealed:

the deceptive appearance (*bhrānti-nimitta*) and the deceptive essence (*bhrānti-svabhāva*) are, respectively, asserted to be the consciousness of form (*rūpa-vijñāna*) and the consciousness that is not form (*arūpa-vijñāna*).
Herein, the deceptive appearance is itself the cause of deception, having the consciousness of form as its essence.
The essence of confusion is precisely the various formless consciousnesses.
If the cause of the confusion of form-consciousness did not exist, the result of formless consciousness would likewise not exist.
The treatise says:

For what reason do the body, the possessor of the body, the consciousness of the experiencer, the consciousness of the experienced, and the consciousness of the experiencer all exist together in a state of union within every body?
This is because they can fully accomplish birth, experience, and manifestation.
For what reason do the various consciousnesses, such as those of time and so forth, evolve in their distinct forms?

It is because the flow of saṃsāra has been uninterrupted since beginningless time; because the realm of sentient beings is immeasurable; because the receptacle worlds are immeasurable; because the successive verbal expressions regarding all activities are immeasurable; because the individual apprehension and experience of distinctions are immeasurable; because the experience of the maturation of the fruits of karma—whether desirable or undesirable—is immeasurable; and because the various distinctions of death and birth experienced are immeasurable.
The commentary states:
It is for the sake of bringing about the complete enjoyment [of objects] by one's own self.

The three consciousnesses—the body (*kāya*), the possessor of the body (*kāyika*), and the experiencer (*vedaka*)—are admitted to exist simultaneously within all bodies; because they arise together in harmony at one time, they are called "simultaneous" (*sahabhū*).
Regarding the phrase "because it is that which is manifested," this refers to its nature as the cause.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, how are these various consciousnesses established so as to constitute the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*)?
Briefly, it is established by three characteristics:
first, by consciousness-only, because there are no external objects;
second, by the nature of duality, because there is a distinction between the two types of consciousness, namely the aspect (nimitta) and the seeing (darśana).
Third, it is by way of variety, because it arises with various modes of appearance (*ākāra*). Why is this so?

Because all these consciousnesses lack external objects, they are established as "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*); yet, because they possess the aspects (*nimitta*) and the seeing [faculty] (*darśana*), they are established as being twofold.

If the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth take the consciousnesses of form and so forth as their aspect (*nimitta*), and take the cognition of the eye-consciousness as their vision (*darśana*), up to taking the cognition of the body-consciousness as their vision;
and if it is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it takes everything from the eye as its first [object] to dharmas as its last.

The various consciousnesses constitute the aspect (nimitta), while the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) constitutes the seeing (darśana); this is because this mental consciousness possesses discrimination and arises appearing as all the [other] consciousnesses.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"The two kinds of variety within consciousness— The meditator’s mind can enter them;
By realizing and entering 'mind-only,' One is likewise able to subdue and transcend them."
The commentary states:
Herein, both the prose and the verse demonstrate that consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) is established by way of three aspects.
Within the prose, regarding "by way of consciousness-only": because there is only consciousness, all cognitions are merely consciousness, since the objects of cognition do not exist.

Regarding "by way of the two natures": because the aspects (*nimitta*) and the vision (*darśana*) are established within a single consciousness, that very same consciousness has one part become the aspect and the second part become the vision.

Regarding the various consciousnesses such as the eye-consciousness and so forth, they are established as having these two natures; that is to say, upon a single consciousness, according to what is appropriate, one part transforms into the appearance of various objects, while the second part transforms into the various subjects that grasp them.

If we consider it in terms of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), then with the visual consciousness as the first and the consciousness of phenomena (*dharmavijñāna*) as the last, all these [sensory] consciousnesses constitute the "aspect" (*nimitta*), while the mental consciousness constitutes the "seeing" (*darśana*). This is because the mental consciousness performs universal conceptualization and arises appearing as all the other consciousnesses.

Furthermore, among these three [consciousnesses], it is only with respect to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that one establishes the "various aspects" (*nānākāra*), because its apprehended objects are indeterminate.

The objects of the other consciousnesses are determinate and lack discrimination, whereas the mental consciousness is discriminative; therefore, it is only here that the third aspect—the various aspects of the perceived—is established. Consequently, it is within this mental consciousness that the doctrine of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) is fully established.
Regarding the ability to enter *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) within the verses: it is because one realizes that the apprehended objects (*grāhya-artha*) are eternally non-existent.
Regarding the ability to enter the "two": it is because one realizes that this consciousness possesses both the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*).
"Capable of entering into various [appearances]" means that this consciousness arises manifesting as various semblances.
"The intention of the observer" refers to the underlying purpose of all yogic practitioners.
Question:
Into what does one awaken and enter?
Answer:
By entering into the realization that there is only mind, one is also able to suppress and abandon that [duality].
If one can enter into the realization that there is only mind and no external objects whatsoever, then one is likewise able to suppress and abandon those [objects].
Since there is no object to be grasped, how can there be a mind that grasps?
The teachings on entering the two natures and entering the manifold are all intended to establish the reason for entering *vijñapti-mātratā* (consciousness-only);
other meanings are similar.
The Treatise says:

Furthermore, within this context, there is a class of masters who maintain that there is a single mental consciousness which, as it functions in dependence upon various bases, receives their respective names—just as mental action (manas-karman) is designated by the names "bodily action" (kāya-karman) and "vocal action" (vāk-karman).
The commentary states:
A certain class of Bodhisattvas wishes to maintain that there is only a single substance of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). They further establish and demonstrate this in sequence as follows:

Just as what is called "mental action" (*manaskarman*) is designated as "bodily action" (*kāyakarman*) and "vocal action" (*vākkarman*), so too a single mental volition (*cetanā*), when it operates through the door of the body, receives the designation "bodily action," and when it operates through the door of speech, receives the designation "vocal action"; yet, it remains fundamentally mental action.

Consciousness is likewise; although it is a single entity, when it functions in dependence upon the eye, it receives the name "eye-consciousness," and so on, until when it functions in dependence upon the body, it receives the name "body-consciousness."
There is no other consciousness apart from the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), except for the distinct existence of the *ālayavijñāna*.
The treatise states:
Furthermore, when it evolves upon all bases, two kinds of images appear as various characteristics; namely, the image resembling objects and the image of conceptualization.

Furthermore, in all places, it also manifests as an image resembling the tangible; within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), this very mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) relies upon the body, just as the other material sense-faculties rely upon the body.
The commentary states:
Some may raise this objection:
"Since the various faculties, such as the eye, lack discrimination, the mental consciousness that functions in dependence upon them should likewise be non-discriminative."
Just as the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) serves as the basis for defilement and causes defilement to proceed, so too should this [storehouse consciousness] be understood.
Therefore, the subsequent explanation states:
"Furthermore, when it evolves upon all bases, two kinds of images appear that resemble various characteristics; namely, the image of the object alone and the image of conceptualization."
In this context, "all bases" refers to the bases such as the eye and so forth.
"The two images that manifest resembling various characteristics" refers to the two phrases: the image resembling the object and the conceptualized image.

By these two phrases, it is taught that there is only a single consciousness: one part manifests as the images of objects alone, while the second part discriminates the arising of the characteristics of those objects; therefore, what was stated previously is without fault.

Furthermore, in all instances, it arises as a semblance of a tangible object-image; that is to say, when one is in a state of meditative concentration where the five consciousnesses are absent, there arises an internal experience within the physical body, just as other material sense-faculties depend upon the body—just as the other material sense-faculties, such as the eye and so forth, depend upon the body.
Because these faculties depend upon the body, they are able to produce benefit or harm to their own basis;
the mental consciousness is likewise, and it should be understood that because it depends upon the body, it can effect transformations within the body.

Furthermore, there is another meaning: just as the body-faculty (kāyendriya) relies upon the body, when an external object of touch is present before it, the body-faculty arises as if possessing the characteristics of that which is touched.
Just as when this [sensation] arises, it can produce benefit or harm for its own physical basis, so too is it with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*):
when it arises in the likeness of an image of what was touched, depending upon the body, it can produce benefit or harm for that very body which serves as its support.
The treatise states:
Regarding this, there is a verse:
That which travels far and wanders alone, Bodiless, it slumbers in the cave.
"One who tames this mind so difficult to tame—him I call a true Brahmin.
The commentary states:
Those Bodhisattvas, in order to establish this meaning, cite a verse from the Āgama as proof.
It is called "far-reaching" because it is able to take all objects of cognition as its objective support.
It is called "solitary" because there is no second [entity].
It is called "bodiless" because it is detached from the body.
"Dormant in the cave" means dwelling within the cave of the body.
"To tame this" means to exercise mastery over it.
"The mind difficult to tame" refers to its nature being violent and evil.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, as the Sūtra states:
"The objects traversed by these five faculties are each received by the mind; the mind is their support."
The commentary states:
Furthermore, other teachings are cited to establish this meaning.

Regarding the statement that "the mind is able to individually experience the objects traversed by these five faculties," the term "objects" (*viṣaya*) refers to that which is traversed by the various faculties.
Such objects are each received by the respective mental consciousnesses, because they are all capable of discerning all phenomena.
Because each one individually experiences them, they are called "each capable of receiving."
The mind is the basis for those [faculties] because it is the generative cause of those various faculties; for if the mind is distracted, they do not arise.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, as stated among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the six groups of consciousness are all called the mind base (*manāyatana*).
The commentary states:

Furthermore, there is scriptural authority that can prove this point, namely, that all six groups of consciousness are designated as "mind" (*manas*), with no other name for consciousness being given.

Since it is taught by the Noble Ones that all six groups of consciousness constitute the sense-base of mind (*mana-āyatana*), one thereby knows that there is only mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*).
The treatise states:

Where the *ālaya-vijñāna* is established as the "object-consciousness" (*artha-vijñapti*), it should be understood that all other consciousnesses therein are its "image-consciousness" (*nimitta-vijñapti*), while the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) and its support are its "perceiving-consciousness" (*darśana-vijñapti*).

Because that object-aspect consciousness (*nimitta-vijñāna*) serves as the causal condition for the arising of this seeing-consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*), when it appears as an object, it is able to perform the function of being the basis for the arising of the seeing-consciousness.
This is what is called establishing the various consciousnesses as the nature of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*).
The commentary states:
Within the *ālaya-vijñāna*, one may also establish the two aspects of the "perceiving" (*darśana*) and the "perceived" (*nimitta*) consciousnesses.

That is to say, the *ālaya-vijñāna* takes that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and its support as its perceiving consciousness, while the visual and other sensory consciousnesses constitute its perceived consciousness, because all phenomena are nothing but consciousness.
"Those consciousnesses that have those as their objects" refers to the various consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth.

"Because they are the objective conditions for the arising of this seeing-consciousness" means they are the causes for the arising of seeing; they are called the causes for the arising of seeing by virtue of their nature as objects of perception (*ālambana*).

Regarding the statement that "when appearing as an object, it can perform the function of being the basis for the arising of the perceiving consciousness": because it is capable of being seen by that [consciousness], it is called the "perceiving consciousness" (*darśana-vijñāna*).

When this very perceiving consciousness appears as an object, those various aspect-consciousnesses (*nimitta-vijñānas*) serve as the cause for the uninterrupted continuity and abiding of both the aspect-consciousness and the perceiving consciousness; therefore, they are said to perform the function of being the "basis for arising."
The treatise says:
How can it be known that various objects appear before one with clear manifestation yet are not existent?
As the Blessed One said:
If bodhisattvas accomplish four dharmas, they are able to realize accordingly that all is representation-only and that external objects do not exist at all.

First, they accomplish the wisdom of the characteristics of contradictory cognitions; for example, hungry ghosts, animals, gods, and humans perceive the same single object, yet there are differences in what each of them cognizes.

Second, there is the realization that consciousness can be perceived even when it lacks an objective referent (*ālambana*), because objects are apprehended within the conditions of the past, the future, dreams, and reflections.

Third, there is the realization that one should abandon effortful activity to attain non-erroneous knowledge; for if consciousness were to perceive objects as having real external referents, it would necessarily be erroneous, whereas true knowledge is attained not through effort but by its very nature.
Fourth is the accomplishment of the sublime wisdom that functions in accordance with the three kinds of superior wisdom.
What are these three?

First, for all Bodhisattvas who have attained mastery over the mind and have attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), objects appear in accordance with the power of their resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
Second, for those who have attained the cultivation of the dharma-contemplation of śamatha, all objects appear as soon as they direct their attention.
Third, for those who have already attained non-conceptual wisdom, when non-conceptual wisdom is present before them, no objects at all appear.

By means of these three types of superior wisdom that function in accordance with reality, as well as the three types of causal conditions previously explained, the principles regarding what is meaningful and what is meaningless are established.
The commentary states:
"Knowledge of the characteristics of contradictory cognitions" means being able to understand the objective characteristics of the objects apprehended by contradictory cognitions.

"Knowledge that cognitions are currently perceived even though they lack an object" means clearly seeing that cognitions arise despite the absence of an object, as in the case of the past and so forth.

Regarding "the non-erroneous wisdom that should be free from effort": this means that if one understands that whatever object appears exactly as it manifests is truly existent, then, without the need to give rise to an antidote, non-erroneous wisdom will be spontaneously accomplished.

"Excellently knowing that which accords with the three kinds of superior knowledge" means being able to understand the meaning of that which accords with the objects of the three kinds of superior knowledge.
"Attaining mastery over the mind" means attaining a mind that is pliant, compliant, and capable.
"Those who have attained meditative concentration" refers to the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others who have already attained dhyāna.
"Various objects appear according to the power of resolute conviction" means that if one wishes for earth to become water, it becomes so as desired; the same applies to fire and the other elements.

One who has attained *śamatha* and has acquired the cultivation of the observation of phenomena (*dharmavipaśyanā*) through *samādhi*, applies diligent investigation to the sūtras and other scriptures.

As soon as one directs the attention (*manasikāra*), various objects appear; according to whichever single object one directs the attention toward, such and such a variety of objective images appears accordingly.

Regarding the statement that when non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is present, no objects whatsoever appear: if objects existed as they appear, then such things would exist in reality, and thus non-conceptual wisdom could not exist.
If non-conceptual wisdom were substantially existent, one must necessarily admit that all objects are non-existent.
The treatise says:
If the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is in reality nothing but consciousness, it is the basis upon which objects appear as if they were real.
How is it established as the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)?
For what reasons and conditions is it called the dependent nature?
It is produced from seeds of its own habitual perfuming; because it arises in dependence upon other conditions, it is called the dependent nature.
Because it lacks the capacity to abide spontaneously after the moment of its arising, it is called *paratantra-svabhāva* (the dependent nature).
The commentary explains:

"That which is truly the basis for the manifestation of objects as if they were real" means that while objects do not truly exist, there is only consciousness; this very consciousness, which serves as the cause for the manifestation of those apparent objects, is termed *paratantra*.
Regarding the question, "How is it established as the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)?", this asks about its own internal constitution.
Regarding the question, "For what reason and by what conditions is it called the dependent nature?", this asks for the sake of explaining it to others.
It is called the dependent nature because it arises from its own causes, and having arisen, it lacks the capacity to remain stable even for a moment.
One should personally internalize this and also explain it to others.
The treatise states:
If the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) depends upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it is in reality non-existent, yet it manifests as if it were an object.
How is it established as the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)?
For what reasons and conditions is it called the thoroughly imagined nature?

Because it is the appearance produced by the inverted conceptualization of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) through immeasurable modes of activity, it is therefore called the thoroughly imagined nature.

Their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) do not truly exist; only that which is grasped through pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) is obtainable. Therefore, it is called "the thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita*).
The commentary states:
"Based upon the dependent-arising" (*paratantra*) means based upon consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
"Truly non-existent" means that there is truly no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"Appearing as an object" means that only the appearance as an object is perceived.
As for "how" and "why," these follow what was stated immediately above.
"Immeasurable modes of activity" refers to the modes of activity of all objective spheres.
"The mental consciousness as pervasive conceptualization" means that the mental consciousness itself is designated as pervasive conceptualization.
The "characteristic of arising from inversion" refers to that which can produce the characteristic of an object of perception that is false and inverted.
"Its own-characteristic is truly non-existent" means that its substantial entity is truly non-existent.
"Only that which is grasped by the parikalpita-svabhāva can be apprehended" means that only that which is grasped by the deluded consciousness can be apprehended.
The treatise states:
"If it is the pariniṣpanna-svabhāva, it is the eternal absence of any characteristic of the parikalpita-svabhāva."
How is it established as the thoroughly perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)?
For what reasons and conditions is it called the thoroughly perfected nature?
It is called the thoroughly perfected nature because of its unchanging character (*avikāritva*).

Furthermore, because it is the nature of the pure object of focus and because it is the most supreme among all wholesome dharmas, it is called "perfected reality" (pariniṣpanna) in the sense of being supreme.
The commentary explains:
"That which is the eternal non-existence of the characteristics of the imagined nature" means that the imagined nature has non-existence as its very essence.
Regarding "what" and "why" and so forth, these have already been explained previously in the section on the *paratantra-svabhāva*.
"By virtue of being unchanging" means having no deceptive nature, just as [the term] "non-deceptive nature" implies.
Furthermore, because it is the object of purification and because it is the most supreme among all wholesome dharmas, it is called "perfected reality" (*pariniṣpanna*) in the sense of being supreme.
That is to say, it is called "perfected reality" because it is the object of purification and because it is of the nature of supreme excellence.
The treatise says:

Furthermore, there must be that which performs the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) and that which is the object of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpya*), for the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) to be established.
In this context, what is that which performs the pervasive conceptualization?
What is that which is the object of pervasive conceptualization?
What is the nature of pervasive conceptual construction?
One should know that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is that which performs pervasive conceptualization, because it possesses discrimination.

Why is this so? Because this mental consciousness (manovijñāna) takes the habitual perfuming of its own names and expressions as its seeds, and also takes the habitual perfuming of the names and expressions of all [other] consciousnesses as its seeds; therefore, the mental consciousness evolves through infinite modes of conceptualization and engages in universal discrimination and deliberation regarding all things—hence it is called "universal imagination" (parikalpa).
Furthermore, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is called the "object of pervasive conceptualization" (*parikalpya*).
Moreover, that characteristic by which the dependent nature becomes the object of pervasive conceptualization is here termed the "imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
"By these characteristics" means "in this manner.
Furthermore, how does the pervasive imagination (parikalpa) engage in pervasive conceptualization?
What is its objective referent?
What characteristics are grasped?
By what is there attachment?
By what are words produced?
By means of what discourse?
What is it that is superimposed?

It refers to taking names as objects, grasping their characteristics within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), through the adherence of views, through the arising of speech via discursive thought (*vitarka*), and through the four kinds of discourse such as seeing and hearing; thus one engages in discourse and superimposes existence upon that which lacks objective reality. By this, the pervasive imagination (*parikalpa*) is able to perform its universal conceptualization.
The commentary states:

Furthermore, as for how the pervasive imagination (*parikalpa*) is able to engage in pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpayati*), it means that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is called the "pervasive imaginer," while the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is called the "object of pervasive conceptualization."
In order to demonstrate that it is by means of these categories that one performs pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*), it is further stated that "the object-condition is names" and so forth.

To "grasp the characteristics within the dependent nature" (*paratantra-svabhāva*) means that, within this very dependent nature, one grasps those characteristics by means of names such as "eye," and through grasping those characteristics, one performs pervasive conceptualization.
Regarding attachment through views: one adheres in accordance with the characteristics as they are grasped.
Regarding the arising of speech through discursive thought: based on what has been adhered to, one utters words through the cause of discursive thought.

Regarding the arising of discourse through the four kinds of verbal expression—seeing, hearing, and so forth—it refers to the four types of verbal expression consisting of what is seen, heard, sensed, and known, as spoken in speech, along with other forms of verbal expression.
To superimpose existence upon that which lacks objective reality is to grasp at an object where no object exists, just as it is expressed in speech.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, are these three natures different or not different?
One should say that they are neither different nor non-different.

That is to say, the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), by way of one perspective, becomes the dependent; this very same nature, by way of another perspective, becomes the imagined (parikalpita); and this very same nature, by way of yet another perspective, becomes the perfected (pariniṣpanna).
By what alternative perspective does this dependent nature become "dependent"?
Because it arises based on seeds that are dependently perfumed.
By what alternative perspective does this very same nature become "thoroughly imagined"?
Because it is the characteristic of the object of parikalpita (imagined construction), and because it is that which is thoroughly imagined by parikalpita—
by what alternative perspective does this very same intrinsic nature become the pariniṣpanna (perfected reality)?
Because that which is thus thoroughly imagined ultimately does not exist in such a manner.
The commentary explains:

"By virtue of being the characteristic of the object of thorough imagination" means that this mental consciousness is called "thorough imagination" (*parikalpa*); it is the nature of the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and the objective field (*ālambana*), capable of producing thorough imagination; therefore, it is also termed "the thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita*).

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because it is that which is thoroughly conceptualized by the pervasive imagination": the mental consciousness itself is termed "pervasive imagination" (parikalpa); it takes those appearances as its apprehended object (grāhya) and as that which is thoroughly conceptualized (parikalpya).
For this reason, the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is also called the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva).
It is "like that which is imagined," just as it is the object of the mental consciousness's imagination.

Regarding the phrase "because it ultimately does not exist in this way": since that which is the object of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) upon the basis of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpya*) is ultimately non-existent, by virtue of this meaning, this very nature constitutes the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The treatise says:
How many types does each of these three natures have?
Briefly stated, the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) has two types:
First, because it arises dependent upon seeds perfumed by others; second, because its nature as either afflicted or purified is not established independently of others.
Due to these two kinds of dependence, it is called "other-dependent" (*paratantra*).
The thoroughly imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) is also of two kinds:

first, because it is the thorough imagination of intrinsic nature; second, because it is the thorough imagination of specific distinctions. For these reasons, it is called the "thoroughly imagined nature."
The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) also has two types:
first, because it is the perfected nature by way of its own essence;
second, because it is the perfected nature by way of purity. It is on account of these that it constitutes the perfected nature.
The commentary states:

Regarding the phrase "because the natures of affliction and purification are not established," it means that this very *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) constitutes affliction when it is the object of universal conceptualization (*parikalpa*), and constitutes purification when it is free from such conceptual construction.
Because it consists of two parts, its unity is not established; therefore, it is called the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).

Regarding "because of the pervasive conceptualization of self-nature": this refers to, for example, the pervasive conceptualization of the eye and so forth as being the self-nature of the eye and so forth.

Regarding "due to the pervasive conceptualization of distinctions": this refers to how, with respect to the very nature of those [factors] such as the eye, one pervasively conceptualizes them as having infinite distinctions, such as being permanent or impermanent.
"Because it is the perfected nature by way of its intrinsic nature" refers to stained *tathatā*.
"Because it is the perfected nature by way of its purity" refers to stainless *tathatā*.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, there are four types of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*):

first, conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); second, conceptualization of specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*); third, conceptualization with awareness (*sa-vitarka*); and fourth, conceptualization without awareness (*a-vitarka*).
Those with discernment refer to those skilled in linguistic expression;
those without discernment refer to those unskilled in linguistic expression.
Thus, there are five further types of pervasive conceptualization:
First, the nature of the object as it is conceptually constructed based on the name, which means that such a name has such an object.
Second, the nature of the name as it is conceptually constructed based on the object, which means that such an object has such a name.
Third, based on names, one imaginatively constructs the intrinsic nature of names; that is, one imaginatively constructs names whose referents are not yet understood.
Fourth, based on referents, one imaginatively constructs the intrinsic nature of referents; that is, one imaginatively constructs referents whose names are not yet understood.

The fifth [point] relies on the two types of pervasive conceptualization and the two natures; that is, the pervasive conceptualization of "this name" and "this object," as well as their suchness (tathatā).
The commentary states:
Those skilled in terminology refer to those who understand terminology.
Those unskilled in terminology refer to those such as cattle and sheep; although they possess discrimination, they are unable to comprehend written characters.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, there are briefly ten types that comprehensively subsume all forms of conceptualization (*vikalpa*):
first, fundamental conceptualization, which refers to the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
Second is the discrimination of the characteristics of the object, which refers to the consciousnesses of form and so forth.
Third is the discrimination of the manifesting characteristics, which refers to the eye-consciousness and so forth, together with their supporting consciousnesses.
