Fourth is the discrimination of the transformation of the characteristics of the object, which refers to transformations such as aging and so forth; transformations of pleasant feelings and so forth; transformations of greed and so forth; transformations due to affliction, seasonal changes, and the passage of time; transformations among the various destinies such as the hells; and transformations among the various realms such as the desire realm.
Fifth is the discrimination of manifesting characteristics as change, which refers to all the various modes of change as previously described.
Sixth is the discrimination induced by others, which refers to the discrimination arising from hearing categories of non-orthodox teachings as well as hearing categories of orthodox teachings.
Seventh is improper conceptualization, which refers to the conceptualization arising from hearing non-orthodox teachings, as in the case of various non-Buddhist outsiders.
Eighth is proper conceptualization, which refers to the conceptualization arising from hearing the true Dharma within the authentic teaching.

Ninth is the discrimination of clinging, which refers to the category of improper mental attention (ayoniśomanasikāra), rooted in the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and associated with the sixty-two types of speculative views (dṛṣṭigata).
The ten types of discursive conceptualization refer to the ten kinds of conceptualization of bodhisattvas.
The commentary states:
"Briefly summarized, all conceptualizations comprise ten types" is the general heading, which will be explained in detail hereafter.
Fundamental discrimination refers to the ālayavijñāna, which is the root of all discriminations, and whose own essence is also discrimination.
Discrimination of objective signs refers to the discrimination arising from the objective signs of the consciousnesses of form and so forth.

Discrimination of manifested images refers to the discrimination arising from the visual consciousness and so forth, together with their supporting consciousnesses, which manifest as images resembling those objects of perception.
Because it either possesses an object of discrimination or acts as a subject of discrimination, it is called "discrimination of the perceived image."
Discrimination of transformation refers to the very transformations that occur in relation to the signs [of objects].
Because one discriminates based on these transformations of the signs, it is called discrimination of the transformation of signs.

Regarding "the differentiation of the transformation of aging and so forth": the decay and alteration of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) within the body is called the differentiation of the transformation of aging.
For this reason, it is termed the differentiation of the transformation of the characteristics of conditions.
The term "and so forth" includes the transformations of aging, illness, and death.

The same applies to the transformations of pleasant feelings (*sukha-vedanā*) and so forth; that is, the body undergoes alteration due to pleasant feeling. The term "and so forth" includes painful (*duḥkha*) and neither-painful-nor-pleasant (*aduḥkhāsukha*) feelings.
The same applies to the transformations caused by greed and so forth; "and so forth" includes anger and delusion.

The same also applies to the transformations caused by affliction, the passage of time, and seasonal changes—namely, the conceptualization that arises with the transformation of the body as its objective referent.
“Affliction” refers to killing, binding, and so forth.
“The shifting of seasons” refers to the changing of seasons, such as the cold season and others.

“The transformation of the various destinies, such as the hells (*naraka*),” includes by implication the animal (*tiryagyoni*) and hungry ghost (*preta*) destinies; the same applies to the transformation of the various realms, such as the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), where “and so forth” includes the form (*rūpadhātu*) and formless (*ārūpyadhātu*) realms.

Regarding the discrimination of the manifestation of transformational characteristics: this refers to the various transformations that appear as the objective images of those objects of perception within visual consciousness and so forth. Based on these manifestations of transformational characteristics, there is further discrimination; this is also like the various transformations previously mentioned, such as aging, because transformation arises therein even during states such as old age.

Regarding "discrimination induced by others," this refers to discrimination arising from the instruction of others. This, in turn, is of two types: first, that which arises from hearing what is not the true Dharma;
second, that which arises from hearing the true Dharma.

This latter type is further divided into two kinds of discrimination regarding phenomena: namely, hearing the true Dharma that is either wholesome or unwholesome. The same explanation applies to hearing what is not the true Dharma.
Improper conceptualization refers to the conceptualization by non-Buddhists and their disciples based on hearing categories of non-orthodox teachings.
Proper conceptualization refers to the conceptualization by the disciples of the Buddhas within the True Dharma based on hearing categories of the True Dharma.

"Adherence to conceptualization" refers to the conceptualizations associated with the sixty-two types of wrong views that arise based on the view of a self, caused by improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), as explained at length in the sutras.
Regarding "distraction and conceptualization," this refers to the ten types of conceptualization as explained later in the treatise.

The commentary states: (1) distraction regarding the signless; (2) distraction regarding signs; (3) distraction through superimposition; (4) distraction through denial; (5) distraction regarding identity; (6) distraction regarding difference; (7) distraction regarding intrinsic nature; (8) distraction regarding differentiation; (9) distraction regarding grasping objects according to names; and (10) distraction regarding grasping names according to objects.
To counteract these ten types of distraction, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is taught throughout all the *prajñāpāramitās*.
One should understand that this relationship between the objects to be countered and their remedies fully encompasses the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The commentary states:
Herein, "distraction characterized by the signless" refers to this distraction taking the very sign of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object.
To counteract this distraction, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
There truly exists the bodhisattva.
To say "truly exists" indicates that the bodhisattva truly has emptiness as its essence (*śūnyatā-ātman*).
Emptiness itself is the essence; therefore, it is called the "essence of emptiness."
Regarding the distraction of signs (*nimitta-vikṣepa*): this refers to a distraction that takes the signs of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as its object.
To counteract this distraction, that same sutra states:
"One does not perceive a bodhisattva."
The intention of this sutra is to state that one does not perceive the bodhisattva as having the parikalpita (imagined) or paratantra (dependent) natures as its essence;
this is for the purpose of counteracting the conceptual proliferation of superimposition.
That very sutra states:
"Form is empty of intrinsic nature," because form,
as it is conceptually constructed, is empty of intrinsic nature.
Regarding the distraction of diminution, it is for the purpose of counteracting this distraction that the same sutra states:
"Not by means of emptiness."
This means that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and the nature of form (*rūpatā*) are not empty.
Regarding "dispersal and movement toward a single nature," in order to counteract this dispersal and movement, that same sutra states:
"Form is emptiness; it is not [inherently] form."

Why is this? If the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) were of one essence, then this dependent nature should be a pure object, just like the perfected nature.
Regarding distraction toward dissimilar objects (*visabhāga-vikṣepa*), in order to counteract this distraction, that same sūtra states:
"Form is not separate from emptiness. Why is this?
If these two were different, then the phenomenon (*dharma*) and its nature (*dharmatā*) would also have to be different.
If they possessed a difference in nature, it would be illogical, just as [it is illogical for] an impermanent phenomenon to be different from its impermanence.
If one takes the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as the referent, then form is emptiness and emptiness is form.

Why is this? Because the non-existence of the imagined form is itself emptiness, and this emptiness is that very non-existence; it is not like the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), which cannot be said to be identical.
Regarding movement through intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikṣepa*), as an antidote to this movement,
that same sūtra states: "Śāriputra,
this is merely a name called 'form' (*rūpa*)."
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form does not exist.
As for the distraction of differentiation, in order to counteract this distraction, that same sūtra states:
The intrinsic nature is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity.
Arising entails defilement and cessation entails purity; because there is neither arising nor cessation, there is neither defilement nor purity. Such is the meaning of these various phrases.
Regarding "distraction consisting in grasping meaning according to names," this refers to distraction regarding an object in accordance with its name.
To counteract this distraction, that same sutra states:
"One establishes adventitious names and gives rise to conceptualization regarding each respective phenomenon."
Regarding the term "distinctly distinct," it refers to individual names.
For example, as for the discursive movement that grasps at meanings according to names, this refers to the arising of discursive movement toward names based on their referents.
To counteract this discursive movement, that very sutra states:
Provisional guest-names are established to follow along with conventional discourse; it is not that the self-nature of objects possesses such names inherently.
To counteract these ten types of mental distraction, the *Prajñāpāramitā* is taught.
Based on this, it is said that non-conceptual wisdom arises as its cause.
The treatise states:
"If one considers it from another perspective, the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) possesses three natures."
How is it that the three natures do not become indistinguishable?

If something is established as the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) by one aspect, it is not thereby established as the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) or the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).

If something is established as the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) from one perspective, it is not thereby established as the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) or the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
If something is established as the perfected nature from one perspective, it is not thereby established as the dependent nature or the imagined nature.
The commentary states:
This meaning is explained according to the interpretation of the preceding path.
*Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Fascicle Four.
Commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, Fascicle Five.
Composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
2. The Section on the Characteristics of the Knowable, Part Three, Section Two. The treatise says:

Furthermore, how is it known that, just as in the case of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) appears while not corresponding to its actual substance?

Because the cognition arising from a name contradicts [the object's] lack of a corresponding essence; because names contradict [the existence of] multiple essences; and because names contradict [the existence of] indeterminate or mixed essences.
In this regard, there are two verses:
Because prior cognition does not exist before the name, because multiple names are indeterminate,
and because it would entail having many essences or a confused essence, it follows that [the object] is not identical to its designation.
The dharma is non-existent yet can be attained; it is unstained yet possesses purity.
One should know it to be like an illusion and so forth, and likewise similar to space.
The commentary states:
Just as in the case of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), although the imagined aspect (*parikalpita-bhāga*) appears and can be apprehended, it does not correspond to its actual substance.

To clarify this meaning, it is said: "Because prior to the application of a name there is no cognition [of the object], which contradicts the correspondence between the name and the substance," and so forth.
If the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) were of the same character, then cognition regarding an object would arise without depending on names.
For example, just as one conceives of a jar, if one were separated from the name "jar," there would be no cognition of a jar within the referent of that jar.
If the designation "this jar" and the referent "that jar" shared the same characteristic, the cognition of "jar" would arise;
however, because they do not share the same characteristic, it does not arise.

Regarding this designation and its referent, if their essence were congruent, there would be a contradiction. Herein, the name is established as the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) and the referent as the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), because the dependent nature becomes the object of imagination through the power of the name.
Furthermore, a single object has many names. If the name and the object possessed the same characteristic, then the object, like the name, would necessarily be manifold.
If that were so, this object would become multiple entities; yet for a single object to have multiple entities is a contradiction.
Therefore, if the two genders were of one and the same characteristic, it would constitute the second fault of contradiction.
Furthermore, the name would be indeterminate, as the single sound "go" (cow) applies to nine different meanings.

If one were to maintain that name and object possess the same characteristic (ekalakṣaṇa), then multiple objects with contradictory characteristics would have to be of a single substance; this would constitute the third fault of contradiction.
Because [the opponent] maintains that cows and so forth—which do not possess a single characteristic as their referent—are of a single nature, the first verse reiterates this point.

Regarding "that which is established therein," this reveals that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) do not constitute a single, identical reality.
As for the phrase "the dharma is non-existent yet is apprehended," this single *gāthā* uses metaphors such as a magical illusion (*māyā*) to awaken the disciples.
Your disciple has two contradictory doubts:
how can phenomena be non-existent yet perceptible?
And how can there be purity in the absence of defilement?
Two analogies herein explain this doubt. Regarding "like an illusion" and so forth:
for example, although an illusory image has no real existence, it is nonetheless perceived as appearing.
One should know that the meaning here is likewise: although it is perceived as appearing, it does not exist in reality.
Regarding that which resembles space: for example, although space cannot be defiled by clouds and the like because its nature is pure, it is nevertheless said to be "pure" when it is free from them.

One should know that all phenomena are likewise: although they are in reality undefiled because their nature is pure, they are said to be "purified" when adventitious obscurations and stains are extinguished and removed.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, for what reason is it that while things do not exist at all in the manner they appear, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is not entirely and completely non-existent?
If this were non-existent, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) would also not exist.
If this were non-existent, then everything would be non-existent.
If the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature were non-existent, it would result in the fallacy that there is neither defilement nor purification.
Since both affliction and purification are actually perceived, it is therefore not the case that everything is non-existent.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
If the dependent nature does not exist, The perfected nature also does not exist.
If all aspects did not exist, there would never be defilement or purification.
Commentary:
If the dependent nature were not as it is apprehended, then why would everything not be entirely non-existent?
If this did not exist, the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) would also not exist. Why?
Because it exists by virtue of the existence of both defilement and purification.
If both were non-existent, then all aspects would be utterly non-existent.
Now, it must be shown that this is not the case of total non-existence, for there would otherwise be the fault of slandering both affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*).
Since both affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*) are presently perceived, neither of these two natures can be said to be non-existent.
If one were to insist that they do not exist, one would be negating the manifest existence of affliction and purification, asserting that they are utterly non-existent.
The treatise says:
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have taught the Vaipulya doctrine within the Mahāyāna; in that teaching it is asked:
"How should the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) be understood?"
One should understand that "non-existence" is taught through various alternative formulations (*paryāya*).
How should one understand the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)?
One should understand it to be like a magical illusion, a mirage, a dream, a reflection, an optical aberration, a shadow, an echo, the moon in water, and a transformation (*nirmāṇa*).
How should the thoroughly established nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) be understood?
It should be understood through the teaching of the four dharmas of purification.
What are these four dharmas of purification?

First is purity by nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), which refers to suchness (*tathatā*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), signlessness (*animitta*), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Second is purity through the removal of stains (*vaimalya-viśuddhi*), which refers to this very [nature] being free from all obstructive defilements.
Third is the purity of attaining this path, which refers to all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), the perfections (*pāramitā*), and so forth.
Fourth is the purity of producing this object, which refers to the sublime and correct teachings of the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Because it is the pure condition for this teaching of the Dharma, it is not the nature of the imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva);
because it is the outflow from the most pure dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), it is not the nature of the dependent (paratantra-svabhāva).
These four dharmas collectively encompass all pure phenomena without exception.
Regarding this, there are two verses:
"Phenomena such as illusions are taught regarding arising; The non-existence of the imagined nature is taught."
If one speaks of the four purities, these are called the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The natural purity and the purity from stains, as well as the objects of the path of purification—
all dharmas that are pure— are subsumed within these four characteristics.
The commentary states:

"Purity of intrinsic nature" means that this intrinsic nature is primordially pure; it is the very nature of *tathatā* (suchness), which truly exists as the common characteristic shared equally by all sentient beings.
Because this exists, it is said that all phenomena possess the *tathāgatagarbha* (the womb of the Tathāgata).

Regarding "stainless purity": this very suchness is free from the stains of the afflictive and cognitive obstructions; it is through the manifestation of such pure suchness that all Buddhas are realized.

Regarding "attaining the purity of this path," it means that one is able to attain this true suchness (*tathatā*) and the noble path itself, which is purity; namely, the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), such as the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and all the perfections (*pāramitā*).
"Arising in this pure object" means arising in the objective sphere (*ālambana*) of those factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) which are capable of realizing awakening.
Since arising in this sphere is itself purity, it is called "arising in this pure object," namely the twelvefold teaching consisting of the sūtras and so forth.
Why is this? If this holy teaching were of the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva), it would become a cause of affliction (saṃkleśa).
If it were of the nature of the dependent (paratantra-svabhāva), it would be false.
Because it is of the nature of the outflow from the most pure *dharmadhātu*, it is not false.
Since it is free from the two [imaginary and dependent] natures, it constitutes the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) nature.
Furthermore, among these four types, whichever one is mentioned in the Mahāyāna should be understood as referring to the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*.
Among these, the first two are unchanging, and because they are the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), they are called "perfectly accomplished.
The latter two are free from error, and because they are the perfected nature, they are called "perfectly accomplished."
This meaning is fully set forth in the subsequent verses.
Regarding the statement that "illusion and so forth refer to arising," this means that the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) is what is termed "arising" here.
One should understand that whenever all phenomena are described as being like illusions, up to and including magical transformations, such descriptions refer to the *paratantra-svabhāva*.

Regarding the statement that there is nothing to be grasped through conceptual construction: wherever it is stated that "there is no form," and so forth, up to "there are no all phenomena," one should know that this teaching refers to the nature of pervasive conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, for what reason are metaphors such as illusions taught regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), as stated in the Sūtras?
It is in order to eliminate the false doubts of others concerning the dependent nature.
Furthermore, how can there be false doubt regarding the dependent nature?
This is because others harbor such a doubt:
"How is it that objects do not exist in reality, yet they constitute the objective sphere of experience?"
To eliminate this doubt, the analogy of a magical illusion (māyā) is taught:
how can mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) evolve in the absence of an external object?
To eliminate this doubt, the analogy of a mirage (marīci) is taught.
How can there be a distinction in the experience of the desirable and undesirable, despite the absence of external objects?
To dispel this doubt, the analogy of a dream is taught.
How can there arise a distinction between the results—the desirable and the undesirable—of pure and impure karma, even though no external objects exist?
To eliminate this doubt, the analogy of a reflected image is taught.
To address the doubt as to how various cognitions can arise in the absence of external objects,
the analogy of light and shadow is taught.
How is it that various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) and verbal expressions proceed without an objective referent?
To eliminate this doubt, the analogy of an echo is taught.
How is it that there is a real apprehension of the objects of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) proceeding without an objective referent?
To eliminate this doubt, the analogy of the moon reflected in water is taught.

How is it that, although there is no objective referent, various bodhisattvas—with minds free from error—voluntarily take birth for the sake of accomplishing the welfare and happiness of sentient beings?
To eliminate this doubt, the analogy of transformation is taught.
The commentary states:
For this purpose, analogies such as illusions are presented regarding the dependent nature; these shall now be demonstrated.

In this context, "false doubt" refers to all doubts concerning the false dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). To eliminate these doubts, the metaphors of an illusion and so forth are taught to reveal the dependent nature.
If objects do not truly exist, how can they constitute a cognitive domain?
To remedy this doubt, the analogy of a magical illusion is taught to reveal the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
For example, although a magically conjured elephant lacks any real substance, it nonetheless constitutes a cognitive domain; the same applies to [apparent] objects.
He again gives rise to doubt:
"If there is no object, then there is no objective referent; how then do the various minds and mental factors arise?
To remove this doubt, the analogy of a mirage is taught to reveal the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

In this context, the mirage is a metaphor for the mind and mental factors, while the water is a metaphor for the object. Just as a mirage has movement, so too does the cognition of water arise even though no such object exists.
It is the same with all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*): because they are in a state of agitation, although no object exists, the cognition of an object arises.
Regarding this, those foolish people again raise a doubt:
"If no object exists, how can the various distinctions in the experience of pleasant and unpleasant things be obtained?"
To eliminate this doubt, the analogy of a dream is taught to reveal the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Just as in a dream, although there is no real object, various distinctions in the enjoyment of the pleasant and the unpleasant are perceived as manifest and obtainable, so it is with this [dependent nature] as well.
Regarding this, a further doubt arises:
"If the reality of pure and impure karma does not exist, how can the reality of desirable and undesirable fruits arise?
To eliminate this doubt, the metaphor of a reflection is taught to reveal the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).
For example, although a reflection has no real object, a cognition of a reflection arises with respect to its source; yet, no separate object corresponding to the reflection can be found.
This case is likewise: one should know that although there is no real fruit of the desirable or undesirable, it nonetheless appears as if obtainable.
Regarding this, a further doubt arises:
"If there is no external object, how can various consciousnesses arise?
To eliminate this doubt, the analogy of light and shadow is taught to reveal the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Just as one who plays with shadows may perceive various kinds of light and shadows, and although many such light and shadows can be perceived, in reality the meaning of "light and shadow" does not exist at all.
Consciousness is also like this: although there are no various objects, the appearance of various objects is perceived.
Regarding this, a further doubt arises:
if there are no objects, how do the manifold categories of conceptual proliferation and verbal expression proceed?
To eliminate this doubt, the analogy of an echo is taught to reveal the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Just as an echo, though lacking any objective referent, is nonetheless perceived, so too are conceptual proliferations and verbal expressions; although they lack any real meaning, they are nonetheless perceived.
Regarding this, there arises further doubt:
If objects do not exist, how is it that the world perceives objects in concentrated states of mind and mental factors?
For it is said that a concentrated mind can know things as they truly are and see them as they truly are.
To eliminate this doubt, the analogy of the moon in water is taught to reveal the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
For example, although the moon in water has no real existence, it is nonetheless perceived due to the moist, smooth, and clear nature of the water.
The concentrated mind is likewise: although the object of its focus has no real existence, it is nevertheless perceived as present.
Water serves as a metaphor for this concentration, because of its nature of being moist, supple, and clear.
Regarding this, a further doubt arises:

if the referent of "sentient beings" does not truly exist at all, how is it that bodhisattvas who have realized the truth first employ the wisdom of benefiting and bringing happiness to them, and then assume a physical body within various realms of existence?
To eliminate this doubt, the analogy of a magical transformation (*nirmāṇa*) is taught to reveal the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

For example, although a magical creation has no real objective referent, all its functions are accomplished through the power of the creator; yet, the object of the transformation is not non-existent.

One should know that it is likewise here: although the meaning of the appropriated self-body does not exist, the meaning of the appropriated self-body that is capable of bringing about the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings is perceptibly present.
Furthermore, there is another meaning; the Blessed One’s intention in teaching the eight similes, such as that of an illusion, shall now be revealed.

Herein, the simile of the illusion is intended to eliminate [the misconception regarding] the six internal bases, such as the eye; it should be understood as demonstrating the six sense-bases, for example, that although illusory forms do not truly exist, they are nonetheless perceived as appearing.
The simile of a mirage is taught to eliminate [the misconception regarding] the receptacle world, because it is so vast.
Within a mirage there is actually no water; yet, due to the power of its flickering movement, it appears as if water were obtainable.

The analogy of the dream is taught to eliminate the notion that the objects of experience, such as form and so forth, are real; it demonstrates that just like a dream, form and the rest do not exist in reality, yet they can act as causes for the arising of various experiences of the desirable and the undesirable.

The simile of the reflected image is taught to eliminate [the misconception that] physical karma is the fruit; it demonstrates that conditioned by wholesome and unwholesome physical karma, other forms arise as reflections.
The simile of the echo is taught to eliminate [the misconception that] vocal karma is the fruit; it demonstrates that the cause of vocal karma brings about the fruit of vocal karma just like an echo.
There are three types of mental karma (*manas-karman*):
first, that of the non-concentrated stage (*a-samāhita-bhūmi*); second, that of the concentrated stage (*samāhita-bhūmi*); and third, that which is of the nature of hearing (*śruta-maya*).

The metaphor of light and shadow is taught to exclude the fruits of mental karma belonging to the non-concentrated stage, thereby demonstrating that the various fruits obtained from this [concentrated] mental karma are like light and shadow.

The analogy of the moon in water is taught to eliminate [the misconception regarding] the fruits of mental karma belonging to the stage of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*), demonstrating that the fruits of mental karma in the stage of equipoise are like the moon reflected in water.

The analogy of transformation (*nirmāṇa*) is taught to eliminate [the misconception regarding] mental karma of the "hearing-type" (*śruta-maya*); "hearing-type" refers to that which is perfumed by hearing and reflection. This demonstrates that the distinctions of mental karma of the hearing-type proceed in a manner similar to a magical transformation.
The treatise says:
Based on what underlying intention did the Blessed One, in the *Brahmaparipṛcchā-sūtra*,
state that the Tathāgata neither attains saṃsāra nor attains nirvāṇa?

Within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), with reference to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), there is the intentional meaning (*saṃdhi*) that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are without distinction.

Why is this? It is because this very other-dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) constitutes saṃsāra through its aspect of the thoroughly imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), and constitutes nirvāṇa through its aspect of the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
The commentary states:
These three types of phenomena characterized by intrinsic nature are all in accordance with the sūtras that have been taught; they shall now be demonstrated.

Regarding the secret intention (*saṃdhāya*) by which the Blessed One stated in the *Brahmaparipṛcchā-sūtra* that the Tathāgata neither attains saṃsāra nor attains nirvāṇa—the question concerns the secret intention that, within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), there is no distinction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa in terms of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). The answer will be explained extensively hereafter.
The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is not definitively saṃsāra, because it constitutes nirvāṇa through its perfected aspect (*pariniṣpanna-bhāga*);
nor is it definitively nirvāṇa, because it constitutes saṃsāra through its imagined aspect (*parikalpita-bhāga*). Therefore, it cannot be definitively described as having a single nature.
By virtue of this intrinsic nature, if one part is attained, the remaining parts are not different from it.
With this underlying intention, that sūtra states that the Tathāgata neither attains saṃsāra nor attains nirvāṇa.
The treatise states:
In the *Abhidharma Mahāyāna Sūtra*, the Bhagavat taught that there are three categories of phenomena:
first, the defiled portion; second, the purified portion; and third, the portion consisting of both.
With what underlying intention was this said?

Within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) constitutes the defiled portion, while the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) constitutes the purified portion; thus, the dependent nature itself comprises these two portions.
Based on this underlying intention, it is stated thus.
By what analogy is this meaning illustrated?
It is illustrated by the analogy of a gold-bearing earth deposit.
For example, within a worldly deposit of gold and earth, three things can be found:
first, the element of earth; second, the soil; and third, the gold.
Within that element of earth, the soil is not substantially real yet appears to be obtainable, whereas the gold is substantially real yet is not obtainable.
When smelted by fire, the appearance of earth does not manifest, while the appearance of gold manifests.

Furthermore, regarding this element of earth, when earth appears it is a false manifestation, whereas when gold appears it is a true manifestation; therefore, the element of earth consists of these two parts.

Consciousness is also like this: before it has been burned by the fire of non-conceptual wisdom, all false, imagined natures (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) manifest within this consciousness, while all true, perfected natures (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) do not manifest.

When this consciousness is incinerated by the fire of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), the true perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) within this consciousness manifests, while the false imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) does not manifest.

Therefore, this consciousness of false discrimination possesses those two parts within its dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), just as the earth element exists within a deposit of gold and soil.
The commentary states:
In the *Abhidharma-mahāyāna-sūtra*, it is with this underlying intention (*saṃdhi*) that three dharmas are taught:
First is the defiled portion, meaning that the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) is defiled.
Second is the purified portion, meaning that the nature of the perfected (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is purified.
Third, it has two aspects, because the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) pervades both of them.
To clarify this meaning, the metaphor of gold in its ore is employed.
In this context, the "store" refers to those seeds.
What is called the "earth element" is solidity and hardness.
Earth and gold are derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
In this analogy, three factors are discernible: namely, within this treasury, first there is the appearance of earth, and only later is the characteristic of gold perceived.
To demonstrate that the characteristic of gold can only be obtained after [processing], it is said that gold truly exists because it can be obtained after being refined by fire.
The treatise states:

In some places the Blessed One says that all phenomena are permanent; in some places he says that all phenomena are impermanent; and in some places he says that all phenomena are neither permanent nor impermanent.
With what underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) was this said?

It means that with respect to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it is permanent in its aspect as the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), impermanent in its aspect as the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), and neither permanent nor impermanent by virtue of those two aspects combined.
Based on this underlying intention (*saṃdhi*), it is said as follows: Just as permanence and impermanence are non-dual, so too are suffering and pleasure non-dual;

purity and impurity are non-dual; emptiness and non-emptiness are non-dual; self and selflessness are non-dual; tranquility and non-tranquility are non-dual; having intrinsic nature and lacking intrinsic nature are non-dual; arising and non-arising are non-dual; ceasing and non-ceasing are non-dual; primordial peace and non-primordial peace are non-dual; and natural nirvāṇa and non-natural nirvāṇa are non-dual. It is likewise with the non-duality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.

All such various intentional expressions (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*) of the Buddhas should be understood according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), following the previously explained categories of permanence and impermanence, and so forth.
Regarding this, there are many verses:
"In reality, phenomena do not exist as they appear; They are not of a single kind, nor are they non-phenomena or non-non-phenomena;
Therefore, it is said that their meaning is non-dual."
Based on one aspect, it is revealed as either existent or non-existent;
based on two aspects, it is said to be neither existent nor non-existent.
Since it does not exist in the manner that it appears, it is therefore called "non-existent."
Because they manifest in this way, they are said to exist.

Yet, their own essence is naturally non-existent; their intrinsic nature does not persist, and since they do not exist in the manner they are grasped, they are held to be without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Because it is devoid of intrinsic nature, it is established; It serves as the basis for each subsequent stage.
Without arising or ceasing, it is primordially quiescent; Its very nature is parinirvāṇa.
Commentary:

Regarding the meaning of the verse: "In reality, phenomena do not exist as they appear, for they are not of a single kind," this explains the causes and conditions for what is neither dharma nor non-dharma according to their respective order. Because they do not exist in reality, they are not dharma; because they appear in more than one way, they are not non-dharma. Since they are neither dharma nor non-dharma, it is said that they have the sense of being non-dual.
"Relying on one part" means relying on one side.
"Revealing and clarifying" means explaining and demonstrating.
"Either existent or non-existent" refers to either having the nature of existence or the nature of non-existence.

Regarding the statement that it is "neither existent nor non-existent" based on its two aspects: this refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which possesses these two aspects, and is thus described as being neither existent nor non-existent.
Regarding "that which appears does not exist": it means that what is perceived as appearing does not exist in the manner in which it appears.
Therefore, when it is said to be "non-existent," it is designated as non-existent for this reason.
"By appearing in such a manner" means by appearing merely as if it possessed a semblance of existence.
Therefore, when it is said that "it exists," it is said to exist on the basis of this very meaning.
The intention behind the statement that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature shall now be elucidated.

Regarding "naturally non-existent": because all phenomena do not possess an intrinsic nature that exists independently of various conditions, this is called the first sense of the absence of intrinsic nature.
Regarding "the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)," because phenomena, once ceased, do not arise again, they lack intrinsic nature; this is another sense of the absence of intrinsic nature.
Regarding "intrinsic nature does not endure," because phenomena lack the power to remain for even a single moment after arising, they lack intrinsic nature.
This principle that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature is shared with the śrāvakas.
However, if one maintains that they lack intrinsic nature because the grasping [of them] does not exist, this [specific] absence of intrinsic nature is not shared with the śrāvakas.

Because the nature of the imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) as apprehended by fools does not exist in that way, it is with this intention that, according to the principles of the Mahāyāna, it is said that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva).
Regarding "established by way of non-existence": because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the absence of arising, ceasing, and so forth is fully established. Why is this so?

Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are without arising; because they are without arising, they are also without cessation. Because they are without arising and cessation, they are quiescent from the beginning; because they are quiescent from the beginning, their intrinsic nature is nirvāṇa.
Regarding "the basis for each subsequent [level]," this means that each subsequent [level] is obtained by virtue of the preceding one.
The treatise states:
Furthermore, there are four kinds of intentions (*abhiprāya*) and four kinds of secrets (*saṃdhāya*); all the words of the Buddha should be understood through these.
Regarding the four intentions (*abhiprāya*): first is the intention of equality (*samatābhiprāya*), which refers, for example, to the statement:
"In that time and at that juncture, I was the perfectly awakened one named Vipaśyin."
Second is the intention regarding another time (*kāla-antara-abhiprāya*), which refers, for example, to the statement:
"If one recites the name of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, one has already attained certainty regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Furthermore, as it is said:
"By merely making a vow, one attains rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss.
Third, the intentional meaning regarding specific distinctions refers to what is said, for example:
If one has already served as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, one is then able to understand the meaning of the Mahāyāna teachings.
There are four types of intentions regarding the dispositions of individuals (*pudgala*), such as when, for the sake of a single individual, one first praises generosity and later disparages it.
As it is with generosity, so it should be understood for ethical discipline (*śīla*) and a portion of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
These are called the four intentions (*abhiprāya*). Regarding the four secrets (*saṃdhi*):

first is the secret of introduction (*avatāraṇa-saṃdhi*), which refers to the teaching, within either the Śrāvaka Vehicle or the Mahāyāna, that there exist persons (*pudgala*) and the distinct intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of phenomena (*dharma*) based on the principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Second is the secret of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-guhyaka*), which refers to those instances where the characteristics of all phenomena are taught to reveal the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Third is the secret of remedies (*pratipakṣa-guhyaka*), which refers to those instances where the eighty-four thousand practices that serve as remedies are taught.
The fourth is the secret of transformation (*pariṇāma-guhya*), which means that in certain instances, various words and syllables reveal a distinct meaning through a specific sense.
As a verse says:
"Perceiving the non-solid as solid, One abides well within inversion."
"Afflicted by the most extreme afflictions, one attains the supreme bodhi.
The commentary states:

Regarding the distinction of the "intentional secret" (*ābhiprāyika-guhyaka*), it refers to when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, first contemplates a certain matter and subsequently teaches it to others; this is called "intentionality."
By means of this, one is definitively led to enter the holy teaching; this is called the "secret" [intention].
As for the "intention of equality," it refers, for example, to someone who takes up a similar phenomenon and says:
"That is precisely me."
The World-Honored One is likewise; having established the equal Dharma-body within his mind, he says, "In the past, I was among them.

This is not to say that the Buddha Vipaśyin of former times is identical to Śākyamuni of today; rather, such a statement is made based on the underlying intention arising from the principle of equality.

The intention regarding another time refers to this underlying purpose: to cause those who are indolent to diligently practice various dharmas through various causes, so that their respective roots of virtue may all attain increase.

The underlying intention here is to show that reciting the name of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna is a cause for spiritual advancement; it does not mean that by merely reciting the name, one has already attained certainty regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
As it is said:
"By means of a single coin, one obtains a thousand coins.
Could this happen in a single day?
The intention [of this teaching] refers to a different time; because a single coin can become the cause for obtaining a thousand, this statement was made.
This case is likewise: one should know that by merely making a vow, one will attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and it is exactly so.

Regarding the intention of another meaning (*arthāntarābhiprāya*), that which can be understood only within the Mahāyāna teachings refers to personally realizing the characteristics of the principles of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
If it were merely the case that understanding the meanings according to conventional designations constitutes the Buddha’s intention, then even foolish worldlings would be able to understand it.

Thus, one should know that the statement here regarding "understanding the meaning" intends to demonstrate that such understanding necessarily depends on having encountered and served many Buddhas in the past.
Regarding the "intention and underlying purpose of the individual," this refers, for example, to first praising generosity and later disparaging it.
The intention here is as follows: first, for those who are excessively stingy, generosity is praised;
later, for those who take pleasure in practicing giving, [the teaching] again disparages it in order to lead them to cultivate superior practices.
Without this underlying intention, praising and then disparaging a single act of giving would constitute a contradiction.
Because of this intention, praise and blame are appropriate.
One should know that the same applies to ethical discipline (*śīla*) and so forth.
"Partial cultivation" refers to mundane cultivation.

"Introducing [beings] to the secret" means that in cases where, based on the principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is said to be a person (*pudgala*) and the intrinsic natures and distinctions of all phenomena, this is called "introducing to the secret" because it is intended to lead sentient beings into the Buddha's holy teaching.
The "secret of characteristics" refers to teaching the three natures within the exposition of the characteristics of all phenomena.

The "secret of antidotes" refers to teaching the antidotes for the various activities of sentient beings in specific contexts, with the intent of establishing antidotes for the afflictive activities of sentient beings.
Regarding the secret of transformation (*pariṇāmanā-guhya*): it refers to cases where various phrases and syllables that express one meaning are transformed to reveal another meaning.

In the verse, "perceiving the non-solid as solid": "non-solid" refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*); because it is not rigid and is difficult to tame due to its tendency toward distraction, it is called "non-solid.
To give rise to a sense of reverence toward this very [concentration] is what is meant by "perceiving it as solid."
"Being well-established in the inverted" means being well-settled within that which is inverted and capable of causing inversion.

To regard the impermanent and so forth as permanent and so forth is called "the inverted"; to regard the impermanent and so forth as impermanent and so forth is "that which is capable of inversion. It means being well-settled therein.
Regarding "being afflicted by extreme afflictions": diligence and exertion are termed "afflictions.
For the sake of sentient beings, one is afflicted by the diligence and exertion of long-term toil, as it is said in a verse:
"To dwell long in saṃsāra is an affliction, which arises solely from great compassion."
Regarding such cases as these,
the meaning of "attaining supreme enlightenment" is easy to understand.
The Treatise says:
If one wishes to compose an exposition of the Mahāyāna Dharma, one should briefly compose that exposition by means of three aspects:
first, by explaining dependent origination; second, by explaining the characteristics of phenomena arising from conditions; and third, by explaining the meaning of the words.
The commentary states:
Based on these three characteristics as appropriate, one should compose commentaries on all Mahāyāna teachings.
The treatise says:
Regarding the explanation of dependent origination herein, it is said:
"Produced by the permeation of speech, all phenomena arise from that;
the ripening consciousness and the evolving consciousnesses arise through mutual conditioning."
The commentary states:

Regarding the phrase "all dharmas produced by perfuming," because external conceptualization perfumes the *ālayavijñāna*, all dharmas arise with this perfuming as their cause; these are precisely the intrinsic nature of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "this arises from that": this refers to the fact that the activity of this discriminative perfuming takes those various dharmas as its cause; this demonstrates that the *ālaya-vijñāna* and those evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) serve as mutual causes for one another.
The Commentary states:

Furthermore, those phenomena characterized by the evolving consciousnesses possess both the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), with consciousness as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Moreover, these [aspects] take the basis (*āśraya*) as their characteristic, the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita*) as their characteristic, and the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as their characteristic; thereby, the characteristics of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are revealed.
As it is said:
"From that which has characteristics and that which has vision, one should know those three characteristics.
Furthermore, how should those characteristics be explained?

This refers to the fact that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*) is truly non-existent within the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*), whereas the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*) is truly existent therein.
Due to these two types of non-existence and existence, non-attainment and attainment—the state of not having seen and the state of having already seen the truth—occur simultaneously.
This means that within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is absent and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is present,
when one realizes the former, one does not realize the latter, and when one realizes the latter, one does not realize the former.
As it is said:
"The dependent nature lacks the imagined; the perfected nature exists therein.
Therefore, attainment and non-attainment—within this, both are equal."
The commentary states:

Regarding those dharmas characterized by the evolving consciousnesses, which have both aspect (*nimitta*) and vision (*darśana*) as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this means that those consciousnesses take both aspect and vision as their essence (*tattva*).
Furthermore, regarding those very characteristics, there are three kinds of bases that serve as their characteristics; these are the *paratantra-lakṣaṇa* (dependent nature).
By means of these three natures thus explained, those characteristics are revealed, and this meaning is precisely what is made manifest in the verse.
Regarding the statement that "one should know those three characteristics from the perspective of having marks and having vision," this is as explained and demonstrated above.

As for the phrase "by these two kinds—non-existence and existence, non-attainment and attainment—the one who has not yet seen and the one who has already seen the truth do so simultaneously": the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) and the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) are what are called the "two kinds."
Of these two kinds, the first does not exist, while the second does exist.
Those who have not yet seen the truth perceive the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) and do not attain the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
One who has already seen the truth attains the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) at this very moment, but does not attain the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
This meaning is revealed in the verse by stating that the dependent nature is devoid of the imagined nature, and so forth.
"Equality" refers to a single moment.
"Within it" refers to within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
"The two" refers to those who have not yet seen reality and those who have already seen reality.
The term "therefore" (hence) signifies "by reason of this cause.

That is to say, within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it is because the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is non-existent and because the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is existent.
Furthermore, because ordinary worldlings grasp through inversion, their views function in this manner.
For the noble ones, however, by virtue of right view, their views function in this manner.
The treatise says:

To explain the meaning of the words means that one first states the initial phrase and subsequently elucidates it through further phrases, either by way of its qualities (*guṇa*) or by way of its meaning (*artha*).
The commentary states:
Since the meaning of the words has been explained according to the interpretation provided, it shall now be further elucidated, either by subsuming their qualities or by subsuming their meanings.
The treatise says:
Regarding the basis of qualities, it refers to the teaching of the Buddha’s qualities:
his most pure awakening; the non-dual manifestation; the inclination toward the signless dharma; abiding in the Buddha-abode;
the attainment of the equality of all Buddhas; reaching the state of non-obstruction; and the unshakeable dharma.
Their conduct is unimpeded, and their established state is inconceivable; they roam within the equal dharma-nature of the three periods of time.
Their bodies are distributed throughout all worlds, and regarding all phenomena, their wisdom is free from doubt or obstruction.
Having achieved great awakening in all practices, they possess no uncertainty regarding the wisdom of all dharmas. Whatever...
The manifested body is beyond conceptual differentiation; it is the wisdom sought by all bodhisattvas alike.
Having attained the Buddha’s non-dual dwelling on the supreme further shore, it reaches the ultimate, wondrous wisdom of the Tathāgata’s liberation, which is free from mutual confusion.

It realizes the equality of the Buddha-ground, which is without middle or limit, extending to the furthest reaches of the dharma-realm, exhausting the nature of space, and reaching the end of the future.
The "limit" (*koṭi*) refers to the most pure awakening (*suviśuddhabodhi*).
It should be understood that this phrase is analytically revealed by the remaining phrases; thus, it constitutes a well-spoken exposition.

Regarding the "most pure awakening of the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā-suviśuddhabodhi*), this refers to the most pure awakening of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, which should be understood as being comprised of the twenty-one qualities of a Buddha.
That is to say: the merit of proceeding without obstruction toward all that is to be known;

the merit of being able to enter the most supreme purity of suchness, which is free from the two characteristics of existence and non-existence; the merit of abiding without cessation in effortless buddha-activities;
and the merit of there being no distinction between the basis, the intention, and the activity within the dharmakāya—[all] these are cultivated in their entirety.
The merit of counteracting hindrances; the merit of subduing all non-Buddhists; the merit of being born in the world without being obstructed by worldly dharmas;
the merit of establishing the True Dharma; the merit of receiving predictions of enlightenment;
the merit of manifesting the enjoyment body and transformation bodies in all worlds; and the merit of severing doubts.
The merit of causing [beings] to enter into various practices; the merit of generating sublime wisdom regarding future phenomena;
the merit of manifesting according to their respective resolute beliefs; the merit of the application of means to discipline sentient beings through immeasurable bases;
the merit of fulfilling the perfections of the equal Dharma-body; and the manifestation of distinctions according to their respective resolute beliefs.
The merits of the Buddha-field include: the merit of the three bodies of the Buddha being without spatial limitation;
the merit of constantly manifesting benefit and peace for all sentient beings until the end of cyclic existence; and the merit of inexhaustibility, and so forth.
The commentary states:
Regarding "the non-manifestation of duality," this means that the manifestation of duality does not exist herein; therefore, it is called the non-manifestation of duality.

This refers to the merit of proceeding toward the objects of knowledge with absolute freedom from obstruction, unlike the wisdom of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, which is characterized by both obstruction and non-obstruction.

Regarding "entering the signless dharma": pure *tathatā* (suchness) is called the signless dharma; "entering" means to penetrate it, which refers to the supreme quality of being able to enter the most purified *tathatā* that is free from the dual characteristics of existence and non-existence.
That is to say, this *tathatā* (suchness) does not have the characteristic of existence, because it takes the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) as its characteristic;
nor is it without characteristic, because its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) exists.
One can enter this *tathatā*, which is without characteristics, through supreme purity; that is, by means of supreme entry and pure entry.

"Abiding in the Buddha-abode" means abiding in the place where the Buddha abides, which is the state of non-abiding; that is, the merit of abiding in effortless buddha-activity without cessation, meaning that within this abiding, one constantly performs buddha-activities without rest.
"Attaining the equality of all Buddhas" refers to the merit of non-differentiation in the basis, intention, and activity within the *dharmakāya*.

"Reaching the state of non-obstruction" refers to the merit of cultivating the remedies for all obstacles; that is, because one constantly cultivates awakened wisdom at all times as the remedy for all obstacles.
The "unreversible dharma" refers to the merit of subduing all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

"Unimpeded conduct" refers to the merit of being born in the world without being obstructed by worldly dharmas; that is, although one is born in the world and acts within the spheres of worldly activity, one is not defiled by the eight worldly concerns, such as gain and so forth.

That which is established as inconceivable is precisely the establishment of the merit of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), because the True Dharma—consisting of the sūtras and so forth—is immeasurable and inconceivable, and thus cannot be understood by ordinary fools.
For this reason, it is called the most pure awakening; this phrase of the most pure awakening is universally applicable throughout every single phrase.
To "roam within the equal dharma-nature of the three periods of time" is precisely the merit of receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
"The body pervading all worlds" refers to the merit of manifesting the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) in all worlds.
"Possessing unimpeded wisdom regarding all phenomena" refers to the merit of severing doubt.
"One who has attained great awakening through all practices" refers to the merit of entering into various types of practice.

"One who has no doubt regarding the wisdom of all phenomena" refers to the merit of the sublime wisdom that arises regarding future phenomena; that is, knowing that such future phenomena will arise through the sublime wisdom of the Tathāgata.
That which cannot be conceptually differentiated regarding all manifested bodies is the merit of manifesting in accordance with the inclinations [of beings].

That which is the wisdom sought by all bodhisattvas and others is the merit of the application for training sentient beings based on immeasurable supports; that is to say, it refers to the immeasurable supports of bodhisattvas that are capable of performing the work of training all sentient beings. This is not a case where Buddhas, having already attained equality between self and others, further seek this wisdom; rather, it is only that Buddhas have already performed such supreme acts of training.
"Attaining the supreme other shore of the Buddha’s non-dual abiding" refers to the merit of the fulfillment of the *pāramitā* of the equal *dharmakāya*.
That is to say, the non-dual *dharmakāya* is called the "equal *dharmakāya*," and it is within this very non-dual *dharmakāya* that one attains the perfectly pure *pāramitā*.
"Unmixed and ultimate in the wondrous wisdom of the Tathāgata’s liberation" means that within the unmixed wisdom of the Tathāgata, one reaches the culmination of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
Here, this resolute conviction is termed "liberation," which refers to the manifestation of various distinguished qualities in accordance with that resolute conviction.

Realizing the equality of the Buddha-ground, which is without middle or extremes, refers to the merit of the three bodies of the Buddha being without spatial limitation; that is to say, the Buddha’s Dharma-body cannot be delimited by such-and-such a location, and likewise, the Enjoyment-body and Transformation-bodies cannot be said to occupy such-and-such worlds.

"Reaching the limit of the dharmadhātu" refers to the utterly pure dharmadhātu; this is called reaching the limit of the dharmadhātu, which is the merit of constantly manifesting benefit and happiness for all sentient beings until the very end of the cycle of birth and death.
That which exhausts the nature of empty space is the merit of inexhaustibility; this means that the Buddha’s wisdom is as inexhaustible as empty space.
That which reaches the furthest limit of the future is the merit of ultimate perfection.
The word "etc. implies that this Buddha-wisdom is ultimately uninterrupted until the end of the future; therefore, it is called the "most pure awakening.
The Commentary says:

Furthermore, regarding the basis of meaning, as it is said: if bodhisattvas accomplish thirty-two qualities, they are then called "bodhisattvas," namely, because they give rise to the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.
Because it causes one to enter into the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*); because one knows for oneself what provisional wisdom one currently possesses;
because it subdues pride; because it is a firm and superior resolve; because it is not a mere pretense of compassion; because it maintains a mind of equanimity toward both friends and enemies;
because it acts as a true spiritual friend until the very end of *nirvāṇa*; and because it is appropriate to the measure [of the recipient].
Because of his speech; because he speaks first with a smile; because of his boundless great compassion;
because he does not retreat or weaken regarding the tasks he has undertaken; because he has no sense of weariness; because he never tires of hearing the meaning of the Dharma;
because he perceives his own committed transgressions as deep faults; because he instructs others for their transgressions without anger; and regarding all modes of conduct...
Because they constantly cultivate and purify the bodhicitta; because they practice generosity without desiring karmic maturation;
because they uphold the precepts without relying on any realm of existence; because they practice patience without harboring anger or obstruction toward sentient beings;
because they exert diligence in order to gather all wholesome dharmas; and because they abandon the formless realms while practicing meditation.
Because of meditative concentration; because of cultivating wisdom in conjunction with skillful means; because of gathering [beings] through the four means of attraction as skillful means;
because of being without dualism toward spiritual friends who are either observant or transgressing the precepts; because of listening to the true Dharma with a reverent mind;
because of dwelling in forest hermitages with a reverent mind; and because of having no attachment to worldly distractions.
Therefore, because they have never taken pleasure in the inferior vehicles; because they perceive the profound merits within the Mahāyāna;
because they distance themselves from evil friends; because they draw near to virtuous friends; because they constantly cultivate and purify the four Brahma-abodes;
because they perpetually sport in the five supernormal powers; because they rely upon wisdom; and because they abide in right conduct—
Because they do not abandon sentient beings who abide in right practice, because their speech is definitive, because they revere truth and reality,
and because the great bodhicitta is always held as primary.
It should be understood that all these phrases are variations of the first phrase; that is, the superior intention (adhyāśaya) to bring about the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.
It should be understood that these phrases concerning the superior intention for benefit and happiness consist of sixteen distinct types of activity.
Among them, the sixteen activities are: first, the activity of successive application;
second, the activity free from error; [and so forth].
Third, the activity of spontaneously engaging without waiting for the request of others;
fourth, the activity of being unshakable and indestructible;

fifth, the activity of being free from seeking defilement—this should be understood as having three distinct aspects: namely, because it is not bound by defilement; because it is free from both attachment and aversion toward those who have been kind or unkind; and because it continues to function consistently throughout successive births.
Sixth, bodily action that is appropriate in speech; this should be understood as having two distinct phrases.
Seventh, impartial action toward pleasure, suffering, and that which is neither; eighth, non-inferior action;
ninth, non-regressive action.
10. The activity of gathering through skillful means;
11. The activity of revulsion toward that which is to be countered, which should be understood as having two distinct phrases;
12. The activity of uninterrupted mental attention.

Thirteenth is the activity of superior progress; it should be understood as having seven distinct points: namely, the correct application of the six *pāramitās* and the correct application of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).

Fourteenth is the activity of perfecting practice; it should be understood as having six distinct points: namely, associating with virtuous persons, hearing the true Dharma, dwelling in forest hermitages (*āraṇya*), abandoning unwholesome thoughts, and the merit of mental attention (*manasikāra*). Regarding this last point, it should be understood as having two further distinctions: the accompaniment and the merit. Regarding these two, they should again be understood as having two further distinctions.
Fifteenth is the activity of perfection; it should be understood as having three distinct points: namely, immeasurable purity, attaining great power, and the realization of merit.

Sixteenth, regarding the establishment of that activity, one should know that there are four distinct points: namely, the quality of governing the community; providing instruction and admonition that is definitive and free from doubt; gathering [disciples] through both material goods and the Dharma; and possessing a mind free from defilement.
It should be understood that all these phrases are differentiations of the first phrase.
The commentary states:

Regarding the phrase "because, within the sphere of meaning, one generates the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings," the meaning of this phrase is revealed by the remaining phrases through sixteen types of activity.
By what kind of action is the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) of benefit and happiness manifested?

It refers to the action of successive application; that is, causing others to enter the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). This means leading all sentient beings to enter the wisdom of omniscience through successive transformation and guidance, just as one lamp transmits its flame to a thousand lamps. This is what manifests the superior intention of benefit and happiness.
In all the remaining phrases such as these, they should all be correlated with the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) for benefit and happiness.
Regarding "action without inversion," this refers to knowing for oneself: "What is the provisional wisdom that I now possess?"

That is to say, although there may be an altruistic intention (*adhyāśaya*) for benefit and happiness, it is nonetheless inverted, such as when one initiates an altruistic intention for benefit and happiness but exhorts others to drink alcohol and the like.

Only if one possesses right knowledge and knows things as they truly are can one properly assess and instruct sentient beings; it is not the case that one with overweening pride, who lacks such true knowledge, would give rise to a mind of benefit while encouraging others to perform harmful deeds.

To spontaneously engage in practice without waiting for others to request it means that one has subdued pride; that is to say, because one has subdued the mind of arrogance, one preaches the Dharma of one's own accord without waiting for exhortation.

Regarding "the karma that is unshakable and indestructible": because it is a firm and superior resolve, the bodhisattva’s firm mind of the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings is not shaken or destroyed by the fact that those sentient beings engage in wrongful conduct.

Regarding "not seeking defiled actions": this is because it is not based on artificial compassion; because one maintains a mind of equanimity toward both friends and enemies; and because one acts as a virtuous friend forever until reaching the ultimate limit of nirvāṇa.

That is to say, the latter three phrases explain these [first] three phrases: acting for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings without being motivated by gain, honor, and the like; therefore, it is called the "superior intention of beneficial and happy action free from the stain of seeking."
How is this to be known?
It is by means of corresponding vocal and bodily actions; that is to say, because one speaks in moderation and because one speaks first with a smile.
Within these two phrases, speaking in moderation and speaking first are vocal actions, while smiling is a bodily action.
"Measured speech" means speaking only words that accord with the Dharma. "Speaking with a smile" means approaching others with a relaxed countenance to perform acts of benefit.

"Equanimity in action toward pleasure, suffering, and the non-dual" refers to infinite great compassion. Because this infinite compassion takes pity on the three types of suffering: it takes pity on sentient beings experiencing suffering for their *duḥkha-duḥkhatā* (the suffering of suffering); it takes pity on sentient beings experiencing pleasure for their *vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā* (the suffering of change); and it takes pity on sentient beings experiencing neither suffering nor pleasure for their *saṃskāra-duḥkhatā* (the suffering of conditioned existence). It is called "non-dual" because it pertains to that which is neither suffering nor pleasure.

"Having no inferior activity" means that one does not retreat or weaken in regard to the tasks undertaken; that is to say, one does not disparage oneself by thinking, "I am unable to attain the fruit of Buddhahood," and so forth.
The action of non-retrogression consists in the absence of weariness; that is to say, one exerts diligent effort in cultivating the causes for attaining Buddhahood with a mind free from weariness.
The action of gathering skillful means consists in the absence of satiety in hearing the meaning; that is to say, through extensive learning, one achieves skillful wisdom to benefit sentient beings.

Regarding "aversion toward the objects to be remedied": this refers to seeing one's own committed transgressions as deeply flawed, and not being resentful toward the transgressions committed by others but instead instructing them; through these skillful means, one is then able to truly subdue sentient beings.
Regarding the activity of uninterrupted mental attention (*manasikāra*), it consists in constantly cultivating and purifying the bodhicitta throughout all modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*).
The meaning of these phrases, concerning the purity of such practice, is explained at length in the sūtras.
The practitioner of superior progress is one who practices giving without desiring karmic maturation, and so forth, up to employing the means of the four bases of sympathy (*saṃgrahavastu*).

That is to say, relying upon the aforementioned superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) for benefit and happiness, one cultivates this application (*prayoga*) as the cause for increasing and advancing toward the fruit.

Regarding the practice of fulfilling the stage of application (*prayoga*), this refers to being without dualism toward virtuous friends who uphold the precepts and those who violate them, up to and including the cultivation of intimacy with virtuous friends.
That is to say, the final six phrases explain these eight phrases.
If one practices and approaches such application, one will swiftly achieve fulfillment.
Regarding "dwelling in an araṇya with a sincere mind," it is because by dwelling in this place, one is free from evil discursive thoughts.
"Worldly diversions" refers to such things as singing and dancing.
"Accomplishing activities" refers to the constant cultivation of the four Brahma-abodes, the perpetual sporting in the five supernormal powers, and the reliance upon wisdom.
This means that the latter three phrases explain these [first] three phrases, which constitute the characteristics of the karma of fulfillment (*pariniṣpanna-karman*).
"Great majestic power" refers to the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).

"Because of relying on wisdom" means relying on wisdom and not relying on consciousness; because internal wisdom arises, one dwells in accordance with the Dharma through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of this internal wisdom.
The establishment of those activities refers specifically to abiding in right practice and so forth;
that is, the latter four lines explain these four lines.
By means of the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) for benefit and happiness, one establishes the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.

Regarding "the merit of governing the assembly": because one does not abandon even those who have broken the precepts, but establishes them and does not expel them, causing them to emerge from unwholesomeness and abide in wholesomeness.

Regarding "because of teaching, instructing, and admonishing with certainty and without doubt": this means that because one is able to give instructions to others in a definitive manner, rather than speaking oneself and then subsequently saying, "What I have said was not good," for this reason, one's words possess a solemn authority.

Regarding "the unification of material wealth and the Dharma": because one's speech is truthful, one gathers material goods such as clothing through the Dharma and gives them back in that same manner.

Regarding "due to the absence of a defiled mind": because one properly embraces the great bodhicitta for the benefit of sentient beings, rather than seeking to have them serve as one’s own attendants.
How do sentient beings, by virtue of this goodness, swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
