It is by thus gathering in all sentient beings.
The treatise says:
As it is said:
"By means of the initial phrase, there is the distinction of the category of qualities;
by means of the initial phrase, there is the differentiation of the meaning of the phrases."
The commentary states:
This verse serves to reveal the meaning previously explained, and thus these words are spoken.
*Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Fascicle Five.
Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Scroll Six.
Composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
4. The Section on Entering the Characteristics of the Knowable (Jñeyalakṣaṇapraveśa). The Treatise says:
Thus, the characteristics of the knowable have already been explained.
How should one view the entry into the characteristics of the knowable?
The basis for the cultivation of extensive learning is not subsumed under the *ālaya-vijñāna*, yet it functions as a seed just like the *ālaya-vijñāna*.

It consists of mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) accompanied by an aspect (*sākāra*), which—being subsumed under correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*)—arises resembling phenomena and their meanings, and appearing as the objects of apprehension (*grāhya*).
The commentary states:
The manner in which one can gain entry into the characteristics of the objects of knowledge (*jñeyalakṣaṇa*) of this kind shall now be explained.
"Entering the characteristics of the objects of knowledge" means being able to gain entry into the meaning of the objects of knowledge.
"The basis for the perfuming of extensive learning" refers to the self-substance that is perfumed by the Mahāyāna teachings.
"Not subsumed under the ālayavijñāna" means that it serves as the antidote to the ālayavijñāna.
Regarding how the ālayavijñāna functions as a seed: just as the ālayavijñāna is the cause of all defiled phenomena, so too is this [the *tathatā-vyavadāna-bīja*] the cause of all pure phenomena.
"Encompassed by correct mental attention" means that its intrinsic nature is correct mental attention.
"Arising as something resembling the phenomenon and its meaning" means at the time it arises with the appearance of the phenomenon and its meaning.
"Resembling the object of apprehension" means resembling objects such as form (*rūpa*).
"Possessing vision" means resembling the act of seeing; this establishes the existence of consciousness with both aspects (*sanimittaka-sadarśana-vijñāna*).
The treatise says:
Among these, who is capable of realizing the characteristics of that which is to be known?

It is the bodhisattva whose mental continuum has been permeated by extensive hearing of the Mahāyāna, who has already encountered and served immeasurable Buddhas appearing in the world, who has attained resolute and one-pointed conviction, and who has well accumulated all roots of virtue, thereby being fully prepared with the provisions of merit and wisdom.
The commentary states:
Such categories can be entered through these skillful means; this shall now be demonstrated.
Regarding "the continuity of the permeation of extensive learning in the Mahāyāna," this distinguishes it from the continuity of the permeation of extensive learning possessed by Śrāvakas and others.

"Having already encountered and served immeasurable Buddhas appearing in the world" means that one has already encountered and served, face-to-face, Buddhas appearing in the world in numbers exceeding all calculation.

One who has attained a resolute and definitive conviction means that the conviction attained regarding the Mahāyāna cannot be shaken or destroyed by any evil associates; because they have already well accumulated all roots of goodness through the three causes just explained, they are called a bodhisattva who is well-provided with the provisions of merit and wisdom.
Furthermore, how are these very accumulations of merit and wisdom gradually brought to fulfillment?
It is said: by the power of the cause, by the power of virtuous friends, by the power of mental attention, and by the power of the support.
In this context, these two phrases correspond to two powers, which should be understood according to their respective order.
The power of mental attention (*manasikāra*) refers to one-pointed, decisive resolve (*adhimukti*).

Taking the Mahāyāna熏習 (*vāsanā*, perfuming) as its cause and service to the Buddha as its condition, because of this one-pointed, decisive resolve, one is able to cultivate correct practice; by cultivating correct practice, one accumulates roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*). This is called the thorough cultivation of the two provisions of merit and wisdom through the power of mental attention.

Because one gradually and skillfully cultivates the two provisions of merit and wisdom through this process, one is able to enter the Great Grounds; this is what is called "by the power of the support.
The treatise asks:
Into what does one enter?

This refers to the mental verbalization that appears as phenomena and objects within those very states; it occurs during the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*)—which is produced by the Mahāyāna Dharma-characteristics—as well as during the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the ultimate path (*niṣṭhā-mārga*). It consists of the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*) regarding all phenomena, due to the resolute belief in accordance with what has been heard, the thorough penetration according to reality, the remediation of all obstacles, and the departure from all obstacles.
The commentary states:
The entry into such categories and the entry into their modes of activity shall now be demonstrated.

Mental investigation on the level of mind is termed "mental discourse" (*manojalpa*). Such mental discourse arises with the Mahāyāna Dharma as its cause; herein, the distinctions of mental discourse are demonstrated.
That which is "produced by the characteristics of the Mahāyāna Dharma" refers to the meaning that this teaching arises as a condition.

Alternatively, one may be said to "enter" while still at the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*); because one hears that all phenomena are nothing but the nature of consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*) and thereby gives rise to deep faith and understanding, one is called "able to enter."
The manner of entering [into reality] within the path of seeing shall now be demonstrated.
"Because of thorough comprehension according to reality" means that one thoroughly comprehends, in accordance with reality, the mental expressions.
How does one penetrate this through correct reasoning? It is by penetrating it thus:
these mental expressions are neither phenomena (*dharma*) nor objects (*artha*), neither the apprehended (*grāhya*) nor the apprehender (*grāhaka*). This is how one penetrates it.
The manner of entering into realization during the path of cultivation shall now be demonstrated.

Regarding "because it remedies all obstacles": this means that when one contemplates this mental discourse as being neither dharma nor meaning, neither the apprehended object nor the apprehending subject, one is thereby able to remedy all obstacles.
The manner of such realization within the ultimate path shall now be demonstrated.
Regarding the phrase "because of being free from all obscurations," this refers to the stage of perfectly pure, sublime wisdom, wherein even the most subtle obscurations no longer exist.
The treatise says:
By what means can one enter?

It is by being sustained by the power of the roots of goodness; that is to say, by means of three ways of refining the mind, by abandoning four points, and by practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* with constant, earnest application toward the objects of the Dharma and its meaning, without negligence.
The commentary states:
By means of this, one is able to enter; this shall now be demonstrated.
By what means is one able to enter?

"Because it is sustained by the power of the roots of goodness" means that one is sustained by the power of the roots of goodness through being well-aligned with and corresponding to these eight phrases, namely: "by way of refining the mind through three aspects" up to "by constant, earnest application and non-negligence. This is what is meant by being sustained by the power of the roots of goodness.
"Constant" means practicing without interruption.
"Vigorous" means practicing with reverence.
If one practices in such a manner, one will then be able to remain free from negligence.
The treatise says:
That in immeasurable worlds, immeasurable persons and sentient beings realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment moment by moment—this is the first way of tempering the mind.

By means of this intention, one is able to practice the perfections such as generosity; having already attained such an intention, I shall, through it, achieve the fulfillment of the perfections such as generosity by expending little effort—this is called the second exercise of the mind.
If those who have accomplished wholesome deeds that are subject to obstacles are reborn with a complete and desirable physical form immediately at the time of death,
then since I possess sublime and unobstructed wholesome deeds, why should I not obtain every perfection at that time?
This is called the third refinement of the mind.
The commentary states:
herein, because one counteracts three kinds of despondent minds, one cultivates only these three refinements of the mind.

Why is this? Because when bodhisattvas hear that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is most supreme, profound, vast, and difficult to realize, their minds become discouraged and retreat.
To counteract this, one cultivates the first refinement of the mind.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas hear that the cultivation of the perfections (pāramitās) is most supreme, profound, vast, and difficult to realize, their minds may become discouraged and retreat.
To counteract this, one cultivates the second refinement of the mind.
Regarding the statement that "by means of this intention one is able to practice the perfections such as generosity," the "intention" here refers to faith and aspiration.

When a bodhisattva develops profound faith and understanding that the perfections possess true intrinsic nature, the nature of possessing merit, and the nature of being capable, this is called "faith."
Having attained deep faith and understanding, one takes delight in practicing; this is called "desire" (*chanda*).

Once a bodhisattva has attained such faith and desire, through their natural inclination and with little exertion of effort, they shall bring the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) to full completion through cultivation.
Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas skillfully engage in reflection and discernment regarding the Buddha’s profound and vast teachings, they deliberate thus:
"This unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is difficult to realize; it can only be realized after the interval of a single moment of mind."
The mind then becomes discouraged.
To counteract this, one cultivates the third refinement of the mind:
"I possess sublime excellence," meaning that I have accumulated the provisions of merit and wisdom—the sublime excellence found throughout all ten stages.

Regarding "wholesome without obstruction": this refers to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), which is able to shatter the subtle and extremely difficult-to-break obstructions consisting of the coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) residing within the bones; immediately following this concentration, one attains the fundamental transformation (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) that is the dissociation from all obstructions.

Regarding the question, "Why would one not attain all perfections at that time? the intended meaning here is that through liberation from obstacles, the omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*)—which resembles [the state of] death—is perfected in its essence, just like that [attainment].

Furthermore, regarding the three kinds of mental refinement within this context: it means that bodhisattvas possess no deficiency in their roots of goodness and are sustained by the power of those roots; by virtue of this power, they are able to refine their minds in these three ways, so that their minds do not succumb to despondency or retreat.

First, one should demonstrate the first kind of mental fortitude (*cittaparicaya*): "In the human realm, within immeasurable worlds, immeasurable sentient beings are able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment moment by moment; why then am I alone unable to realize it?"
Next, the second refinement of the mind shall be demonstrated. This refers to the bodhisattvas’ reflection:

"This intention of mine is free from all obstacles, for there are no obstacles such as stinginess regarding the perfections (*pāramitā*). Thus, without effort, the perfections shall become fully perfected; and through this perfection, I shall realize the Buddha’s *bodhi*."
Next, the third refinement of the mind shall be demonstrated. Regarding those whose virtue is obstructed, this means their virtue is accomplished through worldly merit.

Even such obstructed virtue results in the birth of one who possesses a desirable and complete physical form at the time of death; how much more so for me, whose virtue is accomplished through unobstructed merit—there is no possibility that I should not attain the unsurpassed enlightenment of Buddhahood.
The treatise says:
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"The sentient beings within the human realm / Are infinite in number and location."
In every thought-moment one realizes equal enlightenment; therefore, one should not succumb to despondency.
Since these superior ones have already attained the pure mental dispositions that enable the practice of generosity and the like, they are thus able to cultivate generosity and the rest.
When a virtuous person dies, they attain the fulfillment of their own wishes according to their pleasure;
since supreme goodness arises from eternal cessation, how could such perfection not exist?
The commentary states:
Furthermore, this meaning is clarified by means of a verse.
Therefore, one should not be discouraged; by means of the aforementioned causes and conditions, one should sustain the mind so that it does not become timid or weak, giving rise to this thought:
"I am unable to realize unsurpassed bodhi."
The phrase "those with pure minds" does not mean that these are non-unwholesome or neutral states of mind.
This refers, for instance, to those who practice giving and so forth with a distracted, neutral mind, or to such non-Buddhists (tīrthika) who practice giving and so forth with an unwholesome mind.
If one seeks unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, this is the most supreme goodness; therefore, it is called the "pure mind.

Regarding the statement that "this victor, having already attained [it], is able to practice generosity and so forth": the most supreme bodhisattva is termed a "victor. Since this bodhisattva has already attained such an intentionality (*āśaya*), he is therefore able to cultivate the various perfections (*pāramitā*) such as generosity.

"Having already attained the meaning of the mind that is able to sever the objects of abandonment such as stinginess (*mātsarya*) and so forth" refers to taking [the stages] beginning from ethical discipline (*śīla*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

"The virtuous one attains fulfillment according to their wish at the time of death" refers to the meaning of having attained even the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Regarding the question, "How can there be no supreme goodness through the perfection of eternal abandonment?"—it means that how could it be meaningless for the fruit of Buddhahood to be accomplished as the perfection of supreme goodness by way of the eternal abandonment of hindrances?
The treatise says:
Because one has abandoned the mental orientations (*manasikāra*) of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
and because, through the removal of doubt regarding the Mahāyāna, one is able to permanently sever the doubts arising from divergent views.
Because one abandons the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self regarding the dharmas that are heard and reflected upon, one severs attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).

Because one is without volitional engagement (*manasikāra*) and without conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) regarding all manifest, present, and established marks (*nimitta*), one severs conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Regarding this, there is a verse:
Abiding naturally in the presence [of reality], Establishing all appearances,
The wise do not engage in conceptual discrimination, And thus attain supreme enlightenment.
The commentary states:
Now, the abandonment of the four points shall be demonstrated.
"Because of abandoning mental attention" means because of abandoning the various forms of mental attention belonging to the śrāvakas and others.

Regarding the phrase "because it can forever sever divergent wisdom and doubt": this means that with respect to the profound and vast Mahāyāna, one is able to forever eliminate divergent wisdom and doubt.
Herein, "divergent wisdom" refers to base and corrupt wisdom that wavers from the truth.
"Doubt" refers to indecision.

Regarding the phrase "those who have abandoned doubt concerning all doubts about the Mahāyāna": this refers to the teachings on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) established as the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) within the Mahāyāna—namely, that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), unarisen and unceasing, originally quiescent, and by nature in *nirvāṇa*. Such statements are not merely alternative formulations; they are definitive.

This is spoken in reliance upon the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva); it refers to various such false designations as the fact that all phenomena are like illusions, mirages, dream-images, reflections, shadows, echoes, the moon in water, and magical transformations.

It is spoken of in dependence upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), when one speaks of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, the reality limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), signlessness (*animitta*), the ultimate (*paramārtha*), the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
All such true synonyms are spoken in reliance upon the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); regarding this, all divergent views and doubts shall never again arise.

Regarding the phrase "by abandoning the grasping at self and what belongs to self within the phenomena that are heard and contemplated," the intended meaning here is the abandonment of the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

Because one abandons the grasping at phenomena, as long as one clings to self and what belongs to self within the phenomena that are heard and contemplated, one will ultimately never gain authentic realization and entry into them.

Regarding "because there is no mental engagement and no conceptualization among all established aspects that are present and currently abiding": this means that when non-conceptual wisdom of application (*prayoga-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) functions, one dwells in all meditative concentrations through correct mental engagement (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), whereby all mental engagements with and conceptualizations of aspects are severed.

Regarding "by means of severing conceptualization": this refers to not directing the mind toward or making any conceptual distinctions regarding any objective signs of the spheres of perception—whether they are the forms and so forth currently present before one, or those established through meditative concentration such as the skeleton and so forth. One is able to enter [the state] by means of this non-conceptualizing method; if one were to engage in other types of conceptualization, one would ultimately be unable to enter.
The verses beginning with "Abiding naturally before one's eyes" (*pratyakṣa-svayaṃ-sthita*) manifest only the meaning of what is to be abandoned last.
The treatise asks:
By what means and in what manner does one attain realization?
The commentary states:
This question is posed in order to demonstrate that one enters [into reality] by means of this very [method].
The treatise says:

The commentary states: "By means of mental verbalization that appears as the dharma and its meaning, which is comprised of correct attention of the type derived from the perfuming of hearing—through this, one enters [into reality];
this shall now be demonstrated."

In this context, that which belongs to the category of the perfuming of hearing refers to that which arises from the aforementioned entry into and maintenance of the Mahāyāna perfuming, taking the perfuming of hearing as its cause; it should be understood as being subsumed within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The treatise says: Through the four types of investigation— namely, the investigation of designations based on names, objects, intrinsic natures, and distinctions—

and through the four types of thorough knowledge as it truly is— namely, thorough knowledge as it truly is regarding names, things, intrinsic natures, and distinctions— all such [designations] are equally unapprehendable.

Because Bodhisattvas thus cultivate the preparatory application (*prayoga*) in accordance with reality in order to enter into representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), they investigate the mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) that appears as words and appears as meanings; they investigate that words and names are merely mental verbalization; they investigate that the meanings based upon these words and names are also merely mental verbalization; and they investigate that the intrinsic nature and specific differences of names and meanings are merely conceptual designations (*prajñapti*).

When one realizes that there is only mental discourse (*manojalpa*), at that time one realizes and knows that whether it be names or objects, their intrinsic natures and distinctions are all merely provisional designations; because the characteristics of intrinsic nature and distinction do not exist, they are equally unapprehendable.

By means of the four investigations and the four kinds of thorough knowledge of reality as it is, one is able to penetrate this mental verbalization—which appears as words and appears as meanings—and realize that there is only the nature of consciousness.
The commentary states:
This manner of realization shall now be demonstrated.
"By means of the four investigations" refers to that which is elucidated by the scriptural expressions concerning name, object, intrinsic nature, and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the four kinds of thorough knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*), these are explained by means of the textual expressions concerning the designation of names, things, intrinsic natures, and distinctions.

As it truly is, one thoroughly knows that whether it be names, things, intrinsic natures, or distinctions, all are merely provisional designations; within them, no real referent can be found. Therefore, it is said that they are all alike unfindable.

Furthermore, first one investigates whether names, meanings, intrinsic natures, or distinctions are merely provisional designations; subsequently, one knows as it truly is that such realities are all unfindable. This process of investigation is termed "investigation" (vitarka).
When one knows, as it truly is, that [the object] is unobtainable, this is called the fourfold thorough knowledge of reality (*yathābhūta-parijñāna*).
The treatise says:
"In this context of entering into the nature of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*)."
What is realized and entered?
How is it realized and entered?

One enters the nature of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*), wherein the two natures of appearance and seeing, as well as various natures—namely, the six types of objects consisting of names, referents, intrinsic natures, distinctions, conventional designations of intrinsic nature, and conventional designations of distinction—are all non-existent. This is because the natures of the grasped and the grasper manifest before one, arising simultaneously as if resembling various appearances and referents.
It is like a rope appearing as a snake in the darkness; for example, the snake upon the rope is not real because it does not exist.
If one has already understood that its object is non-existent, although the cognition of the snake ceases, the cognition of the rope remains.

If one analyzes it by way of subtle categories, since this too has the false appearance of color, odor, taste, and touch as its characteristic, this cognition should be sublated by the cognition of the rope upon which it depends.

In this way, when the unreal sixfold aspects of meaning are suppressed within those mental verbalizations that appear as words and meanings, the awareness of the nature of consciousness-only must likewise be eliminated—just as the awareness of a snake [is eliminated]—by means of the awareness of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The commentary states:
Herein, the question concerns that which is realized and the analogy for realization.
"The nature of representation-only" means the state of being merely representation-only.

Regarding "the two natures of the grasped and the grasper," this reveals that consciousness possesses both the aspect of the grasped (*nimitta*) and the aspect of the grasper (*darśana*). It is called the "grasped" because it manifests as if it were a cause or as if it were an established object.

As for "various natures," these are merely the manifestation of a single consciousness appearing as if various aspects of the grasped were present; they do not appear as distinct entities because they do not arise with rapid succession.
Within this entry into the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), these three types are that which is to be entered.

Regarding "arising simultaneously as appearing like various objects of meaning": this means arising as appearing like various signs of names, phrases, and syllables, and arising as appearing like various bases upon which those meanings depend.
In this context, the analogy of the rope demonstrates the entry into the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Regarding the phrase "when suppressing the six aspects of unreal meaning," this refers to the time when the six aspects of unreal meaning are eliminated; here, "elimination" is termed "suppressing."
The Commentary states:

In this way, because the bodhisattva realizes that mental discourse appears as the semblance of objects, he realizes the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva); because he realizes that there is only consciousness (vijñapti-mātra), he realizes the nature of the dependent origination (paratantra-svabhāva).
How does one awaken to and enter the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)?

When the conceptualization of consciousness-only—which is of the same category as the mental verbalization and the permeation of hearing the Dharma—has been eliminated, at that time the Bodhisattva has already discarded the conceptualization of objects; since no semblance of objects can arise, even the semblance of consciousness-only cannot arise.

By means of these causes and conditions, one abides in the name that is non-conceptual regarding all objects; within the dharmadhātu, one then attains direct perception and dwells in accordance with it. At that time, the Bodhisattva’s non-conceptual wisdom—in which the object of cognition and the cognizing subject are perfectly equal—has already arisen. By virtue of this, the Bodhisattva is said to have realized and entered the pariniṣpanna-svabhāva (the perfected nature).
The commentary states:

"To enter into the imagined nature by means of realizing that mental discourse appears as the semblance of objects" means to know that all objects are merely the products of imagined conceptual construction.
For this reason, it is said that one enters into the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Regarding the statement that "one enters into the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) by entering into consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*)," the mention of "consciousness-only" refers to mental verbalization (*manojalpa*); by realizing that all things are of the nature of mental verbalization, one thereby enters into the dependent nature.
"That nothing resembling an object can possibly arise" means that there is no such real object of that category for which [consciousness] could arise as a resemblance.
"Therefore, even that which resembles representation-only cannot arise" means that the characteristic of representation-only itself cannot manifest.
Why is this? Because it is reckoned that at the very moment consciousness arises, there is already an object.
From this point onward, one directly realizes suchness; this stage of direct realization cannot be described, for it is internally self-realized.

At that time, when the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*)—in which the object of cognition (*ālambana*) and the cognizing subject (*ālambaka*) are both equally equal—has already arisen for the Bodhisattva: the "object" refers to suchness (*tathatā*), and the "cognizing subject" refers to true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). These two are equal like space; this is precisely the meaning of not abiding in the dual nature of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*).
Because one does not conceptually differentiate between the grasped object and the grasping subject, it is called non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
In this way, one enters into the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The treatise states:
Regarding this, there is a verse:
The Dharma and the person, The nature of the Dharma and its meaning—concise and extensive, Impurity, purity, and the ultimate;
These are the distinctions of the objects of the name.
The commentary states:
Regarding what was previously explained as "dwelling in the name that is non-conceptual with respect to all objects," what is this "name"?
And how many categories of objects does it comprise?
To answer this question, the distinctions between names and categories are demonstrated by means of verse.
Herein, "names of phenomena" (dharma-nāman) refers to such things as form, sensation, eye, ear, and so forth.
"Names of persons" (pudgala-nāman) refers to the Buddha, those who follow through faith (śraddhānusārin), and others.
Furthermore, "name of the phenomenon" refers to the sūtras and so forth;
"name of the meaning" refers to the meaning based upon these phenomena;
and "abbreviated name" refers to [terms such as] "sentient beings" and the like.
"Extensive names" refers to those individual designators for each [phenomenon].
"Names of personal identity" refers to the primary phonemes (*mātṛkā*).
"Impure names" refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
"Pure designation" refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth.
"Ultimate designation" refers to the objective referent (*ālambana*) that is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
Briefly stated, there are ten types of designations that serve as the objective referents for these bodhisattvas:
First is the designation of phenomena (*dharma-nāman*), such as the eye and so forth;
second is the designation of persons (*pudgala-nāman*), such as the self and so forth;
third is the designation of the teachings (*dharma-nāman*), namely the twelvefold division of the scriptures.
Fourth is the name of meaning (*arthasaṃjñā*), which refers to all the meanings elucidated by these twelve divisions of the teaching.
Fifth is the abbreviated name (*saṃkṣiptasaṃjñā*), which refers to categories such as all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.
Sixth is the detailed name (*vistārāsaṃjñā*), which refers to [specific categories] such as form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth, as well as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth.
Seventh is the name of designation (*nāman*), which begins with the letter *a* and ends with the letter *ha*.
Eighth is the name of the impure (*aśuddha-nāman*), referring to all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Ninth is the name of the pure (*śuddha-nāman*), referring to those who have realized the truths (*dṛṣṭasatya*).
The ten names for ultimate reality refer to the objective support of the general characteristics of all phenomena; that is, they are the objective spheres of two types of wisdom.

These are supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). This is because supramundane wisdom takes the suchness (*tathatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all phenomena as its objective support, whereas subsequently attained wisdom takes the various distinct characteristics of all phenomena as its objective support, as is the case with the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and so forth.

In this context, the intended meaning refers to the objective sphere of the wisdom that takes the general characteristics of all objects as its focal point; such categories constitute the specific range of activity for these bodhisattvas.
The Commentary states:
Because such a bodhisattva awakens to and enters the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), they awaken to and enter the characteristics of the knowable (*jñeyalakṣaṇa*).

By entering this, they enter the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*); they skillfully penetrate the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), are born into the family of the Tathāgatas, attain the mind-nature equal to all sentient beings, attain the mind-nature equal to all bodhisattvas, and attain the mind-nature equal to all Buddhas. This is precisely what is called the bodhisattva’s path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The commentary states:
"Born into the family of the Tathāgatas" means that by this, the lineage of all Buddhas is rendered unbroken.
"Attaining the mind-nature equal to that of all sentient beings" is due to forming this thought:
Just as I myself desire parinirvāṇa, so it is for all sentient beings;
one who attains the state of equality of mind with all bodhisattvas does so by attaining the equal intention (*āśaya*) of a bodhisattva.

Regarding "attaining the mind-nature that is equal to all Buddhas": because one attains the Buddha-dharmakāya within this stage, and by realizing it, one attains the mind-nature that is equal to all Buddhas.

Furthermore, "attaining the state of mind that is equal toward all sentient beings" means realizing the equality of self and others; thus, just as one desires to exhaust all suffering for oneself, one does so for others as well.
To attain the state of mind that is equal with all bodhisattvas means that one’s intention and application are entirely equal to those of all bodhisattvas.
To attain the state of mind that is equal with all Buddhas means that one perceives no distinction between their *dharmadhātu* and one’s own *dharmadhātu*.
The Commentary states:
Furthermore, for what purpose does one enter the nature of consciousness-only?

It is by means of supramundane śamatha and vipaśyanā wisdom that takes all-encompassing phenomena as its object, and by means of the subsequently attained wisdom that recognizes the various marks of consciousness.

In order to sever the seeds of the various characteristics of the *ālayavijñāna*, in order to cultivate the seeds capable of touching the *dharmakāya*, in order to transform the basis (*āśraya*), in order to realize all Buddha-dharmas, and in order to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), one enters the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*).
Furthermore, subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) perceives, without error, the nature of all objects of cognition produced from the ālayavijñāna as being like an illusion and so forth.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva is like a magician who, regarding the illusory phenomena, the various signs, and the teaching of cause and effect, is always free from error.
The commentary explains:
"By means of the supramundane wisdom of calm abiding and insight that takes all-encompassing phenomena as its object" refers to the wisdom manifested through calm abiding and insight.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of severing the seeds of the various characteristics of the ālayavijñāna and its associated [factors]": here, "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "associated with causes. The seeds of all defiled phenomena within the ālayavijñāna are called "the seeds of the various characteristics of the ālayavijñāna."
Furthermore, regarding the mention of "characteristics" (*nimitta*): it is intended to demonstrate that those very seeds are the objective characteristics (*ālambana-nimitta*).
Having stated this, it is shown that both the cause and the fruit of those seeds are severed.
If non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) severs all obscurations and realizes the Buddha-dharmas, what further use is there for subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*)?
Non-conceptual wisdom cannot expound upon the dharmas of cause and effect, because it is non-conceptual.

For this reason, one must rely on subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) to proclaim all dharmas of cause and effect without ever erring, just as a magician does with his magical illusions.
"Arising from all ālayavijñāna" means that the ālayavijñāna serves as the cause. "Within all aspects of discernment" means that consciousness serves as the cause;

thus, when perceiving the object-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-aspect (*darśanabhāga*) through subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) as being like an illusion and so forth, as well as when explaining them, there is no error whatsoever.
The treatise says:

When entering into this realization of the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), there are four kinds of samādhi that serve as the basis for the four stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
How should these be understood?

It should be understood that through the four investigations, within the stage of receptivity to the non-existence of objects at the lower level, there arises the samādhi of "attainment of clarity" (*ālokalabdha*), which is the basis for the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) stage of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

Within the superior stage of patience regarding the absence of external objects, there is the samādhi of increased clarity, which is the basis for the "Summit" stage of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

Furthermore, by means of the four kinds of thorough knowledge of reality as it is, one has entered into representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and attained certainty regarding the absence of external objects; at this point, there is the samādhi of entering a portion of the true meaning, which is the basis for the "Patience" stage of the aids to penetration.

Immediately following this, by subduing the perception of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), there arises the "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) samādhi, which serves as the basis for the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
One should know that such samādhis constitute the stage of the "limits of clear observation" (*abhisamayāntika*).
The commentary states:
Since the four stages conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) are present in all instances when one enters true contemplation (bhūtapratyavekṣā), they should also be demonstrated herein.
Regarding "the basis for the levels conducive to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), this refers to the sense of being the support for the causes of penetration.

As for "the samādhi of attaining clarity (*ālokalabdha*) within the stage of weak receptivity toward the absence of objects," this means that one gives rise to a weak degree of delight regarding the absence of objects; the term "clarity" (*āloka*) reveals the weak cognition of the absence of objects, while the name "samādhi" reveals the meditative concentration that serves as the support for this cognition of the absence of objects.
Regarding "the superior patience toward the non-objective," this means giving rise to a superior degree of attachment and delight toward that which is non-objective.

Regarding "the samādhi of increased clarity," the term "clarity" (vidyā) indicates the superior wisdom regarding the non-objective, while the term "samādhi" indicates the meditative concentration that serves as the basis for this wisdom regarding the non-objective.

Regarding the basis of the patience that accords with the truth (*satyānulomikī kṣānti*): the principle of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) is called "truth" (*satya*); because this patience accords with that, it is termed "patience that accords with the truth.
How is this established?

It means that for one who has already attained certainty regarding the non-existence of the external [object], there is also a profound delight in the non-existence of the grasper (*grāhaka*); one should know that this occurs when the patience that accords with benefit (*hitānulomikī kṣānti*) is operative.
"Regarding 'at the conclusion of clear realization' (*abhisamayāntika*), this refers to the meaning at the time of clear realization.
The treatise says:

Having thus entered the stages (*bhūmi*), having attained the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and having entered into representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), how does the bodhisattva practice within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?"

Within the manifestation of all sūtras as they are established in the ten stages as described above, because of the supramundane and subsequently attained wisdom of śamatha and vipaśyanā that takes the universal dharma as its object, and because of having practiced for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, one attains the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti).
One diligently practices in order to realize the three bodies of a Buddha.
The commentary states:
"Regarding the ten stages established as previously described" refers to the ten bodhisattva stages established according to their respective explanations.
Regarding "taking general phenomena as the object," this means taking general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as the object, rather than taking them through conceptual discrimination.
What is called "supramundane" refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

Subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is that which establishes [the realization]; it should not be said to be exclusively mundane, because it has not yet been fully cultivated within the mundane realm.
Nor should it be said that this is exclusively supramundane, because it manifests in accordance with the mundane; for these reasons, it cannot be definitively stated [as one or the other].
Furthermore, those who attain the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) do so by means of the cognition of the totality (sarvālambana-jñāna).
One who practices with diligent effort desiring to realize the three bodies of a Buddha—that is, one who practices with the thought, "I shall realize the three bodies of a Buddha.
The treatise asks:
What is the distinction between the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of a Śrāvaka and the clear realization of a Bodhisattva?
It should be understood that the clear realization (abhisamaya) of a bodhisattva differs from that of a śrāvaka by way of eleven kinds of distinctions.
First, by way of the distinction of the object of focus (ālambana), because it takes the Mahāyāna teachings as its object of focus.
Second, by way of the distinction of sustenance, because it takes the two kinds of provisions—great merit and great wisdom—as its sustenance.
Third, by way of the distinction of penetration, because it is able to penetrate the selflessness of persons and phenomena.
Fourth, by way of the distinction of nirvāṇa, because it embraces the great non-abiding nirvāṇa;
fifth, by way of the distinction of the stages (bhūmi), because one attains transcendence by relying upon the ten stages.
The sixth and seventh [differences] arise from the distinction of purity, because they purify the Buddha-fields by severing the habitual tendencies of the afflictions.
The eighth arises from the distinction of attaining a mind of equality toward oneself and others, because their application in maturing sentient beings is without rest.
Ninth, by the distinction of birth, because of being born into the family of the Tathāgatas.
Tenth, by the distinction of taking birth, because of constantly assuming birth within the great assemblies of all Buddhas.

Eleventh, by the distinction of the fruit (*phala-viśeṣa*), because the fruits of the immeasurable qualities—the ten powers (*daśabala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the unique Buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*)—are fully perfected.
The commentary states:

Regarding the distinction of *nirvāṇa*, this is because the Bodhisattva’s clear realization (*abhisamaya*) embraces non-abiding great parinirvāṇa (*apratiṣṭhita-mahāparinirvāṇa*), whereas the Śrāvaka does not.

Regarding the distinction of purity: because the bodhisattva’s clear realization permanently severs both the afflictions and their habitual tendencies, they are able to purify buddha-fields; the śrāvaka is not so.
The treatise says:
In this regard, there are two verses:
Name and thing are mutual guests; Their nature should be investigated through analytical inquiry.
These two should also be examined as being merely cognition and merely designation.
When true wisdom contemplates the absence of external objects, there is only the threefold conceptualization;
because that [object] does not exist, this [conceptualization] is absent—this is precisely the entry into the three natures.
The commentary states:
These two verses are spoken as one is about to enter true contemplation (*bhūta-darśana*).

Regarding the phrase "name and thing are mutually guests; their nature should be investigated": this means that name is a guest with respect to the thing, and the thing is a guest with respect to the name, because neither corresponds to the actual essence (*svabhāva*) of the other.
Because one observes through meditative concentration, it is called "investigation" (*vitarka*).

Regarding these two [aspects], one should also infer that they are merely measure (*mātra*) and merely designation (*prajñapti*); one should investigate that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and specific characteristics (*viśeṣa*) of objects do not exist at all, but that there is only the measure of consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*) and only the provisional establishment of intrinsic nature and specific characteristics.

Regarding the term "knowledge of reality," it should be understood as thorough knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta-parijñā*); that is to say, by taking the four kinds of investigation (*paryeṣaṇā*) as causes, the four kinds of thorough knowledge of things as they truly are are produced.

Regarding the statement that "one contemplates the non-existence of objects and the presence of only conceptual construction," this means that one contemplates how objects fundamentally do not exist at all, and that there is only the three kinds of false conceptual construction: namely, conceptual construction of names, conceptual construction of intrinsic nature, and conceptual construction of distinctions.
"Because that does not exist, this does not exist" means that because the object does not exist, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) also does not exist.
Why is this? If there were an object to be conceptually constructed, there could be a conceptual construction that takes it as its objective support (*ālambana*).
Because objects do not exist, one should know that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) also does not exist.

This is precisely what it means to enter the three natures (*trisvabhāva*); that is, within this context, one realizes and enters the three natures by observing and seeing that names and things are mutually adventitious, which is the realization of the nature of the imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Observing that these two kinds [of objects] are fundamentally without objective reality, but exist only as the measure of conceptual discrimination and are merely nominally established through the differentiation of intrinsic natures, one thereby enters into the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, because one does not perceive this discrimination, one thereby enters into the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
This is what is called entering into the three natures.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, there are two verses of instruction as taught in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (Treatise on the Analysis of Yoga):
"When a bodhisattva is in the state of meditative equipoise, They observe that the reflected image is nothing but mind;
Once the conceptualization of external objects has been eliminated, They scrutinize that it is nothing but their own mental representation."
Thus abiding in the inner mind, one knows that the apprehended object does not exist;
next, the apprehending subject is also absent; finally, one touches upon non-apprehension.
Commentary:
To lead them into true contemplation, he bestows the correct teaching; regarding this meaning, he speaks two verses.

When a bodhisattva, relying on the state of meditative concentration, contemplates that the reflected image is merely mind, it means that they contemplate the images resembling phenomena and resembling objects as being nothing other than their own mind.
Who is able to contemplate?
It is the bodhisattva.
In what stage does he abide?

Regarding the phrase "in the state of meditative equipoise, having eliminated the perception of objects, one carefully contemplates that only one's own perception remains": this means that in this state, once the perception of external objects has been dispelled, one carefully contemplates that the perceptions appearing as phenomena and appearing as objects are merely one's own mind.
Thus, for one who abides in the internal mind, just as one withdraws the self-mind and abides in the absence of objects, so too does one cause the mind to abide in the internal mind.
"Knowing that the apprehended object does not exist" means realizing that the apprehended object has no reality whatsoever.

Regarding "next, the grasper is also non-existent": since the object of grasping (the apprehended) is already non-existent, the nature of the mind that grasps it (the grasper) cannot be established either.

Regarding "subsequently touching the non-apprehendable": this means that from this point onward, one touches and realizes suchness; because this suchness is non-apprehendable, it is termed "non-apprehendable."
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, there are five other verses on the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*), as stated in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*:
"The two provisions of merit and wisdom, The Bodhisattva has well prepared them without limit."
Having thoroughly deliberated upon and correctly resolved the Dharma, one realizes that the meaning of objects is merely a category of words.
If one knows that all objects are but words, one then abides in the state of "mere-mind" (cittamātra) which resembles those objects;
thus, one is able to directly realize the true Dharmadhātu, whereby both dualistic appearances are completely eliminated.
Realizing through direct experience that there is no separate entity apart from the mind, one thereby understands that the mind itself does not exist.
The wise person comprehends that both are non-existent and abides equally in the true dharma-realm where both are absent.
The wise possess the power of non-conceptual wisdom, which operates universally and with equanimity in constant accordance with reality;
it extinguishes the thicket of dependencies and the mass of faults, just as a great medicinal elixir neutralizes all poisons.

The Buddha has well established the sublime Dharma; With wisdom and roots settled within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), One understands that the movement of thought is merely conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); With valor, one swiftly returns to the shore of virtue.
The commentary states:
Furthermore, there are verses on clear realization (*abhisamaya*) as taught in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
Those points therein that are difficult to understand are elucidated here.
Regarding the bodhisattva who has well-prepared the two provisions of merit and wisdom, which are boundless:
there are two kinds of provisions—first, the provision of merit; second, the provision of wisdom.

That is to say, the three perfections beginning with generosity constitute the accumulation of merit; the sixth perfection, wisdom, constitutes the accumulation of wisdom; and the perfection of diligence is subsumed within both accumulations.
Why is this? If one practices diligence for the sake of wisdom, it is the provision for wisdom; if one practices diligence for the sake of merit, it is the provision for merit.

In this way, the perfection of meditative concentration also pertains to two types: if one cultivates meditative concentration by taking the immeasurables as its object, it is the provision of merit; otherwise, it is the provision of wisdom.
To whom do such provisions belong? They belong to all bodhisattvas.

That which is long-lasting and difficult to traverse is called "boundless" (*anantapāra*); just as the term "boundless" does not mean that there is no limit at all, but rather receives the designation "boundless" simply because it is so vast, this is also the same.

Regarding the phrase "having thoroughly deliberated upon and resolved the dharmas": one must rely on reflection upon all dharmas following meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in order to achieve such thorough resolution; this is not possible through any other means.

Thus, the statement that "the realization of the meaning consists solely in the category of verbal expression" means that one understands all meanings to have only mental discourse (*manojalpa*) as their cause.

If one knows that all objects are merely words and thus abides in the principle that they are merely mind appearing as those [objects], this means: if one realizes that what appears as objects is merely mental verbalization, one then abides in the correct principle that there is only mind appearing as objects, and is thereby able to directly realize the true dharmadhātu.

Therefore, "the two aspects are entirely eliminated" means that from this point onward one realizes *tathatā* through direct perception, forever departing from the two aspects of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), as will be demonstrated next in the section on direct realization.

"Realizing that there is no separate entity apart from the mind, one thereby understands that the mind itself does not exist": this means realizing that there is no object of cognition apart from the mind; since that [object] does not exist, one thereby understands that the cognizing mind also does not exist.
"The knower who realizes that both are non-existent" means that all bodhisattvas thoroughly realize that these two are entirely non-existent.
"Abiding equally in the true dharmadhātu where both are non-existent" means abiding in equanimity within the true dharmadhātu, which is free from objects and free from mind.
"The power of the non-conceptual wisdom of the wise" refers to the inherent potency of the non-conceptual wisdom possessed by all bodhisattvas.

"Pervasive, equal, and always acting in accordance" means that within the state of equality, they act in conformity with it, because they contemplate all phenomena, such as the sūtras and so forth, as being equal in nature to space.
All internal and external phenomena are viewed in this manner; therefore, it is called "universal.
"Constant" means perpetual throughout time.

Regarding the phrase "extinguishing that which relies upon a thicket of faults and a mass of defects, like a great fine medicine that eliminates all poisons": "extinguishing" (nirodha) refers to eradication; "reliance" (āśraya) refers to the basis, specifically the causes of defiled phenomena within that basis, which are extremely difficult to comprehend.
Just as a mountain stream or a forest thicket is difficult to enter, so too is the accumulation of faults;
this refers to the intrinsic nature of the perfuming of afflicted (*saṃkleśa*) phenomena.

When the Buddha says that the sublime Dharma is well-established within the dharmadhātu along with wisdom and its roots, it means that through the Buddha’s teaching, one properly settles wisdom within true suchness (*tathatā*) and within the fundamental mind that takes that [suchness] as its object.
The fundamental mind refers to taking all the authentic teachings of the Tathāgata as a single characteristic; one should know that this is precisely the non-conceptual mind.

Regarding "knowing that the movement of mindfulness is merely conceptual construction": this means that once one abides in the fundamental mind, the authentic teachings are expounded for them; through subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), one recollects the various meanings and movements [of the teachings], knowing that these movements of mindfulness are solely conceptual construction.

"Bravely and swiftly returning to the shore of the ocean of virtue" refers to how all bodhisattvas, by means of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), as well as skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), quickly proceed toward the shore of the ocean of merit that is the fruit of Buddhahood.

The general meaning of these five verses is as follows: the first verse reveals the path of accumulation (*sambhāramārga*); the first half of the second verse reveals the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), while its second half and the third verse reveal the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); the fourth verse reveals the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); and the fifth verse reveals the path of culmination (*niṣṭhāmārga*).
Commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, Fascicle Six;
Commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, Fascicle Seven.
Composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Part Five: The Section on Entering Its Cause and Result. The Treatise says:
Thus, the entry into the characteristics of the knowable has already been explained. How is that entry into its cause and result to be perceived?
That is to say, by means of the six perfections (pāramitās): generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
How does one enter into consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra) by means of these six perfections?
Furthermore, how do the six *pāramitās* constitute the fruit of that entry?

It means that when this bodhisattva does not cling to wealth or status, does not violate ethical discipline (*śīla*), remains unshakable in the face of suffering, and is untiring in cultivation—such that these causes of distraction do not manifest—the mind becomes one-pointed on a single object. Thereby, one is able to discern all phenomena according to reality and attain entry into *vijñaptimātra*.
Having entered into consciousness-only by relying on the six pāramitās, the bodhisattva realizes the six kinds of pāramitās that are subsumed within the pure superior intention (*adhyāśaya*).

Therefore, in this regard, even if one is separated from the manifest application of the six perfections, by virtue of gaining resolute conviction in the sublime teaching and through the mental engagements of cherishing, sympathetic joy, and delight, one will constantly and uninterruptedly apply the skillful means of cultivation and swiftly bring the six perfections to fulfillment.
The commentary states:
If one attains entry into consciousness-only at that time, then at that very moment one realizes the perfection of the pure superior intention (*adhyāśaya-pāramitā*).
"Manifesting application" refers to the active practice of the perfections.

Regarding those who attain resolute conviction in the sublime teaching: it refers to those who, even though this sublime teaching associated with the *pāramitās* is extremely profound, are nonetheless able to believe and understand it.
The mental attention of cherishing (*premanīya-manasikāra*) refers to generating a profound sense of affection and savoring for those very qualities upon seeing their superior merits.

The mental attention of aspiration (*abhinandanā-manasikāra*) refers to the pure intention (*āśaya*) attained by the Buddhas who have reached the most supreme further shore, with the wish that oneself and all sentient beings may likewise realize it.
The Treatise says:
In this regard, there are three verses:
Having perfected the white dharmas, And having attained sharp and swift patience,
Regarding the profound and vast teachings of their own vehicle,
Bodhisattvas realize that all is mere conceptual construction;
attaining non-conceptual wisdom and seeking pure resolute conviction, their intention becomes pure.
"In the past and within this stream of the Dharma, / All have been able to see the Buddhas;
/ They realize that Bodhi is near, / Because it is obtained without difficulty.
By these three verses, the seven aspects of the pure superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) are revealed in summary:

That is to say: by way of the provisions (*sambhāra*), by way of endurance (*kṣānti*), by way of the object of focus (*ālambana*), by way of mental attention (*manasikāra*), by way of the essential nature (*svabhāva*), by way of the auspicious signs (*nimitta*), and by way of the benefits (*anuśaṃsa*).
One should understand that these phrases in the verses reveal [these topics] in their respective order.
The commentary states:
What are the characteristics of such a purified superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) that enable it to encompass those perfections (*pāramitā*)?
To answer this question, three verses are next spoken to reveal its characteristics.

"Having perfected the white dharmas" means that because one has previously well-prepared the accumulations on the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*), the white dharmas are perfected therein.
Furthermore, regarding "having attained sharp and swift patience": patience is of three grades—mild, middling, and superior; among these, the most superior is called "sharp and swift patience."
One attains purity through this object of focus, which shall now be demonstrated.

Regarding the "profound and vast teachings of one's own vehicle" for a bodhisattva: the Mahāyāna is referred to as "one's own vehicle" because it expounds immeasurable matters that are profound and vast.
The selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) is called the profound matter; the various samādhis such as the *ākāśagarbha* are called the vast matters.
Through this mental attention (*manasikāra*), one attains purification; this shall now be demonstrated.

Regarding the statement that "perfect awakening consists solely in the realization of non-conceptual wisdom through conceptualization": this means that if one realizes that all phenomena are nothing but conceptual construction, one is immediately able to attain non-conceptual wisdom.
The nature of the intention (*āśaya*) shall now be explained.
Regarding "the purity of the intention through the purity of aspiration and conviction": it is the purity of the intention when both desire and conviction are pure.
It should be understood that herein "desire" (*chanda*) means aspiration, and "faith" (*śraddhā*) means resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
The auspicious signs of the mental disposition (*āśaya*) shall now be demonstrated.

Regarding the statement that "in both the former and this stage of the flow of the Dharma, one is able to see all Buddhas": "the former" refers to the stage prior to the purification of the mental disposition, and "this" refers to the stage within the purification of the mental disposition; in both cases, being able to see the Buddhas constitutes the auspicious sign.
Regarding the term "flow of the Dharma" (*dharmasrotas*), it refers to the stage of determination (*niyāma*).
The excellence of the underlying intention (*āśaya*) will be demonstrated next.

As for the phrase "knowing that enlightenment is near because it is easily attained without difficulty," this means that within this stage one perceives that enlightenment is close at hand; because one possesses the superior means (*upāya*) to attain it, its attainment is not difficult.

Within these three verses, the superior intention of purification is revealed, characterized by such accumulations, such forbearance, such objects of focus, such mental engagement, such essential nature, such auspicious signs, and such benefits.
By means of these three verses, the essential characteristics of the pure superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) are established.
The treatise asks:
For what reason and by what causes are there exactly six perfections (*pāramitā*)?

The perfections of generosity and ethical discipline are established because they counteract the obstacles to be remedied, because they serve as the basis for realizing all Buddha-dharmas, because they accord with the ripening of all sentient beings, and because they are intended to counteract the causes for failing to set out on the path.
The causes for not setting forth are attachment to wealth and status, as well as attachment to the household life.
To counteract these causes for retreating even after one has already set forth, the perfections of patience (*kṣānti*) and diligence (*vīrya*) are established.

The cause for regression refers to the various sufferings arising from the transgressions of sentient beings within saṃsāra, as well as the fatigue and indolence arising from long-term application toward virtuous qualities.

In order to counteract the causes of ruin that, despite having already set out on the path, might lead one to regress, the perfections of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are established.
The causes of ruin refer to all forms of mental distraction and erroneous wisdom.
Thus, because they establish the remedies for the obstacles to be countered, exactly six are established.

Furthermore, the first four perfections are the causes of non-distraction; the next one perfection is the accomplishment of non-distraction. Relying upon this non-distraction, one awakens to the true meaning of all phenomena as they truly are, and is thereby able to realize all Buddha-dharmas.
Because they constitute the basis for realizing all the qualities of a Buddha, only six are established.
By means of the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*), one is able to correctly gather in and sustain all sentient beings.
By means of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), one is able to refrain from harming sentient beings;
by means of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), one is able to endure harm even when it is inflicted.
By means of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), one is able to assist in the performance of what ought to be done.
Through such causes and conditions of gathering and benefiting, sentient beings are rendered capable of accomplishing the task of maturation.

From this point onward, those whose minds are not yet settled shall be brought to stability, and those whose minds are already settled shall attain liberation; at the time of awakening, they will reach full maturity.
In this way, one should understand that the number six is established solely for the purpose of maturing all sentient beings in accordance with their needs.
The commentary states:

regarding the establishment of the remedies for the obstacles to be countered, the "cause of ruin" refers to wrong wisdom (*mithyā-prajñā*). Grasping things in a perverted manner is called wrong wisdom; for example, various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) suffer ruin because of such wrong wisdom.
The remaining meanings may be understood.
Regarding the statement that they are the "basis for realizing all Buddha-dharmas," this means they are the causes for realizing all Buddha-dharmas.
By virtue of this second established reason, the number of pāramitās is exactly six—neither more nor less.

Because this non-distraction serves as the basis, one who realizes the true meaning of all phenomena as they truly are relies upon the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) to give rise to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) that realizes the true meaning of all phenomena as they truly are.
The remaining meanings may be understood.

Regarding the third point, establishing the causes and conditions for the number [of perfections], "conforming to the maturation of all sentient beings" means that, in order to conform to the maturation of all classes of sentient beings, exactly six are established, neither more nor less.
To cause those whose minds are not yet settled to attain stability refers to attaining the *dhyāna-pāramitā*.
To cause those who have already attained stability to achieve liberation refers to attaining the *prajñā-pāramitā*.
Regarding those who attain maturation at the time of awakening, it means that they are brought to maturation during the time of instruction.
The treatise asks:
How are these six kinds of characteristics to be perceived?
It is due to six kinds of preeminence:
first, preeminence of basis, meaning that the bodhicitta serves as the basis;
second, preeminence of practice, meaning that it is fully manifested in conduct.
Third, by way of the supremacy of the objective basis (*āśraya*), meaning it takes as its basis the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings;
fourth, by way of the supremacy of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), meaning it is embraced by non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*);
fifth, by way of the supremacy of dedication (*pariṇāmana*), meaning it is dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Sixth, by way of supreme purity, meaning that it arises from being free from the obstructions of both the afflictive and cognitive hindrances.
Is every act of giving, then, a *pāramitā*?
Is a pāramitā necessarily giving?
There are cases of giving that are not pāramitās; thus, one should formulate four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
Just as it is with giving, so it should be understood that the same four permutations apply to each of the other pāramitās.
The commentary states:
By what characteristics are generosity and the other perfections designated as *pāramitās*?
Since worldly beings and even the Śrāvakas also possess generosity and the like, their defining characteristics must certainly be explained.
This refers to the six supreme qualities as the characteristics of giving and so forth.
Regarding the supremacy of the basis: this means that the bodhicitta serves as the basis.
Regarding the supremacy of the object: this means that there is no one other than a bodhisattva who can fully practice [giving] with respect to all internal and external things.
The most excellent basis refers to taking the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings as one's basis.

The most excellent skillful means refers to the purity of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍalapariśuddhi*), which is the skillful means adopted here; this is because there is no conceptual differentiation among the three factors of the gift, the giver, and the recipient.
Thus, when generosity and the other perfections are embraced by non-conceptual wisdom, they receive the name "pāramitā.
Regarding "dedication to the supreme," this refers to dedicating generosity and the others toward the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Regarding "the most supreme purity": this refers to the fact that giving and the other perfections become pure only upon reaching the fruit of Buddhahood, for at that time, one is liberated from the two types of obstacles—the afflictive and the cognitive—which had previously accumulated and arisen.

If one asks whether that which is giving is necessarily a *pāramitā*, or whether that which is a *pāramitā* is necessarily giving, the answer to this question is as follows: there is giving that is not a *pāramitā*, namely, practicing generosity while devoid of the six kinds of excellence.
There are perfections that are not giving, namely the six types of precept and so forth as subsumed under the six supreme qualities.
There are those that are both giving and perfection, namely the practice of giving as subsumed under the six supreme qualities.
There are cases that are neither giving nor a pāramitā; namely, the practice of ethical discipline and so forth when devoid of the six kinds of excellence.
One should understand that in all such instances, the four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) should be applied.
The treatise says:
For what reason are these six perfections (pāramitās) taught in this specific order?
It is because each preceding perfection gives rise to, and is conducive to, the subsequent perfection.
The commentary states:
These six types of pāramitās are explained in this sequence according to their arising, one after another.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, how should one understand the etymological explanations of these *pāramitās*?

Within all the worlds, the roots of virtue such as generosity belonging to the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* are the most excellent, for they are able to reach the further shore (*pāra*); therefore, they are collectively termed *pāramitās*.
Furthermore, because it can shatter stinginess and poverty, and can induce vast wealth, status, merit, and provisions, it is called "giving" (*dāna*).
Moreover, because it can extinguish immoral conduct and the miserable realms, and can attain the happy realms and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is called "ethical discipline" (*śīla*).
Furthermore, because it can extinguish anger, resentment, and enmity, and can skillfully abide in the peace and security of both oneself and others, it is called patience (*kṣānti*).
Moreover, because it can distance one from all laziness and evil, unwholesome dharmas, and can give rise to immeasurable wholesome dharmas so that they increase, it is called diligence (*vīrya*).
Furthermore, because it can eliminate all mental distractions and induce the mind to abide in tranquility, it is called *dhyāna* (meditative concentration).
Moreover, because it can dispel all views and erroneous wisdoms, and can truly discern and distinguish phenomena, it is called *prajñā* (wisdom).
The commentary states:
We shall now demonstrate the etymological analysis of the terminology.
First, we shall explain the general name.
Because all of these enable one to reach the further shore (*pāra*), they are called *pāramitās*.
Because they transcend the further shores of giving and the other perfections of all worldly beings, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas, they are collectively termed *pāramitās*.
Next, the specific names are explained.

It is called "giving" (*dāna*) because at the time of the cause, one overcomes stinginess through generosity; at the time of the fruit, it can tear asunder all poverty; and at the time of the fruit, it draws forth great wealth, status, and vast accumulations of merit.

Furthermore, it is called "precept" (*śīla*) because at the time of the cause it ceases all unwholesome conduct, at the time of the fruit it can extinguish all evil destinies, it can secure a favorable destiny in the future, and it can attain meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in the present life.
In this manner, the etymological explanations for all the *pāramitās* should be stated as appropriate.

Furthermore, regarding "being well-established in the peace and security of oneself and others": it means that by not being afflicted by the fault of anger toward oneself and by not producing suffering for others, one attains peace and security.
The treatise says:
How should one understand the cultivation of these pāramitās?
One should know that this cultivation is, in brief, of five kinds:

First, the cultivation of manifest application; second, the cultivation of resolute belief; third, the cultivation of mental attention; fourth, the cultivation of skillful means; and fifth, the cultivation of the accomplishment of tasks.
Among these, the four types of cultivation have already been explained as before.

Regarding the cultivation for accomplishing activities: it refers to the effortless and uninterrupted performance of the Buddha-activities of all Tathāgatas, wherein they further cultivate the six perfections within their already perfected pāramitās.
Furthermore, regarding the cultivation through mental attention (*manasikāra*), it refers to cultivating six types of mental attention comprised within the six kinds of resolute intention (*āśaya*):

first, the expansive resolute intention; second, the long-term resolute intention; third, the joyful resolute intention; fourth, the gratitude-resolving resolute intention; fifth, the great-vow resolute intention; and sixth, the pure-intention resolute intention.

If Bodhisattvas were to manifest the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment even after the passage of countless great eons, and during every single moment throughout that duration, were to suddenly relinquish all their bodies and lives, and offer to the Tathāgatas worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges filled with the seven treasures—continuing in this way until they sit upon the seat of sublime enlightenment—their intention for giving would still remain insatiable.

Throughout that duration, in each and every moment, even if the great trichiliocosm were filled with blazing fire, and even if one were constantly deprived of all necessities of life during the four postures, if one’s mind of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom were to manifest continuously until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment—such that the bodhisattva’s aspiration regarding these qualities of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom remains insatiable—this is called the bodhisattva’s vast aspiration.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas maintain an insatiable intentionality toward this very practice, continuing without interruption until they sit upon the sublime seat of awakening, this is called the bodhisattva’s intentionality over a long period of time.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings through the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and thereby experience profound joy in what they have done—joy that cannot be matched by those who merely receive the benefit—this is called the bodhisattva’s intention of joy (prāmodyāśaya).

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings through the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), they perceive those beings as having great kindness toward themselves, rather than seeing themselves as having any kindness toward them; this is called the bodhisattva’s intentionality of bearing kindness.
