Furthermore, when bodhisattvas dedicate with a profound mind the roots of virtue accumulated through these six perfections to all sentient beings, so that they may attain desirable, superior fruits of karmic maturation, this is called the bodhisattva’s great resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*).

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas dedicate the roots of virtue accumulated through these six perfections (pāramitās) toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of all sentient beings, this is called the bodhisattva’s purely virtuous intention (*āśaya*). In this way, the bodhisattva cultivates the mental engagement of cherishing (*priyāmanasikāra*) as subsumed within these six types of intention.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas, with deep resolve, rejoice in the immeasurable roots of goodness cultivated by other bodhisattvas through their engagement with the six types of intentionality, such bodhisattvas are practicing the intentionality of rejoicing as subsumed within these six types of intentionality.

Furthermore, bodhisattvas, with deep resolve, take delight in the cultivation of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) as subsumed within the six types of aspiration for all sentient beings; they also vow that their own persons shall never be separated from this cultivation of the six perfections until they sit upon the seat of sublime enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). In this way, the bodhisattva cultivates the mental engagement of delight as subsumed within these six types of aspiration.

If anyone, having heard this cultivation of mental attention encompassed by the six types of bodhisattva intention, should give rise to even a single thought of faith, they will still generate an immeasurable mass of merit and all their karmic obstructions of evil will be extinguished; how much more so for a bodhisattva!
The commentary states:
Among the five kinds of cultivation, "cultivation of the application of manifestation" refers to cultivating the application that brings [the qualities] into manifestation.

"Cultivation of the performance of activities" refers to the fact that when the Tathāgatas abide in the *dharmakāya*, there are buddha-activities performed without effort (*anābhoga*) that are constant and without rest.
Although these six perfections do not manifest [in him], he constantly performs the deeds of accomplishment for the sake of gathering and benefiting all sentient beings.

Regarding each and every moment during that period: even if one were to take the measure of three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) as a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), and accumulate such moments until the attainment of awakening (*bodhi*).

The meaning of "supposing one were to suddenly relinquish all body and life at every single moment throughout that duration" is easy to understand; it should be followed according to the original text.

Accumulating such a measure of time in this sequence until reaching enlightenment, at every single moment throughout that duration, even if for the sake of giving rise to a single thought of morality (*śīla*) or the like, one must remain amidst a great trichiliocosm filled with blazing fire and be constantly deprived of all requisites for life—this statement reveals the difficulty of the dwelling place and the scarcity of material conditions. Within this context, the absence of weariness or satiety constitutes what should be understood as the "vast intention" (*udāra-āśaya*).
That which is constant and uninterrupted over a long period should be understood as the "long-term intention.
"Long" (dīrgha) means "for a duration.
The remaining meanings are easy to understand.

Regarding the statement that "all karmic obstacles of evil shall also be extinguished," the intended meaning here is that it destroys their capacity to produce maturation (*vipāka*), or counters their power to lead one toward the miserable realms (*durgati*).
The treatise says:
How are the distinctions among these pāramitās to be understood?
One should know that each one has three grades.
The three categories of giving are: first, the gift of Dharma; second, the gift of material wealth; and third, the gift of fearlessness.
The three categories of ethical discipline are: first, the discipline of restraint; second, the discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas; and third, the discipline of benefiting sentient beings.
The three grades of patience are: first, patience in enduring enmity and harm; second, patience in accepting suffering; and third, patience in the discernment of dharmas.

The three grades of diligence are: first, the diligence of donning the armor; second, the diligence of application; and third, the diligence that is free from cowardice, free from regression, and free from complacency.
The three categories of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) are: first, the meditative concentration of abiding; second, the meditative concentration of elicitation;

and third, the meditative concentration that accomplishes activities. The three categories of wisdom (*prajñā*) are: first, non-conceptual wisdom of application; second, non-conceptual wisdom; and third, non-conceptual wisdom attained subsequent to realization.
The commentary states:
Within this exposition on the distinctions among the *pāramitās*, the threefold distinction of their essential natures (*svabhāva*) is revealed.
Why, then, are the threefold distinctions of the gift of Dharma and so forth presented here?

That is to say, through the gift of Dharma one sustains the roots of goodness in others; through the gift of material wealth one sustains and benefits their bodies; and through the gift of fearlessness one sustains and benefits their minds. For these reasons, the three types of giving are taught.

Among the three types of precepts, the precept of restraint (saṃvara-śīla) is the basis for maintaining morality; it is established in order to set up the other two precepts, and therefore one dwells securely in it. Why is this so?

One who abides in ethical discipline is able to establish the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas; through this, one cultivates and accumulates all Buddha-dharmas and realizes great enlightenment. Furthermore, one is able to establish the precept of benefiting sentient beings; by means of this, one is able to bring sentient beings to maturity.

Among the three types of patience, the patience of enduring enmity and harm is able to endure the injuries and harms inflicted by others; when diligently practicing deeds that benefit sentient beings, one does not regress due to the suffering of birth and death because of the power of this patience.

The patience of accepting suffering enables one to correctly endure the various sufferings encountered; by the power of this patience, although one undergoes manifold sufferings within saṃsāra, one does not regress.

The patience of discerning phenomena (*dharmanidhyānaksānti*) is capable of thoroughly and accurately examining all phenomena; by the power of this patience, it establishes the two types of patience mentioned previously.
Regarding the distinctions in the essence of the three forms of diligence (*vīrya*), the Blessed One stated in a sutra:
"It possesses force, exertion, valor, firmness and intensity, and does not abandon the yoke of the wholesome."
Those five phrases from that sūtra are the explanation of the three essences of diligence found herein.
By means of armor-like diligence (*saṃnāha-vīrya*), one initially possesses vigor;
by means of applied diligence (*prayoga-vīrya*), one is able to exert effort during the time of application.

Due to diligence that is free from cowardice, free from regression, and free from complacency, there arise, in their respective order, valor, steadfastness, and ferocity, because one does not abandon the yoke of virtue at this subsequent time.
These three explanations clarify those five phrases.

Why is this so? There may be some who, at the very outset, seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; yet, although they possess the capacity, they are unable to exert themselves during the stage of application. Therefore, it is said that they "possess diligence."
Although one may possess diligence, the mind may still be timid or weak; to counteract this, it is said that there is "courage.
Because of this courage, the mind does not succumb to retreat; one should understand that timidity is itself a form of retreat.

Although the mind may lack cowardice, it might still regress when encountering the suffering of birth and death; because of this regression, one would lose the sought-after fruit of Buddhahood. To counteract that, "non-regression" is established.

The absence of turning back or retreating is itself steadfastness and vigor; thus, the absence of retreating demonstrates steadfastness and vigor. Because of this steadfastness and vigor, one does not retreat when encountering suffering.

While there may be those who, though encountering suffering, are able to avoid retreating, they become complacent upon attaining a small amount of goodness. Due to this, they do not realize unsurpassed enlightenment; therefore, it is necessary to speak next of the absence of complacency.
This means not being content with even a slight attainment; it demonstrates the non-abandonment of the yoke of virtue.
For this reason, three types of diligence are taught.
Among the three meditative absorptions (dhyāna), one who abides in meditative absorption is thereby able to dwell securely in the happiness of the present life.
The meditative absorption that induces [supernormal powers] refers to that by which one induces the six types of supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).

The meditative absorption that accomplishes tasks refers to that which, by depending upon it, establishes the performance of activities for the benefit of sentient beings; therefore, it is called "the accomplishment of tasks."
For this reason, there are three types of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Among the three ways of establishing the essence of wisdom (*prajñā*), the meaning is easy to understand.
The treatise says:
How can such mutual inclusion be understood?
It is because this [faith] is able to include all wholesome dharmas, as it is their characteristic, its conformity, and its outflow.
The commentary states:
Regarding the question, "How is such mutual inclusion to be seen?"—this asks how the meaning of the mutual inclusion between these *pāramitās* and all other wholesome dharmas is to be understood.

Regarding the phrase "by this, all wholesome dharmas are subsumed," it should be understood that through these *pāramitās*, all wholesome dharmas are fully subsumed, and they [the wholesome dharmas] likewise subsume the *pāramitās*.
It should be understood that herein all wholesome dharmas are precisely all factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
That which is "their characteristic" refers to the characteristic of *prajñā*.
That which is "conformable to them" should be understood as faith, pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), and so forth.
"Because these are its outflow" refers to the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the ten powers (*daśabala*), and other such remaining qualities.
The treatise asks:
How are the various defilements (*saṃkleśa*) subsumed within these objects of counteraction (*vipakṣa*) to be understood?
"Because it has this characteristic, because it has this cause, and because it has this result.
The commentary states:
As was previously demonstrated, the perfection of wisdom (pāramitā) encompasses all wholesome dharmas (śukla-dharma).
The factors to be counteracted by this also encompass all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*), which shall now be demonstrated.
"Because it has this characteristic" refers to the characteristics of greed and so forth.
"Because it has this cause" refers to the causes of stinginess and so forth, namely, lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) and wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
"Because these are its fruits" refers to the various fruits of stinginess, transgression of the precepts, anger, and so forth.
The treatise asks:
How are the benefits obtained through these six kinds of pāramitās to be seen?

It refers to the fact that when Bodhisattvas circulate through birth and death, they are encompassed by wealth and nobility, encompassed by noble birth, encompassed by great circles of friends and followers, encompassed by the accomplishment of the application of vast undertakings, encompassed by being free from affliction and harm and having naturally thin defilements, and encompassed by their excellent knowledge of all crafts, treatises, and fields of learning. Thus, they attain superior births without fault and eventually sit upon the sublime seat of enlightenment, constantly able to manifest and perform all that is beneficial for the welfare of all sentient beings; this is called "superior benefit."
The commentary states:
Now, the benefits obtained through the pāramitās shall be clearly explained.
Regarding "superior births that are blameless": this is unlike the superior births attained by non-Buddhists, which are termed "blameworthy" because they are defiled by afflictions.
Furthermore, those superior births are all impermanent;
however, the fruit of the *pāramitās* is not impermanent, because it is said that they culminate in sitting upon the sublime seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Furthermore, that superior birth can only benefit oneself and cannot benefit others, because it is not said to be able to constantly manifest for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings.
The supreme fruit obtained through the *pāramitās* is able to constantly manifest for all the various purposes and benefits of all sentient beings.
Thus, these are called the meanings and benefits of the supreme fruits, such as being faultless, attained by those who have reached the perfections (*pāramitā*).
The treatise asks:
How are these six kinds of *pāramitās* to be understood in terms of their mutual determination?

Regarding all these six perfections, the Blessed One has in some instances spoken of them using the term "giving," in some instances using the term "ethical discipline," in some instances using the term "patience," in some instances using the term "diligence," in some instances using the term "concentration," and in some instances using the term "wisdom."
What is the intended meaning of what has been stated?
It means that within the application of practice for all the pāramitās, all the pāramitās mutually assist and bring one another to fulfillment.
Regarding this underlying intention,
the commentary states:
Within the *Prajñāpāramitā* scriptures consisting of three hundred verses and so forth, although originally a single pāramitā was intended to be taught, all pāramitās are in fact taught.
What is the intended meaning of this statement?
It should be understood that the intended meaning here is that at the time of practicing one [perfection], all others act as auxiliaries.

That is to say, when practicing generosity (*dāna*), one restrains body and speech; through this, the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) acts as an auxiliary to bring it to completion.
This continues until one fully understands the causes and effects of giving; through this, the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā) provides assistance and brings it to completion.
One should understand that the remaining perfections provide assistance in a similar manner as appropriate.
The treatise says:
Regarding this, there is a summary verse (*udāna*) which states:
"Number, characteristics, and sequence; etymology, cultivation, and distinctions."
One should know that the subduing of opposing factors and the cultivation of virtues are mutually determined.
The commentary states:
The sequence of the preceding verses is easy to understand.
6. The Section on the Differentiation of Their Cultivation. Commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, Section Six: The Differentiation of Their Cultivation. The treatise says:
Thus, the cause and fruit of their entry [into the Mahāyāna] have already been explained.
How can the distinctions in his cultivation be seen?
They are by means of the ten stages of a bodhisattva. What are these ten?

First, the Ground of Utmost Joy; second, the Ground Free from Defilement; third, the Ground of Radiant Light; fourth, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom; fifth, the Ground of Ultimate Difficult Victory; sixth, the Ground of Manifestation; seventh, the Ground of Far-Going; eighth, the Ground of Immovability; ninth, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence; and tenth, the Ground of the Dharma Cloud—thus these grounds are established as ten.
How is it to be seen?
It is for the purpose of counteracting the ten types of obstacles that are governed by ignorance. Why is this so?
Because there exist ten types of obscurations to be remedied by ignorance regarding the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) that is known through ten aspects.
What are these ten aspects of the dharma-realm that is known?

That is to say: in the first stage, by way of the meaning of universal pervasion; in the second stage, by way of the meaning of supremacy; in the third stage, by way of the meaning of the superior outflow; in the fourth stage, by way of the meaning of non-appropriation; in the fifth stage, by way of the meaning of the non-differentiation of continuity; in the sixth stage, by way of the meaning of non-defilement and purity; in the seventh stage, by way of the meaning of the non-differentiation of various phenomena; in the eighth stage, by way of the meaning of neither increasing nor decreasing, the meaning of the basis for mastery over signs, and the meaning of the basis for mastery over fields; in the ninth stage, by way of the meaning of the basis for mastery over knowledge; and in the tenth stage, by way of the meaning of the basis for mastery over action and the meaning of the basis for mastery over the gates of dhāraṇīs and the gates of samādhis.
In this regard, there are three verses:
The meaning of universal pervasion and supreme excellence, And the meaning of the flow of excellence;
Likewise, the meaning of non-appropriation, And the meaning of continuity without distinction.
The meaning of being free from defilement and purity, The meaning of the manifold being without distinction,
The meaning of neither increasing nor decreasing, And the meaning of being the basis for the four masteries—
These ten meanings exist within the dharmadhātu, Regarding the non-defiled ignorance.
To remedy these obstacles that are to be remedied, the ten stages (daśabhūmi) are established.
Furthermore, it should be understood that such ignorance is non-defiled for śrāvakas and others, yet it is defiled for bodhisattvas.
The commentary states:
Based on the distinctions among the stages of cultivation regarding those causes and effects, the question and answer are thus posed.
What are the ten aspects of the dharma-realm that is to be known?

That is to say, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) by way of the meaning of universal pervasion (*sarvatraga*), up to the tenth stage by way of the meaning of the basis for mastery over karma (*karmavaśitā*) and the meaning of the basis for mastery over the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi, the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is to be known through these ten aspects; therefore, it is called the "dharma-realm to be known through ten aspects."

This means that within each stage (bhūmi) there is a single characteristic of the dharma-dhātu as an object of knowledge, which cannot be fully understood due to the power of ignorance; it is for the purpose of counteracting such ignorance that the ten stages are established.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of obstacles to be remedied; therefore, the ten stages (bhūmi) are established.
What are these ten obstacles to be remedied?
First, the nature of an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva).
Second, improper conduct toward the bodies and so forth of sentient beings;
third, dullness, which involves forgetfulness regarding hearing, reflection, and cultivation;

fourth, the manifestation of subtle afflictions, which are comprised of innate views of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the like—these should be known as "subtle" because they are of the lowest degree, because they do not arise through deliberate attention, and because they persist for a long time even while manifesting.
Fifth, attaining parinirvāṇa through the lower vehicles;
sixth, the manifestation of coarse characteristics;
seventh, the manifestation of subtle characteristics.
Eighth, practicing with regard to the signless;
ninth, not practicing with regard to the welfare of sentient beings;
tenth, not having attained mastery over all phenomena.

The meaning of "pervasive" (sarvatraga) is that this dharma-realm pervades all modes of existence, because there is not even the slightest phenomenon that is not selfless; if one knows it thus, one attains entry into the first stage (bhūmi).
The meaning of "supreme" (*parama*) refers to this *dharmadhātu*, which is the most excellent among all phenomena; if one knows it thus, one enters the second stage (*bhūmi*).
The meaning of "supreme flow" (*pravāha*) refers to the Mahāyāna teaching, which is the most excellent of all that flows from it; if one knows it thus, one enters the third stage.

The meaning of "non-appropriation" refers to the absence of the notion of "mine" and the absence of grasping at what belongs to "me" within this state; it is like the people of the Northern Continent who have no sense of possession. When one realizes this dharmadhātu, there is absolutely no notion of "mine" therein. Knowing it thus, one enters the Fourth Ground.

The meaning of "no distinction in the continuity" refers to the fact that within this state there is no difference in essence; it is not like the eyes and other faculties, which differ individually according to the distinctions in the continuities of various sentient beings. If one understands it in this way, one attains entry into the fifth stage.

Regarding the meaning of neither defilement nor purity: it means that herein there is fundamentally no defilement because its nature is undefiled; since there is no defilement, there is likewise no purity. To know this is to enter the sixth stage.

Regarding the meaning of the non-differentiation of various dharmas: it means that within these, although the dharmas such as the sūtras are established with various distinctions, there is no difference between them; if one knows this, one attains entry into the seventh stage.
The meaning of neither increasing nor decreasing refers to the fact that within this [dharmadhātu], there is no decrease when defilement diminishes, and no increase when purification increases.

The meaning of being the basis for mastery over signs refers to the fact that this dharmadhātu is the basis for mastery over signs; because one attains mastery regarding all signs, it is called "mastery over signs," since any sign desired immediately manifests before one.

Regarding the meaning of the "basis for mastery over the land": it means that this dharmadhātu is the basis upon which mastery over the land rests. One attains mastery over the manifested lands and is thus termed "mastery over the land," because one can, according to one's wish, cause the land to become gold and other such precious substances.
If one knows in this way, one enters the eighth stage.

Regarding the meaning of the basis for mastery over wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā-adhiṣṭhāna*), it means that this dharmadhātu is the basis for mastery over unimpeded eloquence and wisdom; if one knows in this way, one enters the ninth stage.

Regarding the meaning of being the basis for mastery over karma and so forth: it means that this dharmadhātu is the basis for mastery over the karma of the body and so on, as well as the basis for mastery over the gates of dhāraṇīs and samādhis; if one knows it thus, one attains entry into the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
If such ignorance is not an affliction for Śrāvakas and others because they do not desire to enter the various stages (*bhūmi*),
then since one is already able to penetrate all stages within the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), for what reason are the stages established in succession?

To resolve this objection: although one penetrates all stages within the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), it is by means of this dwelling that one attains stable abiding, and it is by the power of this dwelling that the various stages are established.
The Commentary states:
Furthermore, for what reason is the first stage named "Supreme Joy" (*pramuditā*)?
It is because, for the first time, one attains the superior capacity to accomplish the welfare and benefit of both oneself and others.
Why is the second stage called "Stainless" (*vimalā*)?
Because it is extremely far removed from the stain of transgressing the precepts.
Why is the third stage called "Luminous" (*prabhākari*)?
Because it is the basis for non-retrogressive meditative concentrations and attainments (*samādhi-samāpatti*), and because it is the basis for the great light of the Dharma.
For what reason is the fourth stage called "Blazing Wisdom" (*Arciṣmatī*)?
Because all obstacles are incinerated by the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), why is the fifth stage called "Extremely Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjayā*)?

It is because the wisdom of ultimate truth and worldly wisdom are mutually contradictory; this stage is so named because it brings these two difficult-to-unite elements into conjunction and makes them correspond.
Why is the sixth stage called "Manifestation"?
Because, by relying on the wisdom of dependent origination, it causes the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to manifest before one.
For what reason is the seventh stage called "Far-Reaching"?
Because it reaches the final limit of the stage of effortful practice (*prayoga*).
For what reason is the eighth stage called "Immovable"?
Because it cannot be moved by any conditioned activity involving effort regarding all signs,
why is the ninth stage called "Excellent Intelligence" (Sādhumatī)?
Because one has attained the most supreme unimpeded knowledge (pratisaṃvid).
Why is the tenth stage called the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*)?

Because by attaining the wisdom that takes all phenomena as its collective object, it contains and stores all *dhāraṇī* gates and *samādhi* gates; just as a great cloud can cover vast obstructions as extensive as space, so too does it bring the *dharmakāya* to full completion.
The commentary says:
Why is the first stage named "Utmost Joy" (*pramuditā*)?
Because at this time, one first attains the supreme capacity to accomplish the welfare of both oneself and others.

When the śrāvakas and others attain true direct realization (*abhisamaya*), they only acquire the capacity to accomplish their own benefit, but do not acquire the capacity for the benefit of others; therefore, unlike the bodhisattvas, they do not give rise to such joy.
For what reason is the second stage called "Stainless" (*vimalā*)?
Because in this stage, natural morality (*prakṛti-śīla*) is perfected; it is not, as in the first stage, a morality maintained through deliberate discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*).
Since natural morality is perfected, all stains of transgressing the precepts are utterly removed.
For what reason is the third stage called "The Luminous" (*prabhākari*)?
Because in this stage one is never separated from *samādhi* and *samāpatti*, and due to the absence of regression, one is able to produce light for the Mahāyāna teachings.
Why is the fourth stage called "Blazing Wisdom" (Arciṣmatī)?

Because in this stage one dwells in the most excellent factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), and by dwelling therein, one is able to incinerate all root afflictions (kleśa) and secondary afflictions (upakleśa) until they are reduced to ashes.
Why is the fifth stage called "Extremely Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjayā*)?

Because within this stage, the knowledge that realizes ultimate truth is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), whereas the knowledge of worldly crafts, sciences, and so forth is conceptual (*savikalpa*). These two are mutually contradictory and must be cultivated until they are unified; because it can bring together what is difficult to harmonize and cause them to correspond, it is named "Extremely Difficult to Conquer."
Why is the sixth stage called "Manifestation" (*abhimukhī*)?

It is because in this stage one dwells in the wisdom of dependent origination; by the power of this wisdom, one abides in non-conceptuality, and the most supreme *prajñāpāramitā* becomes manifest. One realizes that all phenomena are neither defiled nor pure, and while in the seventh stage one shall achieve "with-effort" (*sābhoga*), in the eighth stage one shall achieve "without-effort" (*anābhoga*).
Why is the seventh stage called "Far-Reaching" (dūraṅgama)?

It is because within this stage, one attains the ultimate consummation of effortful practice; although one cannot be shaken by any mental signs (*nimitta*), one is still said to possess "practice" (*saṃskāra*) even regarding the signless (*animitta*).
Why is the eighth stage called "The Immovable"?
Because within this stage, all signs and all conditioned activities cannot cause any movement, and non-conceptual wisdom flows spontaneously.
For what reason is the ninth stage called "Excellent Intelligence" (Sādhumatī)?

Because within this stage, the wisdom of unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) is designated as "intelligence," and since this intelligence is sublime and excellent, it is called "Excellent Intelligence."
Why is the tenth stage called the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*)?

Because within this stage, the wisdom that universally contemplates all phenomena is like a great cloud; the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi are like pure water. This wisdom contains [all things] as a cloud holds water, and it is also like a great cloud that can cover the void.
In this way, the wisdom that takes all phenomena as its universal object is universally able to suppress and destroy all vast hindrances.

Furthermore, regarding its ability to bring the Dharma-body to fulfillment: just as a great cloud arises and pervades the entirety of space, so too does this wisdom pervade the Dharma-bodies upon which all bodhisattvas rely.
In this context, "perfection" (paripūri) means "pervasion" (vyāpti).
The treatise asks:
How are these various stages (bhūmi) to be understood?
By means of four aspects:
first, the attainment of resolute belief (*adhimukti*), which refers to attaining deep faith and understanding regarding the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Second, the attainment of correct practice (*samyak-pratipatti*), which refers to attaining the ten types of correct dharma-practice associated with the various stages.
Third is the attainment of penetration, which means that when one penetrates the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) in the first stage (*bhūmi*), one is able to penetrate all stages universally.
Fourth is the attainment of fulfillment, which means cultivating the various stages until they reach their ultimate consummation.
The commentary states:
Regarding "attaining fulfillment," it should be understood that at this time, the cultivation of the various stages (*bhūmi*) has reached its ultimate consummation.
The treatise says:
How can the cultivation of these stages be understood?
It is said that bodhisattvas, within each stage, cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā by means of five aspects of practice.
What are these five? They are: cultivation through comprehensive accumulation, signless cultivation, effortless cultivation, intense cultivation, and insatiable cultivation.

These five types of cultivation enable bodhisattvas to accomplish five fruits: namely, the moment-to-moment dissolution of all coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*); the attainment of the joy of the Dharma-garden by being free from various conceptualizations; the correct and thorough understanding of the great light of the Dharma, which is infinite, boundless, and characterized by non-differentiation; the unimpeded manifestation of the signless state that accords with the purified portion; and the correct grasping of ever-superior causes for the sake of bringing the *dharmakāya* to full completion.
The commentary states:
Just as each individual stage (*bhūmi*) possesses five aspects of cultivation, these shall now be demonstrated.
Both the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are accomplished through all five aspects simultaneously.

Regarding "the dissolution of all coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*) within every moment of thought": the seeds of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā-bīja*) from beginningless time belonging to both the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are termed "coarse habitual tendencies."
This accumulation of the two hindrances is dissolved moment by moment through the power of wisdom arising from śamatha and vipaśyanā that takes all-encompassing phenomena as its object.
Here, the intended meaning is that it is called "dissolved" because the accumulation of hindrances is destroyed, or because it is rendered weak and diminished.

Regarding "attaining the joy of the Dharma-garden by being free from various conceptualizations": the teachings of the sūtras and other scriptures abide in various natures; to distance oneself from such conceptualizations of various natures is precisely to realize the joy of the Dharma-garden. Because one may dwell therein, it is called a "garden" (ārāma).

Furthermore, there is another meaning: within the dharmas of applied and sustained thought as they are experienced, one does not give rise to coarse and manifest reception or observation; rather, by means of serenity, insight, and mindfulness of light, one gives rise to subtle reception and observation.

To be able to correctly understand the great light of Dharma, which is all-pervasive, immeasurable, and without limits, means to correctly comprehend the boundless and limitless aspects of the ten directions; just as the light of syllables resulting from thorough practice of recitation is called the "light of Dharma."

"Practicing the signless without conceptual differentiation in accordance with the factors conducive to purification" refers to the accomplishment of the task through all associated dharmas; this is termed practicing the signless without conceptual differentiation in accordance with the factors conducive to purification.
In this context, the intended meaning is that the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood is called "the completion of the task" (*kāryapariniṣpatti*).

To ensure the fulfillment and accomplishment of the *dharmakāya* so as to correctly embrace the progressively superior causes, the *dharmakāya* of the tenth stage is termed "fulfillment," while the *dharmakāya* of the eleventh Buddha-stage is termed "accomplishment."
Among all causes, that which gives rise to the stage of Buddhahood is the most preeminent; therefore, it is said that one can correctly embrace each successive superior cause.
The treatise states:
Because they are progressively more excellent, ten distinct types of *pāramitās* are cultivated within the ten stages (*bhūmis*).

Regarding the six types of *pāramitā* cultivated in the first six stages, they have already been explained as before. As for the four cultivated in the subsequent four stages: First is the *upāyakauśalya-pāramitā* (perfection of skillful means), which refers to dedicating the roots of virtue accumulated through the preceding six *pāramitās* toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment together with all sentient beings.

Second is the *praṇidhāna-pāramitā* (perfection of aspiration), which refers to generating various subtle and sublime great vows in order to attract and gather the excellent conditions for the *pāramitās* in the future.

Third is the *bala-pāramitā* (perfection of power), which refers to causing the aforementioned six types of *pāramitās* to manifest continuously by means of the two powers of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

The four wisdoms are the *pāramitās*, meaning that by means of the preceding six *pāramitās*, one establishes sublime wisdom for the enjoyment of the Dharma-joy and for the maturation of sentient beings.

Furthermore, it should be understood that these four types of *pāramitā* are subsumed within the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Moreover, throughout all the stages (*bhūmi*), it is not the case that one does not cultivate all the *pāramitās*.
This Dharma-gate is subsumed within the *Pāramitā-piṭaka*.
The commentary states:

Because they are predominant, it is said that one cultivates ten distinct *pāramitās* throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*). This means that regarding the ten stages, it is taught as follows: in the first stage, the *dāna-pāramitā* (perfection of generosity) is most predominant; however, it is not that the other *pāramitās* are not practiced, for they are cultivated according to one's capacity and portion.

Up to the tenth stage, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is preeminent; however, it is not that the other perfections are not practiced, as they are cultivated according to one's strength and capacity.
Therefore, it is said that because of their predominance, ten distinct types of *pāramitās* are cultivated within the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
However, if explained according to their general characteristics, all *pāramitās* are cultivated throughout all stages.

Regarding the six perfections practiced in the first six stages as previously explained, this indicates that the ten perfections are cultivated sequentially and individually in their respective order.
In the preceding sūtra, the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) was taught first, and the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*) was taught last.

In this treatise, however, there is a slight incompleteness regarding what was previously stated; namely, that the four kinds of perfections practiced in the final four stages (*bhūmi*), which were not mentioned before, are now included.
If, in a certain context, only six perfections are mentioned, then the four perfections beginning with skillful means (upāyakauśalya) are already included therein.
If the ten kinds of pāramitās are taught in this context, it is specifically non-conceptual wisdom that is designated here as the prajñāpāramitā.

The remaining four pāramitās, such as skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) and so forth, are subsumed under subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna); therefore, one cultivates these four pāramitās during the final four stages (bhūmis).
Regarding the perfection of skillful means (*upāyakauśalyapāramitā*): among the latter four [perfections], the first is explained first.
"Shared with all sentient beings" means that one shares this virtue with all sentient beings, just as if it were a common possession.

I shall now explain this: by means of these virtuous aspirations, one seeks unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment to accomplish every benefit and welfare for all sentient beings; it is only upon realizing enlightenment that this intention will finally be fulfilled.

Therefore, if one reflects in this way, dedicating all roots of goodness toward unsurpassed enlightenment and performing every benefit for all sentient beings, this is called "sharing with all sentient beings."

Skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) manifests both wisdom (*prajñā*) and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). This refers to sharing with all sentient beings the roots of virtue accumulated through the first six perfections (*pāramitās*), and seeking unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) by dedicating these through great compassion, rather than seeking fruits such as the wealth and pleasures of Śakra or other deities. Because one understands this, afflictions (*kleśas*) do not arise; this is wisdom.
Furthermore, because one is endowed with skillful means, one does not abandon saṃsāra yet remains undefiled; therefore, it is called the perfection of skillful means (upāyakauśalyapāramitā).

"Namely, to give rise to various subtle and wondrous great vows that attract and gather the excellent conditions for the perfections (pāramitās) in the future" indicates the activity performed by the perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā).
This vow is itself a *pāramitā*; therefore, it is called the "vow *pāramitā*.
Regarding the term "in the future," this refers to that which is for the sake of the future; it is used in the seventh case (the locative).
For the sake of the future, one makes various aspirations.
Other sūtras speak of two kinds of power: the power of analytical reflection (*cintā-bala*) and the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*).

Even if one does not yet possess the power of cultivation, because one practices the *pāramitās* with diligence through the power of analytical reflection, it is said that these *pāramitās* manifest uninterruptedly; this demonstrates the activity performed by the *pāramitā* of power (*bala-pāramitā*).

This means that the establishment of sublime wisdom for enjoying the dharma-bliss and maturing sentient beings through the first six perfections is as follows: by virtue of the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), such subsequent attainment wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is established; furthermore, by means of this wisdom, the aforementioned six perfections are established. Through this, one personally enjoys the dharma-bliss together with those of like practice, and brings all sentient beings to maturity.

Regarding the statement that "this dharma-gate is subsumed within the Pitaka of the Perfection of Wisdom (Pāramitā-piṭaka)," herein all the teachings of the Mahāyāna are collectively designated by the name "Pitaka of the Perfection of Wisdom."
The Dharma-gate of the ten stages thus cited is subsumed within that [bodhisattva] piṭaka, not the śrāvaka piṭaka.
Because it is so subsumed, one cultivates all the pāramitās throughout all the stages.
These stages are thus proclaimed by all Buddhas alike throughout all Buddha-lands; therefore, they are most excellent (*parama*).
Because this Dharma-gate is most excellent, it was taught at the very beginning in the most excellent place. This place is high, vast, sublime, and firm; hence, it is called "most excellent."
The treatise says:
Furthermore, after how long a period of practice must one cultivate the various stages (*bhūmi*) to attain their fulfillment?
There are five types of individuals (*pudgala*) who do so over the course of three incalculable great eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

This refers to the individual on the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-pudgala*), who completes their cultivation after the first incalculable great eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

The individual on the stage of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-caryā-pudgala*), as well as the individuals on the stages of practice with signs (*sanimitta-caryā*) and practice without signs (*animitta-caryā*), complete their cultivation during the second incalculable great eon across the preceding six stages and the seventh stage.
This very person of effortless practice (anābhoga-caryā-pudgala), from this point upward until the tenth stage, completes their cultivation through three incalculable great eons (asaṃkhyeya-kalpa).
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"Through the power of pure supremacy, With a firm mind progressing upward,
This is called the Bodhisattva’s initial cultivation Throughout three incalculable great eons."
The commentary states:

Regarding the five types of *pudgalas* who pass through three incalculable great eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), this refers to the *pudgala* of the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-pudgala*), who completes their cultivation during the first incalculable great eon within the stage of practice through belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).
Once these are perfected, because one has realized suchness, one becomes a person who practices with pure superior intention (*viśuddhādhyāśaya-caryā-pudgala*).

This practice of pure superior intention pervades all ten stages (*bhūmi*): on the sixth stage, one is a person who practices with signs (*sanimitta-caryā-pudgala*), and on the seventh stage, one is a person who practices with effort despite being signless (*animitte sābhisamskāra-caryā-pudgala*).

In this sutra, the cultivation during the second incalculable great eon is brought to completion, and one enters the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), becoming a person (*pudgala*) who practices without effort (*anābhoga*).

Although this practice without effort is not yet fully perfected, it becomes so only upon reaching the ninth and tenth stages; thus, in this sutra, the cultivation during the third incalculable great eon is brought to completion.
In this way, although there is only one *pudgala*, five types are established based on differences in their stages, just as with the *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, and *anāgāmin*.

As it is said that one attains the Buddha-bodhi after three incalculable great eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), and having repeatedly practiced giving and other perfections throughout beginningless saṃsāra and repeatedly encountered various Buddhas—at what point does one come to be called "initially practicing" the three incalculable eons?
Therefore, this question is elucidated by means of verses.

Regarding the "power of pure supremacy," this refers to the power of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) and the power of the great vow (*mahāpraṇidhāna*). By the power of the roots of virtue, one should know that the factors to be countered (*vipakṣa*) cannot overcome him; by the power of the great vow, one should know that he constantly encounters all spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Regarding "advancing with a firm mind," this refers to generating a steadfast resolve and initiating progressive practice.
It should be understood that a "firm mind" is the great bodhicitta that has been generated, which no force of evil associates can cause one to abandon.
Regarding those who practice for increase, it should be understood that within the present life and throughout successive births, wholesome dharmas constantly increase and never diminish.
The remaining meanings are easy to understand; there is no need for further elaboration.
*Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Fascicle Seven and Fascicle Eight,
composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Seven: The Section on Higher Training in Ethics (Adhiśīla-śikṣā-vibhāga). The treatise states:
Thus has been explained the differentiation of cultivation according to cause and effect.
In this regard, how is the excellence of superior ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*) to be seen?
It is as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* within the section on the formal reception of the bodhisattva vows.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this excellence is characterized by four types of distinction:

First, by way of the excellence of distinction; second, by way of the excellence of common and uncommon training rules; third, by way of the excellence of vastness; and fourth, by way of the excellence of profundity.
The commentary states:
Herein, the question and answer clarify that the ethical discipline (*śīla*) studied by bodhisattvas differs greatly from that of the śrāvakas and others; therefore, it is called "superior."

Furthermore, these three trainings—higher ethical discipline and so forth—are subsumed within the essential nature of the perfections previously described; for what reason, then, are they established separately?
I shall now demonstrate the distinct meanings established for these previously mentioned perfections.

The three trainings are established separately to demonstrate their nature of being successive causes for one another; that is to say, based upon ethical discipline (śīla), meditative concentration (dhyāna) arises, and further, based upon meditative concentration, wisdom (prajñā) arises.
The Commentary states:
Regarding the distinctions of excellence, the Bodhisattva precepts are categorized into three types:

first, the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*); second, the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*); and third, the morality of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*).
Among these, the morality of restraint (saṃvara-śīla) should be understood as having the sense of establishing the two types of morality.
The morality of gathering virtuous dharmas (kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla) should be understood as having the sense of establishing the cultivation and accumulation of all Buddha-dharmas.
The ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings should be understood as having the sense of establishing the maturation of all sentient beings.
The commentary explains:

regarding their distinct excellence, it means that while the Śrāvakas and others possess only the single type of restraint discipline (*saṃvara-śīla*), they lack the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) and the ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*).
The Bodhisattva possesses these three, and is therefore preeminent.
The treatise states:

Regarding the preeminence of the shared and unshared training rules, it means that because Bodhisattvas do not manifest any natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), they share [these rules] with the Śrāvakas; [whereas their other rules are unshared].
Because similar prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepaṇasāvadya*) are currently practiced, they are not shared with them.
Within these training rules, there are cases where a śrāvaka commits an offense while a bodhisattva does not, and cases where a bodhisattva commits an offense while a śrāvaka does not.

Bodhisattvas possess the precepts of body, speech, and mind, whereas Śrāvakas possess only those of body and speech; therefore, Bodhisattvas may also commit transgressions of the mind, which Śrāvakas do not.
In brief, all faultless actions of body, speech, and mind that benefit sentient beings—every such action—a bodhisattva should practice and should train in.
Thus, it should be understood that this is called the distinction between the common and the uncommon.
The commentary states:
Among the common and the uncommon, all natural transgressions—namely, killing and so forth—are said to be "common."
Similar offenses of prohibition, such as digging the earth or cutting living grass and so forth, are designated as "unshared" (āvenika).
Regarding this training rule, it refers to the subsequent training rules.

There are cases where a śrāvaka commits an offense while a bodhisattva does not: for example, during the two periods of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), one might observe that it would benefit sentient beings and thus travel overnight.
There are cases where a bodhisattva commits an offense while a śrāvaka does not: namely, when one observes that it would be beneficial but intentionally does not act.

Therefore, there are instances where the bodhisattva’s mind incurs an offense while that of the śrāvakas does not; this refers to cases where, by merely giving rise internally to discursive thoughts such as desire and so forth, the bodhisattva commits an offense, whereas the śrāvakas and others do not.

All bodhisattvas should practice and should cultivate every bodily, verbal, and mental action that is beneficial to sentient beings and free from fault; that is to say, the bodhisattva should cultivate these three types of action such that they are capable of benefiting others and are without fault.

Or, although an action may be beneficial, it might nonetheless be unwholesome; for instance, giving another person such illicit things as women. To preclude such cases, [the text] states that there is no fault.

The Commentary states: Regarding "vast and sublime," it is further due to four kinds of vastness: first, because of the vastness of various immeasurable precepts; second, because of the vastness of encompassing immeasurable merit; third, because of the vastness of the intention to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; and fourth, because of the vastness of establishing unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
The commentary states:

Regarding the "vastness of the various and immeasurable trainings," this refers to the trainings practiced by bodhisattvas, which are both diverse and immeasurable. This is because, through them, they perform the work of ripening and gathering in all sentient beings.
"Embracing immeasurable and vast merit" means that bodhisattvas embrace immeasurable accumulations of merit, whereas śrāvakas do not.
"Embracing the vast intention for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings" means encouraging all sentient beings to cultivate virtue; this is called the intention for their benefit.
If, with respect to this very person, one wishes that they shall attain a superior fruit through those virtues, it is called the "intention for happiness.

Regarding the establishment of the vastness of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment: it means that by means of this ethical discipline (*śīla*), bodhisattvas establish unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and not as śrāvakas do.
The treatise states:

Regarding "profound and sublime," it means that by means of such types of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), bodhisattvas may perform the ten kinds of actions, including taking life, yet remain without fault and generate immeasurable merit, swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Furthermore, one should know that when Bodhisattvas manifest the two types of karma—of body and speech—through transformation, this too is profound ethical discipline (*śīla*).
For this reason, they may act as kings, demonstrating various actions that afflict sentient beings in order to establish those beings within the Vinaya.

Furthermore, he manifests various *jātaka* tales, demonstrating the practice of afflicting other sentient beings while truly benefiting them; first causing their minds to give rise to deep pure faith, and subsequently bringing them to full maturity.
This is called the profound and supreme ethical discipline (*śīla*) in which a bodhisattva trains.
The commentary states:

regarding "profound and supreme," it refers to those bodhisattvas who possess skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of this kind; herein, the functional efficacy of such skillful means of these bodhisattvas is revealed.
That is to say, when bodhisattvas recognize that a person of such a kind is about to initiate the preparatory application for unwholesome and uninterrupted actions.
With the knowledge of others' minds, he understands that mind; there is no other means by which that karma can be diverted.
He understands as it truly is that because of this karma, one is certain to fall from a happy realm and certain to go to an evil realm. Having known this, he gives rise to this thought:
"I shall perform this karma and must fall into an evil realm; I would rather go myself, for I shall certainly deliver him."
Although this may inflict slight suffering upon them in the present, it causes them to experience great peace and happiness in the future.

Therefore, a bodhisattva is like a skilled physician who, with a mind intent on benefiting others, may even kill someone; yet there is not the slightest fault, but rather the generation of much merit. By virtue of this great merit, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Precepts such as these are most profound.

Furthermore, it should be known that the manifest arising of the two types of karma—of body and speech—by means of transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) by bodhisattvas is also profound ethical discipline (*śīla*).
By this principle, he may act as a king and manifest various acts that afflict sentient beings in order to establish them within the *vinaya*.
This manifestation of his own body is called a "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*); herein, one should speak of such matters as King Anavatapta’s guidance of Sudhana and others.
Furthermore, regarding the manifestation of various *jātaka* stories, such as those of Viśvantara and others:
in these instances, the Bodhisattva’s giving away of his son and daughter to the brahmin was entirely a transformation (*nirmāṇa*).

Regarding "manifesting the practice of harassing other sentient beings while truly gathering in other sentient beings": this means that bodhisattvas never actually harass other real sentient beings, because they are truly gathering in those other real sentient beings; such a case is likewise called profound and sublime.
The Commentary states:
Based on these four kinds of excellence briefly explained, one should know that the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline (*śīla-vinaya*) is the most excellent.
One should further understand that there are immeasurable distinctions among such categories of bodhisattva training rules (*śikṣāpada*), as described in the *Vinayakauśalya-vaipulya-sūtra*.
The commentary states:
These four types of brief classifications are explained in detail in the *Vinayakṣudraka-sūtra*, where there are further hundreds of thousands of distinctions. Chapter 8:
The Section on Higher Training in Mind (*adhi-citta-śikṣā*) From the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, Chapter Eight, the Section on Higher Training in Mind, the treatise says:
Thus has been explained the excellence of higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*).
How is the excellence of higher mind (*adhicitta*) to be seen?
Briefly, it should be understood through six types of distinctions:

First, by way of the distinction of the object; second, by way of the distinction of variety; third, by way of the distinction of the antidote; fourth, by way of the distinction of capability; fifth, by way of the distinction of elicitation; and sixth, by way of the distinction of activity.
The commentary states:
This question and answer are formulated to manifest the excellence of the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*).
The treatise says:
Regarding the distinction of the object of focus (*ālambana-viśeṣa*): it means that the Mahāyāna teachings serve as the object of focus.
The commentary explains:
"That which takes the Mahāyāna teachings as its object of focus" refers to the fact that bodhisattvas necessarily take the Mahāyāna as their object, whereas śrāvakas do not.
The Commentary says:

"Various distinctions" refers to the various and immeasurable samādhis, such as the Mahāyāna-āloka (Light of the Great Vehicle), the Puṇyasambhāra-samādhi-rāja (King of Samādhis for Accumulating Merit), the Bhadrapāla (Worthy Protector), and the Vīryapāramitā (Heroic Progression). Thus they are manifold and infinite.
The commentary states:

Regarding "the Mahāyāna-āloka, the Saṃbhāra-samādhi-rāja, and so forth," this reveals that such various distinctions among samādhis exist only in the Mahāyāna, and not even one of them exists in the Śrāvaka-yāna and other vehicles.
The Commentary states:

Regarding the distinction of the antidote, it refers to the wisdom that takes the general characteristics of all phenomena as its object; by means of the principle of "extracting a wedge with a wedge," it eliminates all coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the obstructions within the *ālayavijñāna*.
The commentary states:
The wisdom that takes universal dharmas as its object abides as the antidote to all obstacles, just as a fine wedge is used to remove a coarse wedge.

Within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), the perfumed seeds of various defiled phenomena are called "coarse"; because the various paths of antidote can eliminate them, they possess the sense of being "subtle."
The Treatise says:
Regarding the distinction of capability, it refers to abiding in the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and taking birth according to one's desire.
The Commentary says:

Because they possess the capacity to abide in the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they go to whatever place there is that benefits sentient beings and are reborn there without falling away from their concentration;
such a thing does not occur for the śrāvakas and others.
The Treatise says:
Regarding the differentiation of elicitation, it means that one is able to elicit unimpeded supernormal powers throughout all worlds.
The Commentary says:
"By means of this meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), one brings forth supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) such that there is no obstruction in any world.
The Commentary says:

Regarding the differentiation of their functions, it refers to the ability to shake, to blaze, to pervade, to manifest, to transform, to go and return, to contract and expand, to cause all forms and images to enter into one's own body, to travel among those of the same kind, to appear or disappear at will, to exercise mastery over what is done, to subdue the supernormal powers of others, to bestow eloquence, mindfulness, and happiness, and to emit great radiance—because one thus brings forth such great supernormal powers.
The commentary states:
Regarding the differentiation of karmic activity, this refers to the deeds performed by manifesting supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Among these, because one is able to move all worlds, it is called "vibration" (*kampana*).
Because it is intensely blazing, it is called "blazing.
As for the term "pervasive," one should understand that this refers to the universal illumination of light.

As for "manifestation," by means of this power, other sentient beings who were previously incapable suddenly become able to see immeasurable worlds, as well as other Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth.
Regarding "transformation," one should understand it as transforming all stages [of the elements], such as earth and so forth, into water and so forth.
Regarding "coming and going," it means being able to travel to and return from immeasurable worlds in a single instant.
Regarding "rolling up and unfolding": this means that one may roll up the infinite worlds of the ten directions into a single infinitesimal atom (*paramāṇu*) without the atom increasing in size;
or one may unfold a single infinitesimal atom to encompass the infinite worlds of the ten directions without the worlds decreasing in extent.
"All physical forms enter into the body" means that within the body there appear immeasurable varieties of all manner of activities.

"Going among those of similar kind" means that, for example, when one goes to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, one's physical appearance and speech become identical to theirs; likewise, when going to all other places for the sake of transforming beings, it is exactly the same.
"Manifest" means appearing;
"hidden" means concealed.
Regarding mastery over what is produced: this refers to such acts as transforming the Māra king into the body of a Buddha and so forth.
The supernormal power of prostration refers to the ability to eclipse all other supernormal powers.
Because it bestows eloquence upon those who inquire, it is called "bestowing eloquence" (*pratibhāna*).
Because it bestows mindfulness and bliss upon those who listen, causing them to attain meditative concentration, it is called "bestowing mindfulness and bliss" (*smṛti-sukha*).
"Emitting great rays of light" is for the purpose of summoning bodhisattvas dwelling in other worlds from afar.
"Manifesting such great supernormal powers" refers to the manifestation of the great supernormal powers previously described.
All such qualities are absent among the śrāvakas; therefore, it is preeminent.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, it is able to induce and encompass the ten difficult practices that are hard to perform.
The ten difficult practices are: first, the difficult practice of self-vow, because one vows to undertake the aspiration for unexcelled bodhi;
second, the difficult practice of non-retrogression, because the manifold sufferings of birth and death cannot cause one to regress.
Third is the difficult practice of not turning one's back, because one does not abandon sentient beings even when they engage in perverse conduct.
Fourth is the difficult practice of being present before others, because one manifests all manner of beneficial deeds toward those who are hostile.
Fifth is the difficult practice of non-defilement,
because one is born into the world yet is not defiled by worldly dharmas.

Sixth is the difficult practice of resolute conviction, because although one has not yet attained full clarity regarding the Mahāyāna, one gives rise to faith and understanding toward all that is vast and profound.
Seventh is the difficult practice of thorough penetration, because one is fully able to penetrate the selflessness of persons and phenomena.
Eighth is the difficult practice of subsequent realization, because one is able to subsequently realize the profound and secret terminology spoken by all Tathāgatas.
Ninth is the difficult practice of non-separation and non-attachment, because one does not abandon *saṃsāra* yet remains unstained by it.

Tenth is the difficult practice of application, because one is able to cultivate the abiding liberation of all Buddhas from all obstructions, and until the end of *saṃsāra*, acts without effort to constantly bring about every benefit and welfare for all sentient beings.
The commentary states:
As it is said that Bodhisattvas practice various difficult deeds (*duṣkaracaryā*), what herein is designated as "difficult deeds"?
All difficult deeds are manifested through ten types.
Regarding "not abandoning and not being defiled, which is difficult to practice": it is called "not abandoning" because one does not cast [samsara] aside.
That is to say, neither completely relinquishing birth and death nor being defiled by it—this is extremely difficult.
The meanings of the other nine difficult practices are easy to understand.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, regarding the difficult practice of conforming to awakening (*anubodha-duṣkaracaryā*), what kind of secret words of the Buddha do those bodhisattvas conform to and awaken to?
As it is said in the Sūtra.
The commentary states:
This question is posed in order to clarify the intended meaning of the esoteric terminology.
Regarding what is stated in the Sūtra, this provides a general answer to the preceding question, which will be explained in detail later.
The Treatise says:
How is it that a bodhisattva is able to practice the giving of gifts?
If bodhisattvas do not give even the slightest gift, yet practice extensive giving throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions,
how is it that bodhisattvas delight in practicing giving?
If bodhisattvas have no desire or inclination for any form of giving whatsoever,
how can they develop deep faith and understanding in the practice of generosity?
Furthermore, if bodhisattvas practice giving without placing their trust in the Tathāgata.
What is a bodhisattva’s exertion regarding generosity?
If bodhisattvas do not exert themselves in the practice of giving, how can they be said to delight in generosity?
What is a bodhisattva’s delight in generosity?
If bodhisattvas do not practice even a small act of giving for even a moment,
how can their giving be vast? It is when bodhisattvas,
in the midst of generosity, are free from the notion of *saḷa* (perishability).
How is it that a bodhisattva’s giving is pure?
It is when the bodhisattva has completely abandoned stinginess.
How is it that a bodhisattva’s giving is ultimate?
If bodhisattvas do not abide in the ultimate,
how can their giving be sovereign?
If bodhisattvas lack mastery over the act of giving, [how can they be called masters of generosity?]
How is it that a bodhisattva’s giving is inexhaustible?
It is because bodhisattvas do not dwell in inexhaustibility.
Just as it is with giving, so it should be understood accordingly for everything from ethical discipline at the beginning to wisdom at the end.
The commentary states:

As for the question of how a bodhisattva is able to practice generosity and so forth, it means that bodhisattvas incorporate all sentient beings into their own being; therefore, the giving they perform is the giving of themselves. This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the question, "How does a bodhisattva delight in practicing generosity? it means that bodhisattvas do not delight in practicing generosity characterized by attachment to its flavor, but rather delight in practicing the pure generosity of a bodhisattva.
"Attachment to flavor" refers to the meaning of greedy defilement.
Alternatively, in other contexts, it is called "coming to seek alms.

Regarding the question, "How does a bodhisattva develop deep faith and understanding in giving? it means that bodhisattvas practice giving by generating the mind of generosity themselves, without depending on external conditions.
Regarding the phrase "how a bodhisattva exerts themselves in giving," it means that because all bodhisattvas have naturally severed stinginess, they are able to give by their very nature.
This refers to the intention that they are able to give spontaneously, neither waiting for the exhortation of others nor exerting themselves through self-motivation.

Regarding the phrase "how a bodhisattva delights in giving," it means that because all bodhisattvas practice giving constantly, there is no time when they do not give; and because they give everything, there is nothing small that they do not give.

Regarding the phrase "how the bodhisattva’s giving is vast," it means that when bodhisattvas practice giving based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), this is the sense of practicing giving while free from desire (*vairāgya*).
The term *sala* (娑洛) explicitly denotes solidity and substance, while implicitly signifying the absence of dispersion.
Now, taking the esoteric meaning: because one gives while relying on meditative concentration and remaining free from distracted thoughts, the gift becomes vast and great.
As for the question, "How is a bodhisattva’s giving pure and so forth? it means that all bodhisattvas practice generosity by uprooting the root of stinginess.
*Utpāda* (殟波陀) explicitly signifies "arising," while its esoteric meaning refers to "uprooting.
*Pada* means "foot" (*pāda*), and *ut* means "to uproot.

Here, we take the esoteric sense: it means to uproot the foot of stinginess, causing it to fall face-downward so that one may practice giving; therefore, it is called *utpāda-mātsarya* (stinginess that has been uprooted).

What is meant by "the bodhisattva’s perfection of giving"? It means that bodhisattvas do not abide in the ultimate nirvana without remainder as do the śrāvakas; therefore, they are able to practice giving perpetually until the very end.

Regarding the phrase "how the bodhisattva’s giving is sovereign," it means that bodhisattvas practice generosity such that the obstacles to giving do not attain sovereignty; because the obstacles to be remedied lack sovereignty, their giving attains sovereignty.
How is it that the giving of a bodhisattva is inexhaustible? It means that because bodhisattvas do not abide in nirvāṇa but constantly practice generosity, their giving is inexhaustible therein.
This is because they intend to attain nirvāṇa while not abiding in nirvāṇa like the śrāvakas; therefore, their giving is inexhaustible.
The Treatise says:
How can one kill? It is by severing the cycle of birth and death through which sentient beings transmigrate.
What is taking what is not given?
It is when sentient beings naturally appropriate things for themselves even though no one has given them.
What is sexual misconduct?
If one thoroughly understands that all sensual desires are erroneous and practices correctly,
how could one speak falsely? If one can declare falsehood to be falsehood within falsehood itself.
What is *vaśīnī*?
It is if one can always dwell in the most excellent abiding in emptiness (*śūnyatā-vihāra*). What is *pārṣa*?
If one is well-established in the perfection of what is to be known,
what is frivolous speech?
It is the correct teaching of the various categories and distinctions of the Dharma.
How can one be subject to desire?
If one repeatedly seeks to personally realize unsurpassed meditative concentration (anuttara-dhyāna),
how can one be subject to hatred?
If one is able to correctly loathe and destroy all afflictions within the mind,
how could one hold wrong views? If one perceives,
according to reality, the pervasive nature of perversion in all places, [how could one hold wrong views?]
The commentary states:
As it is said in the Sūtra, "O Bhikṣus, I am one who can kill living beings," etc., this passage clarifies the intended meaning of that statement.
What is meant by "one who practices sexual misconduct"? It refers to one who knows that all sensual desires are inherently perverse, yet nonetheless practices correct conduct.
What is meant by *peśunī*? This term *peśunī* explicitly refers to divisive speech (*paiśunya*), while implicitly it signifies the eternally victorious emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

"Pe" symbolizes victory; "śu" symbolizes emptiness; and "ni" symbolizes eternity. Now, taking the implicit meaning, it corresponds with the answer; therefore, the answer states: "If one can always abide in the most excellent dwelling of emptiness."
Regarding the term *pāruṣya*: this *pāruṣya* explicitly refers to harsh speech (*pāruṣyavāda*), while implicitly it signifies "dwelling on the other shore" (*pāra-sthita*).

*Pā* denotes the other shore, and *ruṣi* denotes dwelling; here, taking the implicit meaning brings it into correspondence with the answer. Therefore, the answer states: "well-established in the knowable other shore."
This refers to the meaning of abiding at the further shore of the knowable.
As for how one can [overcome] wrong views and so forth, it means observing and seeing, in accordance with reality, the pervasive nature of error within form and the other aggregates.
This means that within that *paratantra-svabhāva*, one perceives the *parikalpita-svabhāva* as having the sense of falsity exactly as it is.
Regarding the passage on the ten unwholesome courses of action, the remaining meanings are easy to understand.
The Treatise says:
Regarding "the profound Buddha-dharma," what is meant by the term "profound Buddha-dharma"?
This should now be explained:
That is to say, the eternally abiding dharma is the Buddha-dharma, because the Dharma-body is eternally abiding.
Furthermore, the dharma of cessation is the Buddha-dharma, because all hindrances are forever extinguished.
Furthermore, the dharma of origination is the Buddha-dharma, because the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifests through origination.
Furthermore, the dharma of attainment is the Buddha-dharma, because the eighty-four thousand modes of conduct of sentient beings and their respective remedies are all attainable.
Furthermore, the dharma of greed is a Buddha-dharma, because one vows to take sentient beings possessed of greed as one's own body through embracing them.
Furthermore, the dharma of hatred is a Buddha-dharma; furthermore, the dharma of delusion is a Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the dharmas of ordinary beings are likewise the dharmas of all Buddhas.
Moreover, the dharmas free from defilement are the dharmas of all Buddhas, because they fulfill true suchness (*tathatā*) and cannot be stained by any obscurations or impurities.
Furthermore, the quality of being undefiled is a characteristic of all Buddha-dharmas; for although they arise within the world, no worldly dharmas can defile them.
Therefore, they are called the profound Buddha-dharmas.
The commentary states:
Furthermore, other sūtras elsewhere state that the eternally abiding dharma is a Buddha-dharma, and so on at length until it says that the undefiled dharma is a Buddha-dharma.
The underlying intention herein shall now be revealed.
Because the body of the Buddha’s Dharma is eternally abiding, this Dharma is said to be an eternally abiding dharma.
As for the dharma of cessation, all obstructive defilements are completely extinguished; by virtue of this meaning, this Dharma is said to be a dharma of cessation.

If the existence of attainable dharmas constitutes the Buddha-dharma, then since the eighty-four thousand formations of sentient beings and their respective antidotes are all attainable, this dharma is said to be "with attainment."
Regarding the "stainless dharma" (*anāsrava-dharma*): it is pure *tathatā*, which cannot be defiled by any obscurations or impurities; therefore, this dharma is called the stainless dharma.
The remaining meanings are easy to understand and need no further elaboration.
The treatise says:

Furthermore, because it can induce the cultivation of the perfections (pāramitās) and the various Buddha-dharmas that mature sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields, one should know that this is also a specific activity of the bodhisattva’s meditative concentration (samādhi).
The commentary states:
While the distinctions of the activities previously performed have not been explained, we shall now further clarify the activities of the bodhisattvas’ meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
That is to say, by relying on *samādhi*, bodhisattvas are able to cultivate all the perfections (*pāramitā*).

Furthermore, by relying on this meditative concentration, one is able to skillfully bring all sentient beings to maturity, employing various skillful means such as the supernormal powers to lead sentient beings into the True Dharma.

Furthermore, by this power, one is able to thoroughly purify all buddha-fields; for the mind attains mastery such that, according to one's wish, one can manifest buddha-fields consisting of treasures such as gold and silver.
Furthermore, by means of this power, one is able to correctly cultivate and accumulate all Buddha-dharmas; this is the distinction in the activity of this samādhi.
Chapter 9: The Section on Higher Training in Wisdom (*Adhiprajñāśikṣā*) from the *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Part One of Nine. The Treatise says:
Thus, the excellence of the higher training in mind (*adhicitta*) has already been explained.
How is the excellence of superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā-viśeṣa*) to be seen?

It should be understood that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*)—whether by way of its intrinsic nature, its basis, its causal conditions, its object, its aspect, its support, its companions, its maturation, its outflow, its departure, its culmination, its benefits of preparatory application, non-conceptuality, and subsequent attainment, its distinctions, its metaphors for non-conceptuality and subsequent attainment, its effortless activity, or its profundity—is what is called the excellence of superior wisdom.
The commentary states:
Now we have arrived precisely at the time to explain superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).
Here, the intended meaning is that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is called superior wisdom.
This further consists of three types:
first, preparatory non-conceptual wisdom, which refers to the wisdom of investigation;
second, fundamental non-conceptual wisdom, which refers to the wisdom of direct realization.
Third is the subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom, which refers to the wisdom that initiates activity.
