Part Eleven of the Section on the Wisdom of that Result: Supplementary Discussion. It is said:
Furthermore, the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas is profound, most profound. How can this characteristic of profundity be perceived?
There are many verses on this point.
The commentary states:
Within the Mahāyāna, the profound characteristics of the dharmakāya of all Buddhas shall now be revealed.
By means of twelve verses, the twelve profound characteristics will be demonstrated.
The Treatise says:
The Buddha takes non-arising as his birth, and likewise takes non-abiding as his abiding;
all his activities are effortless, and he takes the fourth nutriment as his food.
The commentary states:
Herein, one verse reveals the profundity of the arising and abiding of activity.
That the Buddha’s non-arising is his arising manifests the profundity of arising.
Because the Tathāgatas possess no karma or afflictions and do not undergo birth through the same processes as ordinary fools, they are said to be "unborn" (*anutpāda*).
However, there is a mode of birth that is contrary to this, whose characteristics are difficult to comprehend; this is called the "profoundness of birth."
"Abiding by means of non-abiding" reveals the profundity of abiding.
Taking non-abiding nirvāṇa as one's place of abiding—such nirvāṇa is called the profundity of abiding.
The phrase "all activities are effortless" reveals the profundity of karma; because all Tathāgatas possess effortless activity that is equal in every respect, it is called the profundity of karma.

Regarding the statement that "the fourth nutriment is his food," this reveals the profundity of his dwelling, because the food consumed by the Buddha belongs to the fourth of the four kinds of sustenance—namely, the nutriment of consciousness—which is an impure basis for dwelling and so forth.

Regarding the four kinds of nutriment: first, the nutriment that sustains an impure basis, namely the four nutriments such as edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), because they cause sentient beings bound by desire to subsist upon an impure basis.

Second, the sustenance that causes the pure and impure bases to abide refers to the three sustenances beginning with contact; this is because they cause sentient beings bound by the realms of form and formlessness to abide by means of their pure and impure bases.

Because this basis has already abandoned the afflictions of the lower stages, it is called "pure"; because it has not yet abandoned the afflictions of the higher stages, it is called "impure. Therefore, it is termed the "basis that is both pure and impure."
In this way, one dwells supported by the food of contact, mental volition, and consciousness, excluding the food of physical morsels.

Third, there is the food that supports a dwelling based on exclusively pure support; this refers to the four types of food, such as physical morsels, because they enable the śrāvakas and others to dwell supported by a pure basis.
Fourth, there is the manifestation of dwelling by relying on food, which refers to the four types of nutriment (*āhāra*). The Buddhas manifest the acceptance of these so as to remain in the world.

Therefore, the Buddhas consume this fourth type of manifested sustenance for dwelling in order to cause the merit of sentient beings who are able to give to increase, with pure faith serving as the cause; although they manifest the act of eating, they do not perform the actual function of eating, and when the Tathāgata eats, the devas receive [the food].
When one gives with the intention that all other sentient beings may attain it, by virtue of this cause, those classes of sentient beings will swiftly realize awakening.
All such cases should be understood as being collectively described as "one profound [aspect]."

Furthermore, by means of ten causes, one should understand that the birth of all Buddhas possesses the characteristic of non-birth: (1) because it does not share the same nature as ignorance; (2) because it does not share the same nature as differentiation; (3) because they have attained mastery over appropriation; (4) because they have attained mastery over maintenance; (5) because they have attained mastery over relinquishment; (6) because they possess the characteristic of non-duality; (7) because they are merely like light and shadows; (8) because they are identical to magical illusions; (9) because they abide in non-abiding; and (10) because they accomplish great deeds.

Furthermore, by virtue of ten causes, one should know that the Tathāgata dwells neither in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa: first, because [saṃsāra] is not omniscience; second, because it is not eternally severed; third, because it is not cultivated; fourth, because its nature is known to be non-existent; fifth, because there is no apprehension and no conceptual differentiation; sixth, because of the mind’s detachment; seventh, because of the mind’s realization; eighth, because of the mind’s equanimity; ninth, because phenomena are unattainable; and tenth, because [nirvāṇa] is realizable.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the effortless activities (*anābhoga-kṛtya*) of all Buddhas are established by virtue of ten causes: first, because of the excellence of their abandonment; second, because they have no basis; third, because their activity is effortless; fourth, because the agent is effortless; fifth, because the action performed is effortless; sixth, because there is nothing [to be attained] and thus it is effortless; seventh, because they are originally without distinction; eighth, because what was to be done has already been accomplished; ninth, because there is nothing further to be accomplished; and tenth, because they have attained mastery over all phenomena through the complete maturation of their cultivation.

Furthermore, by virtue of ten causes, it should be understood that although the Buddhas truly have no food to eat, they manifest the act of eating: first, to demonstrate that they maintain their bodies through food; second, to cause the merit of sentient beings to increase; third, because they wish to demonstrate having commonality with the Dharma; fourth, to cause others to follow and learn proper enjoyment; fifth, to cause others to follow and learn the practice of frugality; sixth, to cause them to initiate the practice of diligence; seventh, to bring all roots of goodness to maturity; eighth, to reveal that their own persons are free from defiled attachment; ninth, to show respect for the assistance provided by karma in sustaining life; and tenth, because they wish to fulfill the birth resulting from their original vows.
The treatise says:
Without distinction and immeasurable, Without number and a single karma,
non-firm karma and firm karma— The Buddhas are endowed with the three bodies.
The commentary states:
This verse reveals the profundity of the establishment of number and activity.
The phrase "neither different nor immeasurable" reveals the profundity of the establishment.

Because the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas is without distinction, it is said to be "undifferentiated"; because it manifests perfect awakening (*abhisambodhi*) in immeasurable bases, it is said to be "immeasurable.
The phrase "a single activity of incalculable number" reveals the profundity of its numerical aspect.
Although the Buddhas are immeasurable, they share a single activity; therefore, it is profound.

Regarding "the non-firm activity and the firm activity of the Buddhas who possess the three bodies," this means that the Tathāgatas are endowed with the three bodies: their enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) activity is firmly established, while their emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) activity is not firmly established. Such activity is called profound.
The treatise says:
Manifest perfect awakening is not existent; all awakenings are not non-existent.
Each and every thought-moment is immeasurable; existence is manifested by way of non-existence.
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates the profundity of manifest perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*).
"Manifest perfect enlightenment is not existent" means that neither the person (*pudgala*) nor phenomena (*dharma*) exist.

The statement that "all-enlightenment is not non-existent" is spoken according to the principle of conventional designation (*prajñapti*), because all Buddhas manifest complete enlightenment (*abhisambuddha*).
How is it known that the Buddha manifests complete and perfect enlightenment?

It is because there are immeasurable Buddhas in each and every moment of thought; this demonstrates that within each and every moment of thought, immeasurable Buddhas manifest complete and perfect enlightenment.
"Existence manifested by non-existence" refers to the manifestation that True Suchness (tathatā) is both existent and non-existent; the Buddhas are those manifested by this True Suchness.
The Commentary says:
"Neither defiled nor free from defilement, yet through desire one attains liberation."
"Fully knowing desire and the absence of desire, one awakens to and enters the dharmatā of desire.
Commentary:
This verse demonstrates the profundity of being free from desire.

"Neither defiled nor free from defilement": because craving does not exist, it is called "not defiled"; and because there is no defilement, freedom from defilement also does not exist. Why is this so?
If there were defilement (*rāga*), there could be freedom from defilement; since defilement itself is non-existent, there is no freedom from defilement.

As for attaining deliverance through desire: because one suppresses and severs the active outbursts of greed (*paryavasthāna*) while retaining the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of greed, one attains ultimate deliverance;
for if the latent tendencies were not retained, one would have to enter parinirvāṇa simultaneously with the śrāvakas and others.

One who understands that desire is non-desire and thereby awakens to the dharma-nature of desire, understands that the greed which is conceptually constructed (parikalpita) has no nature of greed; such a person is then able to awaken to the *tathatā* of the dharma of desire.
The treatise says:
The Buddhas transcend all aggregates, yet they abide within all aggregates;
they are neither identical to nor different from them, remaining perfectly quiescent without abandoning them.
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates the profundity of the abandonment of the aggregates (*skandha*).

"The Buddhas transcend all aggregates" means that the Tathāgatas have surpassed the five kinds of appropriated aggregates, such as form (*rūpa*), and abide within the aggregate of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-skandha*), which is beyond apprehension.

Regarding the statement that it is neither identical to nor different from them: although one has already abandoned the aggregates as they are conceptually imputed, it is not different from them, because it abides precisely within their true nature (*dharmatā*).
Nor are they identical; for if they were identical, the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) would likewise become a pure object, just like the dharmatā.
"Being excellently tranquil without abandoning" means not discarding the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), as it is the very essence of sublime nirvāṇa.
The Treatise says:
The activities of all Buddhas are intermingled, like the waters of the great ocean;
regarding what has been done, what is being done, and what will be done, there is no thought of "this is for the benefit of another."
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates the profundity of maturation.
Regarding the "intermingling of the Buddha-activities," it means that all the activities of the Tathāgatas in maturing sentient beings are entirely equal.
What is this analogy?

It is like the waters of the great ocean: for example, when the many rivers flow into the great ocean, their waters mingle and become a common resource enjoyed equally by fish, turtles, and other creatures.
The Buddhas are likewise; they enter the same dharmadhātu, and their activities are harmonized and non-dual, equally serving as the enjoyment for the maturation of sentient beings.
Regarding what I have done, am doing, or shall do, I act within any one of these three times.
Regarding the absence of such thought for the benefit of others, it means that one does not form the thought:
"I have already performed, am currently performing, or shall perform the benefit of others.
Nevertheless, without effort, one is able to accomplish all matters that bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings, just like the *maṇi* jewel or the celestial drum in the world.
The treatise says:
When the sins of sentient beings are not manifest, it is like the moon in a broken vessel;
yet it pervades all worlds, through the light of the Dharma that is like the sun.
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates the profundity of manifestation.
If worldly beings do not see the Buddhas, yet it is said that the bodies of the Buddhas are eternally abiding, then since the Buddha-bodies are eternal, why are they not seen?

Regarding the statement that "the transgressions of sentient beings prevent [the reflection] from appearing, just as the moon does not appear in a broken vessel": just as water cannot remain within a broken vessel, and because the water does not remain, the moon does not appear; so it is in this case.
Within the bodies of sentient beings, the water of *śamatha* is absent, and thus the Buddha-moon does not appear.
Water is used as a metaphor for meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because its nature is clear and moist.

Regarding the phrase "pervading all worlds through the light of the Dharma like the sun," this means that although the Buddha does not physically appear in this world, he nevertheless pervades everything by performing buddha-activities.
By teaching the Dharma through the sūtras, *geya*, and so forth— just as the sunlight pervades the world and performs the buddha-activities that bring sentient beings to maturity—
the treatise says:
"Either manifesting perfect enlightenment, or entering nirvāṇa like fire."
This has never been non-existent, for the bodies of all Buddhas are eternal.
Commentary:
This verse demonstrates the profundity of manifesting perfect awakening and parinirvāṇa.

Regarding the statement that "manifesting perfect enlightenment or parinirvāṇa is like fire," this means that the Tathāgatas may manifest the attainment of Buddhahood or manifest parinirvāṇa; these matters are like fire, which at times blazes forth and at times subsides.

The Buddhas are likewise: they manifest parinirvāṇa for those classes of sentient beings who are not yet mature, and they manifest the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood for those classes of sentient beings who are already mature, desiring to bring them to liberation.
For example, just as fire has a single nature without differentiation, so too is the Dharma-body; one should know it to be solely one.
The meaning of the remaining half-verse is easy to understand.
The Treatise says:
The Buddha dwells in his most supreme self-nature, Amidst non-noble dharmas, The human realm and the evil destinies, And within dharmas that are not the holy life.
Commentary:
This verse demonstrates the dwelling in profundity.

Within non-noble dharmas, among the human and woeful realms, and within dharmas that are not the holy life, the Buddha dwells in the supreme dwelling by means of his most excellent self-nature, because he abides through the noble dwellings and so forth.
Among these, the noble abodes refer to the abodes of emptiness and so forth;
the celestial abodes refer to the abodes of the meditative concentrations (dhyāna);
and the Brahma abodes refer to the abodes of the immeasurables (apramāṇa), such as loving-kindness (maitrī).
Non-noble dharmas refer to unwholesome dharmas.
The Buddha dwells within these by means of the dwelling in emptiness and so forth; because he dwells in these noble dwellings such as emptiness, they are called "noble dwellings."

Regarding "the human realm and the miserable realms," this refers to sentient beings who, relying on those [realms], dwell in various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*); the meditative absorptions in which they dwell are called "divine abodes" (*brahmavihāra*).
Regarding "dharmas that are not the holy life," this refers to dwelling in the four kinds of sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*), such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth, within those dharmas.

"Abiding in the most excellent self-nature" means that by means of such a most excellent self-nature, one abides in the most excellent dwelling; this reveals that among all dwellings, the Buddhas abide in the dwellings characterized by the most excellent self-nature.
The Treatise says:
The Buddha acts in all places, yet he does not act in any single place;
he manifests in all bodies, yet is not within the range of the six sense faculties.
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates the profundity of the essential nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding the statement that "the Buddha acts everywhere yet does not act in any single place": this means that while subsequent cognition (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) proceeds by making distinctions among the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) does not proceed in any single place.
The second meaning refers to the fact that the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) moves everywhere, whereas the other two bodies do not move to a single location.
As for "manifesting in all bodies," this means that the *nirmāṇakāya* is visible everywhere throughout all places.
That which is not within the range of the six sense faculties is the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
Desiring to transform beings such as those in the hells (*naraka*), it manifests birth therein.

When sentient beings born in the hells and other realms see this emanation body, they do not see it as it truly is and cannot comprehend it; they merely think, "This is [just another] being in the hells. Therefore, the emanation body is certainly not within the range of the six sense faculties of those beings in the hells and other realms.
The treatise says:
Defilements are suppressed but not extinguished, like poison neutralized by a mantra;
retaining these delusions until they are exhausted, one realizes the Buddha’s omniscience.
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates the profundity of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Regarding "the afflictions are suppressed but not extinguished, like poison neutralized by a mantra": within the stage of a Bodhisattva, the active manifestations (*paryavasthāna*) of the afflictions are suppressed, yet the afflictions have not been extinguished because their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) still persist.
For example, when various poisons are neutralized by the power of mantras, although their substance remains, they no longer cause harm.
Afflictions are likewise: because they are fully understood through wisdom, although their substance remains, they no longer cause harm.

Regarding "retaining afflictions until the afflictions are exhausted": because they retain the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of various afflictions, they do not attain parinirvāṇa as quickly as the śrāvakas, but rather reach the ultimate exhaustion of all afflictions.
Regarding "realizing the omniscience of a Buddha": when afflictions are exhausted, one attains all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
The treatise says:
"Afflictions become factors of enlightenment; birth-and-death becomes nirvāṇa."
Because they possess great skillful means, the Buddhas are inconceivable.
Commentary:
This verse demonstrates the inconceivable profundity.

This means that for Bodhisattvas who possess great skillful means (*upāya*), the truth of the origin of suffering (*samudaya-satya*)—the afflictions—is transformed into the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), and the truth of the suffering of birth and death (*duḥkha-satya*) becomes *nirvāṇa*.

All such teachings of the Buddhas are inconceivable due to the three causes and conditions previously mentioned, namely, because they are personally realized within (*pratyātma-vedyatvāt*), and so forth.

The treatise states: It should be understood that the aforementioned profundity is of twelve kinds, namely: the profundity of birth, abiding, activity, and persistence; the profundity of establishment, enumeration, and activity; the profundity of manifest perfect enlightenment; the profundity of detachment from desire; the profundity of the abandonment of the aggregates; the profundity of maturation; the profundity of manifestation; the profundity of demonstrating the attainment of enlightenment and nirvāṇa; the profundity of abiding; the profundity of revealing the essential nature; the profundity of abandoning afflictions; and the profundity of the inconceivable.
The commentary states:
These twelve kinds are all difficult to comprehend; therefore, they are called "profound.
Their individual characteristics have already been explained as before.
The Treatise says:
If bodhisattvas are mindful of the Buddha’s Dharma-body, by how many kinds of mindfulness should they cultivate this mindfulness?
Briefly stated, bodhisattvas who are mindful of the Buddha’s Dharma-body should cultivate this mindfulness by means of seven kinds of mindfulness.
First, one should cultivate this reflection: that all Buddhas attain sovereign mastery over all phenomena, because they have attained unimpeded supernormal powers throughout all worlds.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
Pervading the realm of sentient beings, They possess obstructions yet lack the causes [for liberation].
There are two kinds of definitive transformation, for which even the Buddhas have no mastery.
Second, one should cultivate the mindfulness that the Tathāgata’s body is eternally abiding, because true suchness is the uninterrupted liberation from defilements.
Third, one should cultivate this mindfulness that the Tathāgata is supremely faultless, because he is completely dissociated from all afflictive obscurations and cognitive obscurations.
Fourth, one should cultivate this mindfulness that the Tathāgata is without effortful exertion, because he performs all Buddha-activities without cessation and without the need for deliberate effort.
Fifth, one should cultivate this mindfulness because the Tathāgata experiences great wealth and bliss, due to the great wealth and bliss of his purified buddha-field.
Sixth, one should cultivate this mindfulness because the Tathāgata is free from all defilements, for no worldly phenomena can defile him even while he dwells in the world.

Seventh, one should cultivate this reflection that the Tathāgata is able to accomplish the great task: by manifesting perfect awakening, parinirvāṇa, and so forth, he brings all sentient beings who are not yet matured to maturity, and those already matured to liberation.
Regarding this, there are two verses:
Perfected within one’s own mind, Possessing permanence and purity,
It spontaneously bestows The great Dharma-joy upon sentient beings.
Pervasive and without dependence, Benefiting many beings with equanimity,
The one possessing all-buddha-wisdom— One should cultivate all forms of mindfulness.
Commentary:
Now, it shall be demonstrated that if bodhisattvas are mindful of the Buddha’s Dharma-body, they should cultivate that mindfulness through seven kinds of recollection.
Regarding "attaining sovereign mastery over all dharmas": by attaining the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), one exercises sovereign mastery over all dharmas.
Because all Tathāgatas have attained unimpeded supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) throughout all worlds, unlike the śrāvakas and others who still possess obstructions.
If all Tathāgatas exercise sovereign mastery over all phenomena (*dharma*), why do all classes of sentient beings not attain nirvāṇa?
Therefore, this single verse now clarifies that for this reason, all classes of sentient beings are unable to realize ultimate nirvāṇa.

Regarding the statement that "the realm of sentient beings is pervasively possessed of obstacles and lacks the cause": it means that sentient beings possess obstacles such as karma, which is termed being "possessed of obstacles."
Because they possess such obstructions, even though immeasurable Buddhas appear in the world, it is impossible to bring them to parinirvāṇa; the Buddhas have no mastery over them.
If sentient beings lack the nature for parinirvāṇa, this is called "lacking the cause.
This means that they lack the cause for parinirvāṇa because they lack the spiritual lineage (*gotra*); therefore, the Buddhas have no sovereign power over them.
Regarding the two kinds of determinate transformation, there are two types of determination:
first, determination of action; second, determination of experiencing maturation. It should be understood that it is in this context that they are called "determinate."
The Buddhas have no mastery over these two kinds of determination.

The bodies of the dull-witted and ignorant are called the "determination of the obstacle of maturation" (vipāka-āvaraṇa-niyata), while those destined to fall into the hells and so forth are called the "determination of experiencing maturation" (vipāka-anubhava-niyata); one should understand that there is a distinction between these two types within this context.

Regarding the statement that "the body of the Tathāgata abides eternally because it is the true suchness (tathatā) liberated from all stains without interval": this means that the principle of true suchness, being liberated from all obstructive stains without interval, manifests as the Dharma-body; therefore, the body of the Tathāgata abides eternally.
Regarding the Tathāgata’s enjoyment of great wealth and bliss: it should be understood that the Tathāgata’s pure buddha-field is what is called "great wealth and bliss.

Regarding the Tathāgata’s ability to accomplish the great task: this refers to all Tathāgatas manifesting perfect enlightenment, entering parinirvāṇa, and so forth, thereby accomplishing the great benefit and purpose—causing those already matured to attain liberation and causing those not yet matured to reach maturity.
The meaning of the remaining practices of mindfulness of the Buddha is easy to understand.
Furthermore, these seven kinds of mindfulness of the Buddha are elucidated through two verses.

Within these verses, the sevenfold perfection of all Buddhas is proclaimed for the purpose of cultivating mindfulness of the Buddha; that is to say, first, bodhisattvas practice mindfulness of the Tathāgata as being perfected in its dependence upon their own minds.
Next, one contemplates that the Tathāgata’s body is eternally abiding and perfect;
next, one contemplates that the Tathāgata is endowed with pure goodness and perfection, which is the most supreme state of being faultless;
next, one contemplates that the Tathāgata is perfected in effortlessness, meaning that he performs the Buddha-work without exertion.
Next, one should contemplate that the Tathāgata’s perfection of bestowing the great dharma-joy means he experiences great dharma-joy within a pure buddha-field;
next, one should contemplate that the Tathāgata’s perfection of being free from all defilements means he acts universally without any basis of dependence.

If there were something upon which [the mind] depended while it wandered everywhere, there would be suffering and hardship; because it wanders everywhere without depending on anything, the Buddha is eternally free from suffering, detached from defilements, and all-pervading.

The subsequent recollection of the Tathāgata’s impartiality and the perfection of his manifold benefits is precisely the mindfulness of the Buddha as one who can accomplish great deeds, because he brings all sentient beings to maturity and liberation.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, what are the characteristics of the pure buddha-fields of all Buddhas?
It should be understood as it is stated in the "Introduction Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*) of the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-śatasāhasrika-sūtra*:
namely, that the Bhagavat was dwelling in a place adorned with the seven most excellent radiant jewels, emitting great light that universally illumines all boundless worlds;
a place of immeasurable extent, interspersed with exquisite decorations, circular and limitless, its magnitude difficult to fathom, surpassing...
Transcending the spheres traversed by the three realms, arising from supramundane roots of goodness, characterized by the most supreme mastery of pure consciousness,
it is the capital of the Tathāgatas and the place where the great assembly of Bodhisattvas gathers like clouds,
as well as immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and garuḍas.
Constantly attended by kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others;
sustained by the joy and delight of the vast flavor of the Dharma; performing all that is beneficial for all sentient beings;
eliminating all afflictions and calamities; remaining far removed from all māras; and surpassing all other adornments with the adornments of a Tathāgata.
As for its locus, it has great mindfulness, wisdom, and conduct as its pathways; great tranquility and sublime insight as its vehicle;
and the liberations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness as its gateways.
It is a great palace established upon a king of great jewel-flowers, adorned by a multitude of immeasurable merits.

Thus he manifested the pure buddha-field, perfect in its manifest color, perfect in its shape, perfect in its dimensions, perfect in its location, perfect in its cause, perfect in its fruit, perfect in its sovereign, perfect in its attendants, perfect in its retinue, perfect in its sustenance, perfect in its activities, perfect in its benefit, perfect in its fearlessness, perfect in its dwelling place, perfect in its paths, perfect in its vehicles, perfect in its gates, and perfect in its support.
Furthermore, they enjoy such a pure buddha-field, which is consistently sublime, consistently blissful, consistently faultless, and consistently sovereign.
The commentary states:

As it is taught in the "Introduction Chapter" (*Nidānaparivarta*) of the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-śatasāhasrikāsūtra* regarding the purification of Buddha-fields, what kind of sublime qualities does this purified Buddha-field manifest?
This means that the first two phrases manifest the perfection of the primary color of the purified buddha-field.
Regarding the "seven treasures," they are: first, gold;
second, silver; [and so forth].
Third, vaidūrya;
fourth, musāragalva; fifth, aśmagarbha.
By citing these, one should understand that it includes mārakata and other such jewels.
Sixth is the red pearl-jewel; this red pearl emerges from within red insects and is the most preeminent among all jewels;
seventh is the karketana jewel.
"Emitting great light that universally illumines all boundless worlds" refers to the various great radiances emitted by the seven treasures mentioned immediately prior.

Of these [subsequent] lines, the first two both equally demonstrate the perfection of color (*varṇa-saṃpad*); the next line demonstrates the perfection of shape (*saṃsthāna-saṃpad*); the next line demonstrates the perfection of dimension (*pramāṇa-saṃpad*); the next line demonstrates the perfection of location (*deśa-saṃpad*); and the final line demonstrates the perfection of cause (*hetu-saṃpad*).
What is the reason for this?

It is because there are supramundane non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). This subsequently attained wisdom is designated as "supreme" (*viśiṣṭa*); because it is subsequently attained, it arises from these two kinds of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), and these very roots of goodness are termed the "perfection of causes."
Next, one phrase reveals the perfection of the fruit, namely, the purification of the Buddha-field, which has the extremely sovereign pure consciousness as its characteristic.
Next, one phrase reveals the perfection of the Lord, and next, one phrase reveals the perfection of the retinue.
Next, one phrase reveals the perfection of the retinue; having previously mentioned the *nāgas*, this now further mentions the *mahoragas* to include the great serpents.
Next, one phrase reveals the perfection of sustenance, which refers to food and drink.
Next, one phrase reveals the perfection of activity (*kṛtya-pariniṣpatti*), meaning that having consumed this food, one accomplishes all aims and benefits for all sentient beings.
Next, one phrase reveals the perfection of gathering and benefiting (*anugraha-pariniṣpatti*), because within the pure land, one is free from all afflictions and all suffering.
Next, there is one phrase that reveals the perfection of fearlessness: where there is no enmity, there is no dread.

"Enmity" refers to the four māras; in this Pure Land, the māra of afflictions, the māra of the aggregates, the māra of death, and the celestial māra are all entirely absent, and for this reason, there is fearlessness.
Next, one phrase reveals the perfection of the dwelling place;
next, one phrase reveals the perfection of the path.
By what path does one enter this purified buddha-field?
This refers to the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation within the Mahāyāna;
in their respective order, great mindfulness and wisdom serve as the path for entering.
The subsequent phrase reveals the perfection of the vehicle, because one proceeds by means of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Next, there is one phrase that reveals the perfection of the gateway: by what gateway is this Pure Land entered?
It is through the gateways of liberation—namely, Great Emptiness, Signlessness, and Wishlessness—within the Mahāyāna.
Next, there is one phrase that reveals the perfection of the support, just as the great earth and so forth rest upon the wind-circle.
Upon what does this pure buddha-field rely?
It is adorned by a multitude of immeasurable merits and is established upon a great red lotus flower.
Regarding "enjoying such a pure Buddha-field that is consistently and wondrously pure," this means that within the pure land there are no impure things such as excrement or filth.

Regarding "consistently blissful," this means that within the pure land there are only pleasant sensations (*sukha-vedanā*), and no painful sensations (*duḥkha-vedanā*) or neutral sensations (*avyākṛta-vedanā*).
"Exclusively free from fault" means that within the Pure Land there is no unwholesomeness, nor is there any neutral (avyākṛta) state.
"Exclusively sovereign" means that within the Pure Land one does not depend on external conditions, for everything desired accords with one's own mind.
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, it should be known that this *dharmadhātu* of all Buddhas performs five activities at all times:

first, its activity is to rescue and relieve all sentient beings from calamities; for even upon a momentary sight [of the Buddha], he is able to rescue those suffering from calamities such as blindness, deafness, and insanity.
Second, its function is to provide relief from the miserable realms (*durgati*), for it uproots sentient beings from unwholesome states and establishes them in wholesome states.

Third, its function is to provide relief from improper means, for it causes those of other paths (*tīrthika*) to abandon practices for seeking liberation through improper means and establishes them within the noble teaching of the Tathāgata.
Fourth, its function is to provide relief from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), because it bestows the path capable of transcending the triple world.

Fifth, its function is to provide relief regarding the vehicles (*yāna*), because it rescues bodhisattvas who intend to follow other vehicles, as well as śrāvakas of indeterminate lineage, establishing them so that they may practice the Mahāyāna.
Regarding these five activities, one should know that the functional activities of all Buddhas are equal.
On this point, there is a verse:
Because of differences in cause, basis, object, nature, and practice, The diversity of their activities is acknowledged.
This power in the world is distinct; because it does not exist [in others], he is not a Teacher.
Commentary:
It should be understood that the *dharmadhātu* of these Buddhas is able to perform five activities at all times; that is to say, the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* constantly performs five activities.

Regarding the statement that "its function is to rescue all sentient beings from calamities and misfortunes," this means that those who are blind, deaf, and so forth, immediately regain their sight and other faculties upon briefly beholding the Buddha.

Regarding the statement that "its function is to rescue [beings] from the miserable realms (*apāya*)," this refers to extracting them from evil states and placing them in wholesome states; this is called rescuing the miserable realms.

Regarding the statement that its function is to provide relief from *satkāya* (the transitory collection), this means that for the sake of the world, it teaches the Noble Path capable of transcending the three realms; thus, the three realms themselves are referred to as *satkāya*.
The meaning of the remaining two lines can be understood.
Regarding these five types of activity, one should know that the activities of all Buddhas are equal; concerning this point, another verse is further spoken:

That is to say, regarding causes, bases, and so forth: by virtue of these causes and conditions, the various karmas of all Tathāgatas are equal, whereas the karmas of all worldly beings are unequal. A single verse summarizes and briefly demonstrates the distinctions among the causes of the world.

Therefore, the distinction between karmas is admitted as follows: it is held that various worldly beings are born in the hells due to specific causes, born in the heavens due to specific causes, and born as humans or even as hungry ghosts due to specific causes; because these causes differ, the distinction between karmas is admitted.

Regarding the claim that karma is held to differ based on the difference of the basis (*āśraya*): "basis" refers to the body; it is because of the difference in this basis that karma is held to be different.

Regarding the claim that karma is held to differ based on the difference of worldly affairs: this refers to the various worldly activities such as the distinct business of merchants and the distinct business of farming; because these activities have distinctions, karma is held to be different.

Regarding the claim that karma is held to differ because of differences in worldly disposition (*gotra*): "disposition" refers to intention; it is because intentions differ that karma is held to have differences.

Regarding the claim that karma is held to differ because of differences in worldly conduct: it is because there are distinctions in the performance of karmic actions that karma is held to have differences.

The activities of all Buddhas are entirely effortless (*anābhoga*), and they lack any power of differentiation among causes and so forth; therefore, there is no distinction in the activity of the Teachers.
The Treatise says:

If the *dharmakāya* of the Buddhas is thus endowed with the perfection of these qualities and is not shared with the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, with what intention did the Buddha teach the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*)?
In this regard, there are two verses:
To attract one class of beings And to sustain the rest,
The Buddhas have taught the One Vehicle On account of those with indeterminate lineage.
Because the dharma, selflessness, and liberation are equal, yet their natures differ,
And because they attain two types of mental dispositions and undergo transformation, The ultimate teaching is that of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Commentary:
Among these, two verses clarify the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) behind the Buddhas’ teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Regarding "in order to attract and gather a certain class of beings," this means that for the sake of attracting those of indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*), such as certain *śrāvakas*, and causing them to enter the Mahāyāna, [the Buddha thought]: "How may I cause those of indeterminate lineage among the *śrāvakas* to all attain parinirvāṇa by means of the Mahāyāna?"

Regarding "sustaining the remainder," this refers to sustaining those bodhisattvas of indeterminate lineage so that they may abide in the Mahāyāna; how might one ensure that bodhisattvas of indeterminate lineage do not abandon the Mahāyāna and instead attain parinirvāṇa through the Śrāvaka vehicle?
For this reason, the Buddha taught the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Based on the meaning of the phrases "the indeterminate" and so forth, he has already explained the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and liberation, and so on at length; herein, moreover, by the power of a specific underlying intention (*abhiprāya*), he speaks solely of the One Vehicle.
What is the intended meaning?
It refers to the equality of the Dharma and so forth.

Regarding "the equality of the Dharma": "Dharma" here refers to *tathatā* (suchness). Since all śrāvakas and others equally take this as their destination, and because that destination is equal, it is called the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Regarding the phrase "because of the absence of self and so forth," this means that for persons such as śrāvakas, there is no self at all.
Because of this absence of self, it would be illogical to say, "this is a śrāvaka" or "this is a bodhisattva."
Based on this intention regarding the equality of selflessness, the One Vehicle is taught.
Regarding "equality in liberation," it means that because śrāvakas and others equally attain liberation from the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the One Vehicle is taught.
As the World-Honored One said:
"There is no difference between liberation and liberation.

Regarding the statement that their natures are not identical, this refers to the distinctions among spiritual lineages (*gotra*); for even those śrāvakas of indeterminate lineage shall eventually attain Buddhahood.
It is by virtue of this underlying intention that the One Vehicle (ekayāna) is taught.
Regarding "attaining two types of aspiration": it refers to attaining two kinds of aspirations.
First is the aspiration of inclusive equality; by means of this, one embraces all sentient beings, saying, "They are myself, and I am they."
Having thus taken it up, they themselves become Buddhas and others likewise become Buddhas.
It is with this underlying intention that the One Vehicle (ekayāna) is taught.

Second is the intentionality regarding the equality of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā-samatā-āśaya*): this refers to those śrāvakas who, at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, received the Buddha’s prediction and attained the intentionality regarding the equality of the Buddha’s dharma-nature, yet had not yet attained the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Having attained such an impartial intention (*samāśaya*), one reflects:
"The *dharmatā* of all Buddhas is my own *dharmatā*.
Furthermore, there is another sense: within that assembly, there are bodhisattvas who share the same name as [the Buddha] and have received the prophecy from the Buddha.
Because of this intention of equality regarding the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is said that there is a single vehicle (*ekayāna*).
As for the statement "because of transformation," this refers to the Buddha manifesting as the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth.
As the Blessed One said:
I recall that in the past, I have attained parinirvāṇa by relying on the Śrāvaka vehicle countless hundreds of times.
It is with this underlying intention that I speak of the One Vehicle (ekayāna).
Because sentient beings to be converted by means of the Śrāvaka vehicle attain parinirvāṇa upon seeing this, I manifest this transformation.
Regarding "because it is ultimate": this single vehicle alone is the most ultimate, for beyond this there is no other superior vehicle.
The Śrāvaka vehicle and others have further superior vehicles, namely, the Buddha-vehicle.
Based on this underlying intention, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, proclaim the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
The treatise says:
If all Buddhas possess the same Dharma-body, by what cause can it be seen that there are many Buddhas?
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"In a single realm, two [Buddhas] do not exist; Simultaneously, they are immeasurable and perfect;
Successive succession is illogical; Therefore, it is established that there are many Buddhas."
The commentary states:
We shall now demonstrate that, for this reason, one should understand that although all Buddhas are identical in their *dharmakāya*, they may manifest as either one or as many.

One should know that they are one because the *dharmadhātu* is identical; for all Buddhas take the *dharmadhātu* as their essence, and since the *dharmadhātu* is one, one should know that there is but one Buddha.
Furthermore, regarding the "one Buddha," it is because no two Buddhas appear simultaneously within a single world-system that we know there is but one Buddha.
Furthermore, within the verses it is shown that the Buddhas may be either one or many.
Regarding the phrase "there are not two in a single realm," this sentence demonstrates that there is only one Buddha.
Within a single world-system, two Buddhas do not appear simultaneously; therefore, it is said that there is only one Buddha.
The remaining phrases demonstrate that there are many Buddhas.
Regarding "simultaneously immeasurable perfections": it means that immeasurable bodhisattvas simultaneously bring their accumulations to fulfillment.
If these bodhisattvas were unable to attain Buddhahood despite simultaneously fulfilling their accumulations of merit and wisdom, then such accumulations would be empty and fruitless.
Since the accumulations cultivated by a multitude of bodhisattvas are perfected simultaneously, one should know that many Buddhas appear at once.
As for the claim that sequential succession is illogical, it means there is no principle for attaining Buddhahood through sequential succession.

If bodhisattvas, while cultivating the provisions, were to achieve fulfillment through a sequential order of dependence and succession, then there would be a sequence of before and after at the time they attain Buddhahood;

however, since bodhisattvas do not achieve fulfillment through a sequential order of dependence and succession while cultivating the provisions, there is likewise no sense of sequential order or succession at the time they attain Buddhahood.
Therefore, there are many Buddhas existing simultaneously.
The treatise asks:
How should one understand that within the *dharmakāya*, a Buddha neither ultimately enters parinirvāṇa nor ultimately does not enter parinirvāṇa?
Regarding this, there is a verse:
Because he is liberated from all obscurations, And because his activities are never-ending,
The Buddha has entered ultimate *nirvāṇa*, Yet he has not entered ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
The commentary states:

Other schools maintain that the Buddhas do not undergo ultimate parinirvāṇa, while yet another school of Śrāvakayāna practitioners maintains that the Buddhas do undergo ultimate parinirvāṇa; this verse clarifies these two perspectives.

Regarding the phrase "because of liberation from all obstructions": since the Buddha is liberated from all afflictive and cognitive obstructions (*kleśa-jñeya-āvaraṇa*), it is with this underlying intention that it is said that the Buddhas enter ultimate *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the phrase "because that which is to be done is never finished": since the Buddha universally intends to bring to maturity those sentient beings who are not yet matured, and to bring to liberation those who are already matured—this being his duty—there is no end to this task; therefore, the Buddha ultimately does not enter parinirvāṇa.
If it were otherwise, it would be like the ultimate nirvana of a śrāvaka; in that case, the original vow would be empty and without fruit.
The treatise asks:
For what reason is the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) not identical with the essential nature body (svābhāvikakāya)?

For six reasons, it is illogical that the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) of the Buddha is identical to the Nature Body (*svabhāvakāya*): first, because the Form Body (*rūpakāya*) is visible; second, because the distinctions among the immeasurable assemblies of Buddhas are visible; third, because its nature is seen as indeterminate according to one's resolute belief (*adhimukti*); fourth, because its nature is seen to fluctuate as it appears differently to each individual; fifth, because it is seen interspersed with various assemblies such as Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and devas; and sixth, because it would be unreasonable for the *ālayavijñāna* and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) to undergo transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) [if they were the same as the Nature Body]. Thus, it is not logical that the Enjoyment Body is the Nature Body.
The commentary states:
We shall now demonstrate that it is not logically tenable for the Buddha’s enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) to be identical to the essential body (*svabhāvakāya*).

Regarding the phrase "because the form body is visible": the form body of the Buddha’s enjoyment body is visible, whereas the Buddha’s dharma body (*dharmakāya*) is not; because of this logical inconsistency, the enjoyment body is not identical to the dharma body.
Furthermore, the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) can be perceived as having distinctions among the assemblies of Buddhas, whereas the dharma body (dharmakāya) possesses no such distinctions.
Because this [assertion] is irrational, the enjoyment body is not the essential body (svābhāvikakāya).
Furthermore, the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) is seen according to one's resolute conviction (adhimukti), as stated in the sūtra:
"Some see the Buddha’s body as being only yellow; some see the Buddha’s body as being only blue," and so forth, as explained at length.
If the enjoyment body were identical to the nature body, then this nature body would not be determinate; for it is illogical to designate as the "nature body" that whose essence is indeterminate.
Because this is illogical, the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) is not the essential body (svābhāvikakāya).

Furthermore, regarding the enjoyment body, one class of sentient beings first perceives it as distinct, and at a later time perceives it again as distinct; yet the nature of the Buddha’s dharma-body does not undergo such fluctuation.
Because this is unreasonable, the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) is not the essential body (svābhāvikakāya).
Furthermore, the enjoyment body is constantly interspersed with various assemblies of gods and others, whereas the essential body does not possess such intermixture.
Because this is illogical, the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is not the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*).

Furthermore, the essential body is attained through the transformation of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*); if the enjoyment body were identical to the essential body, then upon the transformation of the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), what other body would be attained?
Because this is unreasonable, the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) is not the essential body (svābhāvikakāya).
Since these six reasons are untenable, the two do not constitute one.
The treatise says:
For what reason is the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) not identical to the essential body (svābhāvikakāya)?
It is because of eight reasons: namely, it would be illogical for bodhisattvas—who have long since attained non-retrogressive concentration—to be born in Tuṣita Heaven or among human beings.

Furthermore, it would be unreasonable for Bodhisattvas, who have long since constantly recollected their past lives, to lack correct knowledge regarding writing, calculation, arithmetic, seals, the treatises on arts and crafts, or the conduct involved in the enjoyment of sensory objects.

Furthermore, it is not reasonable that bodhisattvas, having long since understood the teachings of both false doctrines and well-spoken Dharma, would go to the abodes of non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthika).
Moreover, it is not reasonable that bodhisattvas, having long since been able to skillfully know the right path of the three vehicles (triyāna), would practice erroneous asceticism (duḥkha-caryā).

Furthermore, it would be unreasonable for Bodhisattvas to relinquish hundreds of millions of Jambudvīpas and attain perfect enlightenment and turn the wheel of the true Dharma in only a single location.

If, apart from manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment, one were to perform buddha-activities in other places solely through an emanation body (nirmāṇakāya), then one should attain perfect enlightenment only in Tuṣita; why then is it not established that Buddhas appear simultaneously throughout all of Jambudvīpa?
Since no such designation is established, there is neither scriptural authority nor logical reasoning [for it].

Although there may be many emanations, this does not contradict the statement that two Tathāgatas do not appear simultaneously in the world, because a single world-system is comprised of one four-continent world, just as two wheel-turning monarchs do not appear together.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
The Buddha’s subtle transformation body, Entering many wombs with equanimity,
Manifests all modes [of existence], And turns the wheel of the perfectly awakened one.

To claim that one generates the aspiration for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, practices accordingly, and realizes great enlightenment, yet ultimately enters parinirvāṇa, is unreasonable; for such a vow and practice would be fruitless, resulting in the fault of futility.
The commentary states:
We shall now demonstrate that it is contrary to reason to claim that the Buddha’s transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is identical to his essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*), for eight reasons.

Among these, the first point that is contrary to reason is as follows: since beginningless time, bodhisattvas have attained non-retrogressive meditative concentration (*avaivartika-samādhi*) over immeasurable eons; they should not even be born in Tuṣita Heaven, much less among human beings.
However, those who are currently manifesting birth in this world are *nirmāṇakāyas* (emanation bodies), not *svābhāvikakāyas* (essential bodies).

Furthermore, it would be illogical for bodhisattvas—who have constantly recollected their past lives since time immemorial—to lack correct knowledge regarding writing, arithmetic, and so forth; rather, they manifest such matters as emanations solely for the purpose of disciplining sentient beings.

Furthermore, if Bodhisattvas, having diligently cultivated merit and wisdom throughout three incalculable eons, were unable to correctly discern what is well-spoken and ill-spoken, or what constitutes wrong and right modes of practice regarding suffering, how could they possibly attain sudden enlightenment at the time of realizing Bodhi in their final body?
By this reasoning, it is the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) and not the essential body (svābhāvikakāya).

Furthermore, it would be illogical for all bodhisattvas to abandon hundreds of millions of Jambudvīpas and attain perfect enlightenment and turn the wheel of the true Dharma in only a single location;
however, if the transformation body manifests simultaneously in all places, it accords with correct principle.
Therefore, the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is not the essential body (svabhāvakāya).

If members of other schools hold such a view—that the Buddha attains true awakening (samyaksambodhi) in only one location, while manifesting transformation bodies in other regions to perform buddha-activities—[it is incorrect].

If that were so, why do you not allow that he might dwell solely in Tuṣita Heaven, directly realize perfect enlightenment there, and then manifest transformation bodies throughout all four great continents to perform the Buddha-work?

Furthermore, since there is no scriptural authority nor logical reasoning to support the claim that one does not manifest equal enlightenment within all four great continents, one should not say that in this buddha-field there are four continents where he does not manifest the attainment of buddhahood.

If someone were to say that even if such a thing were possible, it would contradict the sūtras—since the sūtras state that two Tathāgatas do not appear simultaneously—one should know that this sūtra is similar to the case of the Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*).
Just as it is said that no two Wheel-Turning Kings appear together, this is based on a single four-continent world-system (*cāturdvīpaka*), not a single Buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra*).

Just as two Tathāgatas do not appear simultaneously, it should be understood that this case is likewise; here, the intention is to refer to a single world-system consisting of one set of four great continents.
Now, furthermore, he reveals through verse the Buddhas' manifestation of equal enlightenment.

Regarding the Buddha’s subtle transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) and so forth: the meaning here is that if, at that time, the Buddha manifests as dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven and demonstrates passing away from there and entering the mother’s womb, then at that very same time he also creates an immeasurable retinue such as the Venerable Śāriputra and others, and likewise manifests their entry into the womb, birth, and other such events.
One should know that the establishment of such transformed retinues is intended to manifest the preeminent Buddha-activities of omniscient awakening.
It should now be understood that it is unreasonable for the Tathāgata to enter parinirvāṇa in an ultimate sense.
This means that, in order to transform and deliver all sentient beings, one first makes great vows and cultivates great practices, constantly swearing this oath to oneself:
"I shall diligently cultivate correct practice for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings."
If, immediately upon attaining Buddhahood, one were to enter parinirvāṇa, then the vows and practices cultivated would be empty and without fruit.
Since this is illogical, [the Buddha] is the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) and not the essential body (svābhāvikakāya).
The treatise says:
Since the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Buddha are impermanent, why do the sūtras state that the Tathāgata’s body is permanent?
It is because the *dharmakāya*, upon which these two depend, is permanent.

Furthermore, because the flow-body (*niṣyanda-kāya*) and the transformation-body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) are constantly enjoyed without cessation or interruption, and because they repeatedly manifest transformations that never permanently cease, they are like one who constantly experiences pleasure or one who constantly bestows food.
It should be understood that the permanence of the Tathāgata’s body is likewise so.
The commentary states:

The sūtras declare that the Tathāgata’s body is eternally abiding; yet, since both the Buddha’s enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) are impermanent, how can the body be permanent?
Therefore, next, the meaning of the permanence of the two bodies is established.
That is to say, these two bodies abide in the dharma-body; because the dharma-body is permanent, they are also said to be permanent.
Furthermore, the enjoyment body is said to be permanent because its enjoyment is never interrupted.
The transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is also called "permanent" because it constantly manifests the signs of perfect enlightenment, parinirvāṇa, and so forth in an uninterrupted succession.
Furthermore, this permanence of these two bodies is illustrated through analogies.

It is just as when people in the world say, "He constantly experiences pleasure"; although the pleasure he experiences is not exclusively uninterrupted, one may still say that he constantly experiences pleasure.
Or again, it is like when people in the world say, "He constantly gives food"; although this giving of food is not always without interruption, one may still say that he constantly gives food.
It should be understood that the meaning of the permanence of the two bodies is likewise so.
The treatise states:
For six reasons, the transformation bodies manifested by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not abide eternally.
First, because once the task is completed, one is liberated after having matured sentient beings.
Second, it is to cause them to relinquish their lack of aspiration for nirvāṇa and to seek the eternally abiding body of a Tathāgata.
Third, it is to cause them to abandon the slighting and disparagement of the Buddhas, and to lead them to realize the teachings of the profound, true Dharma.
Fourth, it is to cause them to generate a deep yearning for the Buddha, lest those who see him too frequently should give rise to weariness and indolence.
Fifth, it causes one to exert diligent effort toward oneself, because one knows that a true teacher is difficult to find.
Sixth, it causes one’s own diligence not to abandon its yoke, so as to bring all sentient beings to maturity as quickly as possible.
In this regard, there are two verses:
Because their task is completed, they relinquish their lack of delight in nirvāṇa;
Free from disparaging the Buddhas, they give rise to deep yearning and reverence.
Because he internally arouses right effort for the sake of the most rapid maturation,
it is maintained that the Buddha’s transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) does not abide eternally.
Commentary:
These six reasons, presented both in prose and in verse, demonstrate that the Buddha’s transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) does not abide eternally.
Since the text is easy to understand, there is no need for further elaboration.
The treatise states:
The *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas has been non-different and immeasurable from time immemorial; therefore, one should not need to exert further effort in order to attain it.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
Because the cause for the Buddha’s attainment is non-different and immeasurable, If sentient beings were to abandon diligent effort, [the result would follow].
To realize [the truth] while constantly failing to establish the cause, and to sever such a cause, is unreasonable.
The commentary states:
Herein there is an objection:

If the Buddha’s dharmakāya has, from time without beginning, no distinct and immeasurable causes for realization yet is capable of accomplishing all manner of beneficial and blissful deeds for sentient beings, then one should not need to exert further effort or application in order to realize the fruit of Buddhahood.

To resolve this objection, it is shown by verse: This difficulty could arise if sentient beings were to abandon the cause of diligence in seeking the fruit of Buddhahood; however, such a difficulty does not apply here, because the realization attained by all Buddhas has been non-distinct and immeasurable from beginningless time, and thus has never failed to serve as the cause for attaining the fruit of Buddhahood since that very beginninglessness.

However, since the Buddha has realized that which is beginningless, non-distinct, and immeasurable, and which constantly serves as the cause for sentient beings to exert diligent effort toward attaining the fruit of Buddhahood, one should not raise such an objection.

The Dharma-body of all Buddhas has, from time without beginning, no distinct or limited causes for its realization; since it is not necessary to exert further effort or application to realize the fruit of Buddhahood, the Buddhas' realization of the Dharma-body is not such that sentient beings must abandon the cause of diligence in their pursuit of the fruit of Buddhahood.

Furthermore, the Buddha’s realization of that which has been non-differentiated and immeasurable since beginningless time serves as the cause for the diligent application of effort (*vīrya*) in seeking the fruit of Buddhahood.
This is because if sentient beings were to abandon such diligent exertion, this realization would never become the cause [for their attainment].

Furthermore, it is unreasonable to claim that this cause is severed; for the bodhisattvas have their minds enveloped by the vow of compassion, regarding all sentient beings with pity as if they were an only child. Since these sentient beings dwell in a great prison and undergo all manner of hardships, the bodhisattvas therefore act for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.
If one should form the thought:
"Since others are capable of doing it,
I shall not do it," this is not reasonable.
One should constantly maintain this thought:
"Whether others perform this task or not, I shall certainly do it.
Therefore, one should not sever such a cause.
The treatise says:
My brief commentary on the "Mahāyānasaṃgraha" chapter within the *Abhidharmamahāyānasūtra* is hereby completed.
The explanation says:
The *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, composed by the master Vasubandhu for the sake of those correctly entering the Mahāyāna, has reached its conclusion through this brief commentary.
*Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Fascicle Ten.
